topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which condition holds for a firm in long-run equilibrium in perfect competition?
A price = marginal cost = minimum average cost
B price > marginal cost and the firm earns supernormal profit
C marginal revenue = marginal cost at an output below minimum average cost
D price = average variable cost
parts.answer: A price = marginal cost = minimum average cost
parts.working: Free entry and exit remove supernormal profit, so P = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC and the firm earns normal profit. C describes monopolistic competition in the long run (excess capacity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, explaining the assumptions about how rival firms react.
parts.answer: Rivals match price cuts but do not follow price rises, so demand is elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, producing a kink.
parts.working: 1 mark: assumption that rivals do not follow a price rise – demand above the kink is price elastic (firm loses many customers). 1 mark: rivals follow a price cut – demand below the kink is price inelastic (little gain in sales). 1 mark: kink at the current price. 1 mark: MR curve has a vertical discontinuity (gap) below the kink.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the model predicts that prices in oligopoly will be stable even when costs change.
parts.answer: Because MC can shift up or down within the gap in the MR curve without changing the profit-maximising output and price.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit maximisation where MR = MC. 1 mark: the discontinuity in MR means MC can rise or fall within the gap. 1 mark: output and price stay the same – price rigidity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of the kinked demand curve model.
parts.answer: It does not explain how the initial price was set (or: evidence shows oligopoly prices do change; ignores non-price competition and collusion).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A monopolist faces the following prices and total costs.
Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Price ($): 50, 45, 40, 35, 30, 25
Total cost ($): 30, 48, 62, 80, 105, 138
Which output maximises profit?
A 3 units
B 4 units
C 5 units
D 6 units
parts.answer: B 4 units
parts.working: TR = 50, 90, 120, 140, 150, 150 and profit = TR − TC = 20, 42, 58, 60, 45, 12, so profit is greatest at 4 units. Check with marginal values: the 4th unit has MR = 20 and MC = 18 (worth producing), but the 5th unit has MR = 10 and MC = 25 (not worth producing). C and D are wrong: total revenue is highest at 5–6 units, but profit falls there.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a perfectly contestable market.
parts.answer: A market where entry and exit are free and costless, with no sunk costs, so incumbents face the threat of entry whatever the number of firms.
parts.working: 1 mark: no barriers to entry or exit. 1 mark: no sunk costs, so firms can leave without loss. 1 mark: entrants have access to the same technology / incumbents cannot react instantly; number of firms may be small.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the threat of 'hit-and-run' entry affects the behaviour of a firm in such a market.
parts.answer: Supernormal profits would attract entrants who take profits and leave, so incumbents keep prices near average cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: hit-and-run entry described. 1 mark: incumbents therefore limit price to earn only normal profit. 1 mark: they also have an incentive to minimise costs – outcome may be close to productive/allocative efficiency even with few firms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a sunk cost that might make the market for domestic air travel less contestable.
parts.answer: Advertising to build a brand / training of crew / landing slot fees that cannot be recovered.
parts.working: B1 (aircraft themselves can be leased or resold, so are not mainly sunk).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that monopoly is always against the interests of consumers.
parts.answer: Not always: monopoly can bring higher prices and lower output, but economies of scale, dynamic efficiency and regulation may benefit consumers.
parts.working: Knowledge and understanding / analysis (up to 14): diagram comparing monopoly with perfect competition – monopoly sets MR = MC, higher price, lower output, P > MC (allocative inefficiency), possibly not at minimum AC (productive inefficiency), deadweight loss, transfer of consumer surplus to producer; X-inefficiency without competition; less choice. Counter-arguments: natural monopoly and economies of scale may give lower costs and prices than many small firms; supernormal profit funds research and development (dynamic efficiency, new products); contestable markets restrain prices; price discrimination can allow some consumers to be served who otherwise would not; regulation (price caps) and competition policy. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on barriers to entry, the industry (utilities vs consumer goods), whether profits are reinvested, government regulation; reasoned conclusion on 'always'. Level 4 (15–20) requires a well-supported judgement.

practice.stem: A rail company sells peak-time and off-peak tickets on one route (invented data). Peak demand is P = 100 − 2Q and off-peak demand is P = 60 − Q, where P is the fare in dollars and Q is thousands of tickets per week. Marginal cost is constant at $20 per ticket in both markets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit-maximising quantity and price in each market.
parts.answer: Peak: Q = 20 thousand, P = $60; off-peak: Q = 20 thousand, P = $40

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand (as a positive number) in each market at these prices, and explain how this relates to the prices charged.
parts.answer: Peak 1.5; off-peak 2.0; the higher price is charged where demand is less price elastic.
parts.working: For P = a − bQ, PED = P ÷ (a − P). Peak: 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 (B1). Off-peak: 40 ÷ 20 = 2.0 (B1). The firm charges more in the market with lower PED (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the firm's total profit from the two markets, ignoring fixed costs.
parts.answer: $1200 thousand

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two conditions that make it possible for the company to practise this price discrimination.
parts.answer: Some monopoly power; markets can be separated (ticket valid only at that time) with no resale; different PEDs in the two markets.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Two airlines, Alpha and Beta, are the only carriers on a route. Each must choose a high fare or a low fare. The table shows annual profits in $ million (Alpha's profit first, Beta's second) (invented data).
Alpha high, Beta high: 60, 60
Alpha high, Beta low: 20, 80
Alpha low, Beta high: 80, 20
Alpha low, Beta low: 35, 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify each airline's dominant strategy, if it has one. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Both airlines have a dominant strategy of a low fare.
parts.working: If Beta sets High, Alpha earns 80 with Low > 60 with High (1). If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns 35 with Low > 20 with High (1). So Low is dominant for Alpha; by symmetry also for Beta (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the Nash equilibrium and explain why the airlines may be tempted to collude.
parts.answer: Nash equilibrium: both set low fares ($35 million each). If both colluded on high fares they would each earn $60 million.
parts.working: 1 mark: Nash equilibrium (Low, Low). 1 mark: joint profit at (High, High) is 120 > 70. 1 mark: this is a prisoners' dilemma – collusion raises profit but each has an incentive to cheat (80 > 60), so agreements are unstable without trust or enforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether price discrimination by firms such as airlines and electricity suppliers benefits consumers.
parts.answer: Some consumers gain (lower prices, access to services), others lose (higher prices, loss of consumer surplus); overall benefit depends on output effects and use of profit.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): definition and conditions (market power, separation of markets, different PED, no resale); third-degree price discrimination diagram with two markets, higher price in the inelastic market; first-degree discrimination converts all consumer surplus to producer surplus. Benefits: lower prices for students, off-peak users or low-income groups; total output may rise; a service may only be viable with discrimination (covering high fixed costs); off-peak pricing spreads demand and uses capacity better; profits may fund investment. Costs: consumers in the inelastic market pay more; loss of consumer surplus; perceived unfairness; may be used to drive out rivals (predatory). Evaluation (up to 6): judge which consumers, whether output increases, whether profits are reinvested and whether regulation protects captive users; reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Households that install solar panels reduce air pollution for their neighbours. Assuming no government intervention, what is true of the market for solar panels?
A marginal social benefit is less than marginal private benefit, so too many are installed
B marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so too few are installed
C marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, so too many are installed
D marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit at the market output
parts.answer: B marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so too few are installed
parts.working: There is a positive externality (external benefit), so MSB > MPB and the market output, where MPB = MPC, is below the socially optimal output where MSB = MSC. C describes a negative production externality.

practice.stem:
A city government is considering a new metro line. Estimated values over its life, in present-value terms ($ million, invented data):
private costs (construction and operation): 900
private benefits (fare revenue): 600
external benefits (time saved by road users, less pollution, fewer accidents): 520
external costs (noise and disruption during construction): 80

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net private benefit and the net social benefit of the project.
parts.answer: Net private benefit −$300 million (a loss of $300 million); net social benefit +$140 million
parts.working: Net private = 600 − 900 = −300 (B1). Social benefit = 600 + 520 = 1120; social cost = 900 + 80 = 980 (M1); NSB = 140 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the project would not be built by a private firm but might be undertaken by the government.
parts.answer: A private firm only counts private costs and benefits, which give a loss; the government includes externalities, which make social benefits exceed social costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: private firm makes a loss of $300 million. 1 mark: external benefits (time saved, cleaner air, fewer accidents) are not paid for by users, so they are ignored by the market. 1 mark: social benefits exceed social costs, so CBA supports public provision or a subsidy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two difficulties in valuing the external benefits of the project.
parts.answer: Placing money values on time saved and lives saved; predicting future usage; choosing a discount rate; deciding which third parties to include.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained difficulties (identify 1, explain 1).

practice.stem: In a cement market, the marginal private benefit is MPB = 100 − Q and the marginal private cost is MPC = 20 + Q, where Q is output in thousand tonnes and values are in dollars per tonne. Production causes air pollution with a constant external cost of $20 per tonne. There are no external benefits (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
parts.answer: Free market 40 thousand tonnes; social optimum 30 thousand tonnes
parts.working: Market: MPB = MPC: 100 − Q = 20 + Q so Q = 40 (B1). MSC = MPC + 20 = 40 + Q (M1); with no external benefit MSB = MPB, so 100 − Q = 40 + Q gives Q = 30 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight welfare loss caused by the externality.
parts.answer: $100 thousand
parts.working: Triangle between MSC and MSB from Q = 30 to 40: at Q = 40, MSC − MSB = 80 − 60 = 20 (M1); ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the free market overproduces cement in this case.
parts.answer: Producers ignore the external cost of pollution, so they produce where MPB = MPC, beyond the output where MSB = MSC.
parts.working: 1 mark: external cost not included in private costs. 1 mark: so MPC < MSC and the market output (40) exceeds the social optimum (30), where the extra units cost society more than they are worth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether cost-benefit analysis is a reliable method for deciding whether a government should build a large dam for irrigation and electricity.
parts.answer: CBA provides a systematic framework including externalities, but valuations, forecasts, discount rates and distributional issues make results uncertain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): stages of CBA – identify private and external costs and benefits (irrigation, electricity, flood control vs construction, displacement of communities, loss of farmland, ecological damage, downstream effects); place money values (shadow pricing, willingness to pay); discount future values to present value; compare social benefits with social costs. Strengths: considers third parties, makes assumptions transparent, allows comparison of projects. Weaknesses: valuing intangibles (lives, cultural sites, biodiversity); forecasting over 50+ years; choice of discount rate can reverse the decision; who gains and who loses (distribution) is not shown by net figures; political bias in estimates; risks such as earthquakes. Evaluation (up to 6): CBA is better than ignoring external effects but should be combined with sensitivity analysis and consultation; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: A consumer has an income of $1200 to spend on two goods, X and Y. The price of X is $40 and the price of Y is $30 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of each good the consumer could buy, and the slope of the budget line (Y on the vertical axis).
parts.answer: X intercept 30; Y intercept 40; slope −4/3 (−1.33)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The price of X falls to $30. Describe how the budget line changes.
parts.answer: It pivots outwards from the Y intercept (40): the X intercept rises to 40 and the slope becomes −1.
parts.working: 1 mark pivot about the Y intercept. 1 mark new X intercept 40 / slope −1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the condition for the consumer's optimum choice in terms of indifference curves and the budget line.
parts.answer: Where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve (MRS = Px/Py).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For a Giffen good, which describes the effects of a rise in its price?
A the substitution effect and the income effect both reduce quantity demanded
B the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a larger amount
C the substitution effect increases quantity demanded and the income effect reduces it
D the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a smaller amount
parts.answer: B the substitution effect reduces quantity demanded and the income effect increases it by a larger amount
parts.working: A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good: a price rise lowers real income, which raises quantity demanded by more than the substitution effect reduces it, so quantity rises. D describes an ordinary inferior good.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of indifference curve analysis in explaining why demand curves usually slope downwards.
parts.answer: It separates income and substitution effects, explains normal, inferior and Giffen goods without measuring utility, but rests on unrealistic assumptions.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): indifference curves (convex, MRS diminishing), budget lines, optimum at tangency; price fall pivots budget line; derive demand curve from successive tangencies (price-consumption curve); separation into substitution effect (always negative) and income effect (positive for normal, negative for inferior goods); explains why most demand curves slope down and the Giffen exception; uses ordinal not cardinal utility, an advance on marginal utility theory. Limitations: assumes rational, consistent, fully informed consumers; only two goods; preferences fixed; behavioural economics (habits, bounded rationality, framing) challenges it; hard to test. Evaluation (up to 6): a reasoned judgement on usefulness – strong theoretical insight, weaker predictive power; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using indifference curves and budget lines described in words, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of an inferior good that is not a Giffen good.
parts.answer: Substitution effect increases quantity; income effect reduces it; the substitution effect is larger, so quantity demanded rises overall.
parts.working: 1 mark: budget line pivots outwards; new tangency on a higher indifference curve. 1 mark: hypothetical (compensated) budget line parallel to the new one, tangent to the original indifference curve, separates the effects. 1 mark: substitution effect – movement along original curve; always increases quantity of the cheaper good. 1 mark: income effect – parallel shift; for an inferior good, higher real income reduces quantity. 1 mark: substitution effect outweighs income effect. 1 mark: net result – quantity demanded rises, so the demand curve slopes downwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the result would differ for a Giffen good.
parts.answer: The negative income effect is larger than the substitution effect, so quantity demanded falls when price falls (upward-sloping demand).
parts.working: 1 mark income effect outweighs substitution effect. 1 mark quantity falls when price falls.

practice.stem:
A bakery has a fixed number of ovens. The table shows total product (loaves per hour) for different numbers of workers (invented data).
Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total product: 10, 26, 45, 60, 70, 75

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal product and the average product of labour for each number of workers.
parts.working: MP = change in TP for each extra worker (B1 all correct); AP = TP ÷ workers (B1 all correct); accuracy (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State after which worker diminishing marginal returns set in, and explain why they occur.
parts.answer: After the 3rd worker (MP falls from 19 to 15 with the 4th worker).
parts.working: B1 identification. Explanation (2): in the short run at least one factor (the bakery's ovens/space) is fixed; adding more variable labour to the fixed factor eventually gives each worker less capital to work with, so the extra output falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by the minimum efficient scale of production?
A the output at which marginal cost is at its lowest
B the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
C the output at which a firm first makes normal profit
D the highest output a firm can produce before diseconomies of scale stop
parts.answer: B the lowest output at which long-run average cost is minimised
parts.working: Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which the long-run average cost curve reaches its minimum, i.e. where economies of scale are exhausted. A refers to marginal cost, which reaches its minimum before average cost does.

practice.stem:
A perfectly competitive firm has the following total costs (invented data).
Output (units): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Total cost ($): 120, 180, 220, 252, 300, 370, 462

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average variable cost, average total cost and marginal cost for outputs of 1 to 6 units.
parts.working: FC = 120 (TC at zero output). AVC = (TC − 120) ÷ Q (B1); ATC = TC ÷ Q (B1); MC = change in TC (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum price the firm needs in order to continue producing in the short run, and in the long run. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: Short run: $44 (minimum AVC); long run: $74 (minimum ATC)
parts.working: B1 $44: in the short run the firm stays open if price covers AVC, because fixed costs must be paid anyway (B1). B1 $74: in the long run all costs are variable, so price must cover ATC or the firm leaves the industry (B1).

practice.stem: A firm faces the demand curve P = 80 − 2Q, where P is the price in dollars and Q is the quantity per day (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output and price at which total revenue is maximised, and the value of total revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand (as a positive number) when the price is $60, and explain whether the firm should raise or cut its price from $60 to increase revenue.
parts.answer: PED = 3; demand is price elastic, so cut the price.
parts.working: At P = 60, Q = 10; dQ/dP = −½ (M1); PED = ½ × 60 ÷ 10 = 3 (A1). Elastic, so a price cut raises TR (MR > 0) (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the price elasticity of demand at the revenue-maximising output.
parts.answer: Unit elasticity (PED = 1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer buys two goods. Good X costs $2 and its marginal utility is 30 utils. Good Y costs $5 and its marginal utility is 50 utils. To maximise total utility with the same income, the consumer should
A buy more X and less Y
B buy more Y and less X
C make no change
D buy more of both goods
parts.answer: A buy more X and less Y
parts.working: MUx/Px = 15 utils per $ and MUy/Py = 10 utils per $. Each dollar moved from Y to X raises total utility until the ratios are equal. B compares total MU (50 > 30) without dividing by price.

practice.stem:
A consumer has Rs 900 to spend on goods X and Y. The price of X is Rs 100 and the price of Y is Rs 200. The table shows the marginal utility (utils) of each unit (invented data).
Unit: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
MU of X: 400, 300, 200, 150, 100
MU of Y: 1000, 800, 400, 300, 200

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combination of X and Y that maximises the consumer's total utility, and the total utility at that combination.
parts.answer: 3 units of X and 3 units of Y; total utility 3100 utils
parts.working: MU/P for X: 4, 3, 2, 1.5, 1; for Y: 5, 4, 2, 1.5, 1 (M1). Equi-marginal principle: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = 2 at 3X, 3Y (M1); spending 3 × 100 + 3 × 200 = 900 = income (A1). TU = 400 + 300 + 200 + 1000 + 800 + 400 = 3100 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the consumer would not choose 5 units of X and 2 units of Y, even though this also costs Rs 900.
parts.answer: At that combination MUx/Px (1) < MUy/Py (4), so switching spending from X to Y raises total utility (TU = 2950 < 3100).
parts.working: 1 mark: ratios unequal. 1 mark: transferring Rs 200 from 2 units of X to 1 unit of Y adds more utility than it loses; TU would be 1150 + 1800 = 2950.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that consumers rarely behave in the way that traditional utility theory predicts.
parts.answer: Traditional theory explains many broad patterns (downward-sloping demand), but behavioural evidence shows systematic departures; the importance depends on the decision.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): traditional theory – rational utility maximisers, diminishing MU, equi-marginal principle, derivation of demand. Behavioural evidence – bounded rationality and heuristics, anchoring (initial prices), framing ('90 % fat-free'), loss aversion, default choices (pension opt-out), herd behaviour, present bias (saving, unhealthy food), altruism. Governments use nudges based on these ideas. Counter-view: in aggregate, demand still falls when price rises; for repeated purchases consumers learn; some 'irrational' behaviour is rational given information costs. Evaluation (up to 6): weigh the extent – theory useful for predicting market-level responses, weaker for one-off, complex or emotional decisions (health, pensions); reasoned conclusion on 'rarely'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the principle of diminishing marginal utility can be used to derive a downward-sloping demand curve for an individual consumer.
parts.answer: A consumer buys until MU/P is equal across goods; if price falls, MU/P rises, so the consumer buys more until MU falls enough to restore equality.
parts.working: 1 mark: diminishing MU – each extra unit adds less satisfaction. 1 mark: equi-marginal condition MUa/Pa = MUb/Pb. 1 mark: a fall in Pa makes MUa/Pa > MUb/Pb. 1 mark: consumer buys more A, MUa falls until equality is restored – lower price, higher quantity demanded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two limitations of the assumption that consumers behave rationally when making choices.
parts.answer: e.g. bounded rationality (limited information and time), habits, anchoring/framing, herd behaviour, inconsistent preferences over time.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained limitations drawn from behavioural economics: bounded rationality, rules of thumb (heuristics), anchoring, social norms and herd behaviour, present bias (choosing short-term pleasure), and difficulty measuring utility in cardinal units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define allocative efficiency and productive efficiency, stating the condition for each.
parts.answer: Allocative: resources produce the goods consumers value most, P = MC. Productive: output is produced at the lowest possible average cost, at minimum AC (MC = AC).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by dynamic efficiency.
parts.answer: Efficiency over time through innovation and investment that lower costs or create better products.
parts.working: 1 mark: improvements over time. 1 mark: via research and development, new technology and new products, often financed from profits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by Pareto optimality.
parts.answer: A position where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark link: it requires both allocative and productive efficiency in all markets.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm sells its output at a price of $12. At its current output, its marginal cost is $9 and its average cost is $10. What can be concluded?
A the firm is allocatively efficient
B the firm is producing less than the allocatively efficient output
C the firm is producing more than the allocatively efficient output
D the firm is making a loss
parts.answer: B the firm is producing less than the allocatively efficient output
parts.working: P > MC means consumers value an extra unit ($12) more than it costs to produce ($9), so output is below the allocatively efficient level. D is wrong: P ($12) > AC ($10), so the firm makes supernormal profit.

practice.stem: Invented data: a pharmaceutical company spent $1.2 billion over 12 years developing a new medicine. Only about 1 in 10 medicines that reach clinical trials are eventually approved. The new medicine is protected by a 20-year patent. Its marginal cost of production is about $30 per course of treatment, but it is sold for $900 per course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a 20-year patent may reduce allocative efficiency.
parts.answer: It gives the firm monopoly power, so it sets price above marginal cost and restricts output.
parts.working: 1 mark: patent = legal barrier to entry. 1 mark: firm sets MR = MC. 1 mark: price ($900) far above marginal cost ($30). 1 mark: output below the level where P = MC; some patients who value the drug above its cost cannot afford it – deadweight loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With reference to the data, evaluate whether patents increase economic efficiency overall.
parts.answer: Patents trade static allocative efficiency for dynamic efficiency; the overall effect depends on how much innovation they cause and how high prices are.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 6): high R&D costs ($1.2 billion) and a low chance of success (1 in 10) mean firms would not invest without the chance of supernormal profit; without patents, rivals could copy at marginal cost; so patents promote dynamic efficiency (new medicines). Costs: price 30 times MC, large deadweight loss, low-income patients excluded; firms may make small changes to extend patents. After expiry, generic producers lower prices. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement – efficiency gains likely where innovation is costly and risky, but shorter patents, price regulation or tiered pricing for low-income countries could reduce the static losses.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the principal-agent problem that can arise from the divorce of ownership and control in large public limited companies.
parts.answer: Shareholders (principals) want maximum profit, but managers (agents) may pursue their own goals such as high salaries, sales growth or status.
parts.working: 1 mark: divorce of ownership (shareholders) and control (managers). 1 mark: managers have more information than shareholders (asymmetric information). 1 mark: managers may pursue sales/revenue maximisation, growth or perks. 1 mark: result – profits lower than shareholders want.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which shareholders might reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Link managers' pay to profits or share price (share options, bonuses); vote out directors / threat of takeover; independent non-executive directors and audits.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained methods.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'satisficing'.
parts.answer: Aiming for a satisfactory level of profit that keeps shareholders content, while also meeting the goals of other stakeholders.
parts.working: 1 mark: satisfactory rather than maximum profit. 1 mark: balancing competing stakeholder objectives.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms
practice.stem: A firm faces the demand curve P = 120 − 2Q and has total cost TC = 400 + 20Q, where P is in dollars and Q in units per week. Total cost includes normal profit (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output, price and profit if the firm maximises profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output, price and profit if the firm maximises total revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the largest output the firm can sell while still earning at least normal profit (sales maximisation). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.subtopic: Growth, survival and objectives of firms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the vertical integration of firms is likely to benefit consumers.
parts.answer: It may lower costs and secure supply, benefiting consumers through lower prices and reliability, but can increase market power and foreclose rivals.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): distinguish backward and forward vertical integration (with horizontal and conglomerate as contrast); motives – control of supplies and quality, removing intermediaries' profit margins, reducing transaction costs, securing retail outlets, economies of scale; benefits to consumers – lower costs passed on as lower prices, more reliable supply, better coordination and quality. Risks – market power increases; rivals may be denied access to inputs or outlets (foreclosure), raising barriers to entry; reduced competition leads to higher prices; diseconomies of scale and X-inefficiency in a large firm; managers may lack expertise in the new stage. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on market structure at each stage, competition policy, whether cost savings are passed on; reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country in one year: GDP is $380 billion. Income earned in the country by foreign-owned firms and sent abroad is $20 billion. Income earned by the country's residents from assets they own abroad is $8 billion. The population is 240 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's gross national income (GNI).
parts.answer: $368 billion
parts.working: GNI = GDP + net primary income from abroad (M1) = 380 − 20 + 8 = $368 billion (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate GNI per head. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.
parts.working: 368,000 million ÷ 240 million = $1,533 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why GNI per head is a better indicator than GDP per head of the income available to the residents of this country.
parts.answer: GNI excludes income that flows abroad to foreign owners (e.g. repatriated profits) and includes residents' income from abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark: GDP measures output produced in the country, whoever owns it. 1 mark: $20 billion of income goes to foreign firms, so GDP overstates residents' income.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which indicator is NOT used in calculating the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)?
A years of schooling of household members
B child mortality in the household
C household income per person
D access to clean drinking water
parts.answer: C household income per person
parts.working: The MPI measures deprivation in health, education and living standards using non-income indicators (nutrition, child mortality, schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets). Income is deliberately excluded. A, B and D are all MPI indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW) and why it might give a different view of living standards from real GDP per head.
parts.answer: MEW adjusts GDP by adding the value of non-market activities that raise welfare and subtracting activities that do not add to welfare.
parts.working: 1 mark: MEW starts from GDP/GNP. 1 mark: adds value of leisure, household production (unpaid work) and the informal economy. 1 mark: subtracts 'regrettables' such as defence and commuting, and environmental damage. 1 mark: so two countries with the same GDP per head can have very different MEW, e.g. if one has longer working hours or more pollution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difficulty in calculating the MEW.
parts.answer: Valuing non-market items (leisure, unpaid care, pollution) in money terms is subjective.
parts.working: 1 mark difficulty; 1 mark explanation (choice of values / data availability makes comparisons unreliable).

practice.stem: Invented population data for a low-income country: aged 0–14: 72 million; aged 15–64: 150 million; aged 65 and over: 9 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dependency ratio (dependants per 100 people of working age).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two economic characteristics, other than population structure, commonly found in low-income countries.
parts.answer: e.g. large share of employment in agriculture/primary sector; large informal sector; low savings and investment; low productivity; high dependence on primary exports.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained characteristics.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a fall in the birth rate could give this country a 'demographic dividend'.
parts.answer: The working-age share rises relative to dependants, raising output per head, savings and investment.
parts.working: 1 mark: dependency ratio falls as fewer children are born. 1 mark: more workers per dependant can raise income per head and savings, if jobs are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether HDI is a better measure of living standards than real GNI per head.
parts.answer: HDI is broader because it includes health and education, but it still omits inequality, freedom and the environment; the better measure depends on the purpose.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): real GNI per head – adjusts for inflation and population, PPP allows comparison, measures material living standards; limitations – ignores distribution, informal sector, non-market output, leisure, environmental damage, quality of goods, exchange-rate issues. HDI – geometric mean of life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per head; reflects capabilities; shows countries with high income but poor health/education; limitations – only three dimensions, averages hide inequality (inequality-adjusted HDI exists), ignores freedom, security, environment; arbitrary weights and goalposts; slow to change. Other measures – MPI, MEW, happiness indices. Evaluation (up to 6): judgement – HDI generally a better indicator of overall living standards, but GNI still essential for income comparisons; use several indicators.

practice.stem:
The Human Development Index uses these formulas:
life expectancy index = (life expectancy − 20) ÷ (85 − 20)
education index = average of (mean years of schooling ÷ 15) and (expected years of schooling ÷ 18)
income index = (ln GNI per head − ln 100) ÷ (ln 75,000 − ln 100), with GNI per head in PPP$
Invented data for a country: life expectancy 67.5 years; mean years of schooling 8.0; expected years of schooling 11.0; GNI per head PPP$5,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the life expectancy index, the education index and the income index. Give each to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: Life expectancy index 0.731; education index 0.572; income index 0.613

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the country's HDI as the geometric mean of the three indices. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which dimension contributes least to the country's HDI and suggest one policy that could raise it.
parts.answer: Education (index 0.572); e.g. increase spending on schools, teacher training or conditional cash transfers for school attendance.
parts.working: 1 mark education identified; 1 mark appropriate policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a year, a country's nominal GDP rises by 12 %, the general price level rises by 8 % and the population rises by 2 %. What is the approximate change in real GDP per head?
A a rise of about 1.7 %
B a rise of about 3.7 %
C a rise of about 6.0 %
D a rise of about 10.0 %
parts.answer: A a rise of about 1.7 %
parts.working: Real GDP growth = 1.12 ÷ 1.08 − 1 = 3.7 %; per head = 1.037 ÷ 1.02 − 1 ≈ 1.7 %. B ignores population growth; C adds population growth instead of subtracting it.

practice.stem:
Invented data for two countries.
Country P: GNI per head (PPP$) 14,000; HDI 0.70; life expectancy 68 years; mean years of schooling 6.5; Gini coefficient 0.52; oil is 60 % of exports
Country Q: GNI per head (PPP$) 9,000; HDI 0.76; life expectancy 74 years; mean years of schooling 10.0; Gini coefficient 0.34

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which Country P's GNI per head exceeds that of Country Q. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why Country Q has a higher HDI than Country P despite its lower GNI per head.
parts.answer: Q has better health and education outcomes, which raise the other two dimensions of the HDI.
parts.working: 1 mark: HDI combines income, health and education. 1 mark: Q's life expectancy is 6 years higher. 1 mark: Q's mean years of schooling are 3.5 years higher. 1 mark: the higher health and education indices more than offset Q's lower income index; e.g. P's income may be concentrated in an oil sector with little spending on public services.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether HDI shows that living standards are higher in Country Q than in Country P.
parts.answer: Probably, but HDI omits inequality, freedom, environment and other factors; the MPI and inequality data could give a different picture.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 6): HDI is broader than GNI per head and captures capabilities; but it is an average – Gini data show P is much more unequal (0.52 vs 0.34), so typical households in P may be worse off than the GNI figure suggests, strengthening the view that Q is better off; HDI ignores political freedom, environmental quality, working hours, housing, security; equal weighting of the three dimensions is arbitrary; data quality. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement, e.g. evidence supports higher living standards in Q, especially given the lower inequality, but a fuller view needs MPI and other indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that rapid population growth is the main obstacle to economic development in low-income countries.
parts.answer: Rapid population growth can hold back income per head and strain services, but it can also provide a labour force and markets; institutions, investment and human capital may matter more.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): Malthusian view – population outpaces food and resources; diluted capital per worker; high dependency ratio; pressure on schools, health, housing; unemployment and urban slums; lower savings. Counter-arguments – demographic transition and demographic dividend when the working-age share rises; larger domestic markets and economies of scale; young, adaptable labour force; technology raises food output. Other obstacles – low savings and investment, poor infrastructure, weak institutions and corruption, debt, dependence on primary exports, conflict, low human capital, inequality. Evaluation (up to 6): population growth is a consequence as well as a cause of poverty (birth rates fall as incomes, education of women and health improve); 'main' obstacle requires a comparison and a reasoned judgement.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between bilateral aid and multilateral aid.
parts.answer: Bilateral aid is given directly by one government to another; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN agencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tied aid may bring fewer benefits to the receiving country than untied aid.
parts.answer: Tied aid must be spent on goods/services from the donor country, which may be more expensive or unsuitable, and does not support local producers.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of tied aid. 1 mark: recipient cannot buy from the cheapest supplier, so less value is obtained. 1 mark: goods may not suit local needs or use inappropriate technology. 1 mark: money flows back to donor firms rather than local businesses/jobs.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of foreign direct investment (FDI) in Pakistan?
A a Pakistani worker in Dubai sends money home to his family
B a foreign pension fund buys a small number of shares in a Karachi-listed bank
C a foreign car maker builds and operates a new assembly plant near Lahore
D a foreign government gives a grant to build schools in Balochistan
parts.answer: C a foreign car maker builds and operates a new assembly plant near Lahore
parts.working: FDI involves a foreign firm acquiring a lasting controlling interest in productive assets, such as building its own factory. B is portfolio investment (no control); A is a remittance (a transfer); D is aid.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem: Invented data for a copper-exporting country in 2025: external debt service payments (interest and principal) were $9.6 billion and export earnings were $32 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the debt service ratio (debt service as a percentage of export earnings) in 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Export earnings are forecast to fall by 20 % in 2026 because of a fall in copper prices, while debt service payments stay the same. Calculate the new debt service ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rising debt service ratio may reduce the country's prospects for development.
parts.answer: More foreign currency goes on interest and repayments, leaving less for imports of capital goods and for spending on health and education.
parts.working: 1 mark: opportunity cost – foreign exchange and government revenue diverted to creditors. 1 mark: less investment, capital imports, social spending. 1 mark: risk of default, higher borrowing costs, IMF conditions, falling investor confidence.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two possible benefits to a low-income host country of a multinational company (MNC) setting up a factory there.
parts.answer: Jobs and incomes; transfer of technology and skills; tax revenue; exports and foreign currency; investment in infrastructure.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained benefits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by transfer pricing and why it can reduce the benefits to the host country.
parts.answer: MNCs set the prices of goods traded between their own subsidiaries so that profits are recorded in low-tax countries; the host country loses tax revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – prices charged in trade between branches of the same MNC. 1 mark: overcharging the host-country subsidiary for inputs/fees, or undercharging for its output. 1 mark: profits appear in a low-tax country. 1 mark: host government loses corporate tax revenue.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether foreign direct investment by multinational companies is more beneficial to low-income countries than official development aid.
parts.answer: FDI brings capital, technology and jobs without debt, but is driven by profit and may concentrate in extractive sectors; aid can target poverty and public goods but has its own problems; they complement each other.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): FDI – capital inflow, jobs, technology and management skills, exports, tax revenue, multiplier effects; costs – profit repatriation, transfer pricing, enclave production with weak linkages, environmental damage, influence over government, footloose firms, goes to countries with resources or large markets, not the poorest. Aid – grants and concessional loans, can fund health, education and infrastructure (public goods) that attract FDI later; humanitarian relief; problems – tied aid, corruption, dependency, loans add to debt, donor priorities, Dutch-disease effects. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on the country's institutions, sector of FDI, type of aid (project vs budget support); FDI more beneficial for middle-income countries with infrastructure; aid more important for the poorest; reasoned judgement.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)
practice.stem:
Invented data for a small mineral-exporting country in one year:
GDP: $50 billion
profits of foreign-owned MNCs sent abroad: $3.5 billion
income received by residents from assets abroad: $0.5 billion
MNC employment: 40,000 workers, total wages $1.2 billion
average wage in the rest of the economy: $8,000 per worker
MNC exports: $6 billion; corporate tax paid by MNCs: $0.9 billion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's GNI and GNI as a percentage of GDP.
parts.answer: GNI $47 billion; 94 % of GDP

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average annual wage paid by the MNC per worker, in dollars.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate, using the data, whether the MNCs bring more benefits than costs to the country.
parts.answer: The MNCs create well-paid jobs, exports and tax revenue, but large profit outflows and possible environmental costs reduce the net gain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 5): benefits – 40,000 jobs at wages ($30,000) far above the national average ($8,000); $6 billion exports earn foreign currency; $0.9 billion tax revenue; skills transfer. Costs – $3.5 billion profits repatriated reduces GNI (GNI is only 94 % of GDP); dependence on a few foreign firms; possible environmental damage and use of non-renewable resources; little linkage to local suppliers if inputs are imported; possible transfer pricing. Evaluation (up to 2): reasoned judgement, e.g. net benefits appear positive, but depend on reinvestment, linkages and government regulation.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether debt relief is the most effective way to promote economic development in heavily indebted low-income countries.
parts.answer: Debt relief frees resources for spending on development, but its effectiveness depends on governance and on what is done with the savings; trade access, FDI and institutional reform may be more important.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): burden of debt – high debt service ratio, diversion of foreign exchange and tax revenue, debt overhang deters investment, austerity cuts social spending; debt relief reduces payments, allows spending on health, education and infrastructure, improves credit rating. Problems – moral hazard (may encourage future over-borrowing), funds may be wasted through corruption, conditions attached may impose unpopular reforms, relief is a one-off and does not address causes (dependence on primary exports, low productivity, volatile commodity prices). Alternatives – fairer trade and market access, diversification, FDI, aid targeted at human capital, institutional reform, microfinance. Evaluation (up to 6): relief is a necessary condition in some cases but rarely sufficient; reasoned judgement on 'most effective'.

practice.subtopic: Relationships between countries (aid, FDI, MNCs, debt)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the main roles of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in relation to low-income countries.
parts.answer: IMF: short- to medium-term loans for balance-of-payments problems, surveillance, technical advice. World Bank: long-term loans and grants for development projects (infrastructure, health, education) and poverty reduction.
parts.working: 2 marks each: IMF (1 role identified, 1 developed); World Bank (1 role identified, 1 developed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss why the conditions attached to IMF loans are often controversial.
parts.answer: Conditions such as cutting budget deficits, removing subsidies, raising interest rates and privatisation can restore stability but may raise poverty and unemployment in the short run.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): conditions aim to correct the causes of the crisis and ensure repayment; but austerity reduces aggregate demand and social spending, removal of fuel/food subsidies hurts the poor, loss of policy independence, 'one-size-fits-all' criticisms. Judgement (1): e.g. conditions may be needed for credibility but should be phased and protect vulnerable groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate, a fixed exchange rate and a managed float.
parts.answer: Floating: set by market demand and supply with no target. Fixed: the central bank holds the currency at an official rate. Managed float: mostly market-determined, but the central bank intervenes to influence it.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a central bank could prevent its currency from falling below a fixed exchange rate.
parts.answer: Buy its own currency using foreign exchange reserves; raise interest rates to attract capital inflows; (also capital controls or borrowing from the IMF).
parts.working: 2 marks each: method identified (1) and explained in terms of demand for the currency (1).

practice.stem: A Pakistani textile firm sells shirts for Rs 5,600 each. The exchange rate changes from Rs 280 = $1 to Rs 300 = $1 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dollar price of the shirt before and after the change in the exchange rate, and the percentage change. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before $20.00; after $18.67; a fall of 6.7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rupee cost of a $50 machine part before and after the change.
parts.answer: Rs 14,000 before; Rs 15,000 after

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the depreciation might not raise the textile exporter's profits as much as expected.
parts.answer: Its imported inputs (machinery, dyes, fuel) become more expensive, raising costs; foreign demand may be price inelastic.
parts.working: 1 mark point (dearer imported inputs / inelastic demand / competitors' currencies also falling); 1 mark development.

practice.stem: Invented data: a burger costs Rs 900 in Pakistan and $5.50 in the USA. The market exchange rate is Rs 280 = $1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the exchange rate implied by purchasing power parity (PPP) for the burger. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Rs 163.6 per $

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the rupee is undervalued against the dollar on this measure. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: At the market rate the burger costs 900 ÷ 280 = $3.21 in Pakistan; 3.21 ÷ 5.50 = 0.584 (M1); undervalued by 1 − 0.584 = 41.6 % (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a single-product comparison may not give a reliable estimate of the PPP exchange rate.
parts.answer: The burger includes non-traded inputs (rent, wages) whose prices differ; local tastes, taxes and competition differ; one product does not represent the whole basket.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to the Marshall–Lerner condition, a depreciation of a currency will improve a country's current account balance if
A the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than one
B the price elasticity of demand for exports is less than one
C the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is less than one
D the income elasticity of demand for imports is greater than one
parts.answer: A the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than one
parts.working: If the sum of PEDs (in absolute value) exceeds 1, export revenue rises and import spending falls by enough to improve the balance. C describes the case in which the balance worsens, as at the start of the J-curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a fixed exchange rate system is better than a floating exchange rate system for a developing economy.
parts.answer: A fixed rate gives certainty and can control inflation, but needs large reserves and removes monetary policy independence; a floating rate adjusts automatically but can be volatile; the better choice depends on the economy.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): fixed – certainty for traders and investors, reduces speculation (if credible), imposes discipline and can anchor inflation; costs – need for large foreign currency reserves, loss of independent monetary policy (interest rates set to defend the peg), risk of speculative attack and forced devaluation, misalignment can harm competitiveness. Floating – automatic correction of current account imbalances, no need for reserves, monetary policy free to target domestic goals; costs – volatility and uncertainty, depreciation raises import prices (imported inflation, cost of fuel and food), raises the burden of foreign-currency debt, speculation. Managed float as a middle way. Evaluation (up to 6): depends on reserves, inflation history, openness, credibility of the central bank, size of foreign-currency debt, commodity dependence; reasoned judgement.

practice.stem:
Invented data: a country's currency depreciated by 15 % at the start of Quarter 1. Its current account balance ($ billion) was:
Quarter 0: −2.0
Quarter 1: −2.6
Quarter 2: −2.9
Quarter 3: −2.1
Quarter 4: −1.2
Quarter 5: −0.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the quarter in which the current account deficit was largest, and calculate the improvement from that quarter to Quarter 5.
parts.answer: Quarter 2 (−$2.9 billion); improvement of $2.5 billion
parts.working: B1 Quarter 2. −0.4 − (−2.9) = $2.5 billion (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the J-curve effect to explain the pattern in the data.
parts.answer: In the short run demand for exports and imports is price inelastic, so the deficit widens; over time demand becomes more elastic and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met, so the balance improves.
parts.working: 1 mark: depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. 1 mark: in the short run contracts and habits mean quantities change little (PEDs sum < 1), so import spending rises and the deficit worsens (Q1–Q2). 1 mark: over time buyers switch, PEDs rise and the sum exceeds 1. 1 mark: the deficit narrows (Q3–Q5), giving the J shape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason, other than the depreciation, why the current account might have improved.
parts.answer: A recession in the country reducing import demand / rise in world prices of its exports / faster growth in trading partners.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a free trade area, a customs union and a common market.
parts.answer: Free trade area: no tariffs between members, each sets its own external tariffs. Customs union: free trade area plus a common external tariff. Common market: customs union plus free movement of labour and capital.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem that can arise in a free trade area that does not arise in a customs union.
parts.answer: Trade deflection: imports enter through the member with the lowest external tariff and are moved to other members; rules of origin are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: trade deflection. 1 mark: rules of origin/border checks needed, adding cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a feature of a customs union but not of a free trade area?
A removal of tariffs on trade between member countries
B a common external tariff on imports from non-members
C free movement of labour between member countries
D a single currency used by all members
parts.answer: B a common external tariff on imports from non-members
parts.working: Both arrangements remove internal tariffs (A), but only a customs union adds a common external tariff. Free movement of labour (C) is a feature of a common market; a single currency (D) of a monetary union.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country ($ billion):
2015: exports 12, imports 18, GDP 40
2025: exports 15, imports 20, GDP 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the trade openness ratio ((exports + imports) as a percentage of GDP) for 2015 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A newspaper said the data show the country 'became less involved in globalisation'. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
parts.answer: Trade grew in absolute terms (from $30 billion to $35 billion); the ratio fell only because GDP grew faster; other aspects of globalisation (FDI, migration, technology, capital flows) are not shown.
parts.working: 1 mark: exports and imports both rose in value. 1 mark: the ratio fell because GDP rose by 25 % while trade rose by about 17 %. 1 mark: globalisation also includes FDI, capital and labour flows not in the data. 1 mark: real vs nominal values / exchange-rate changes may distort figures.

practice.stem: Country A imports a good. It can buy the good from Country B at $10 per unit or from Country C at $8 per unit. Before joining a customs union, Country A charges a 50 % tariff on imports from all countries. Country A then forms a customs union with Country B, keeping a 50 % common external tariff on goods from Country C (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain from which country Country A imports the good before and after joining the customs union.
parts.answer: Before: from Country C ($8 + $4 tariff = $12, cheaper than B at $10 + $5 = $15). After: from Country B ($10, no tariff, cheaper than C at $12).
parts.working: 1 mark each, with prices shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is trade creation or trade diversion, and calculate the extra resource cost per unit to the world of buying from the new supplier.
parts.answer: Trade diversion; extra resource cost $2 per unit
parts.working: B1 trade diversion: imports switch from a more efficient non-member to a less efficient member. M1 cost per unit B $10 − C $8; A1 $2 per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why consumers in Country A may still gain even though the government of Country A loses.
parts.answer: Consumers pay $10 instead of $12, but the government loses the $4 per unit tariff revenue it used to collect.
parts.working: 1 mark consumers' price falls by $2. 1 mark government loses tariff revenue of $4 per unit, which is greater than consumers' gain per unit on existing imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that globalisation has reduced inequality between countries.
parts.answer: Globalisation has helped many emerging economies converge, but some low-income and commodity-dependent countries have fallen further behind; effects vary.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 14): features of globalisation – trade liberalisation, FDI and MNCs, capital flows, migration, technology transfer, global supply chains. Arguments for reduced inequality between countries – rapid growth in China, India, Vietnam and others through export-led manufacturing; technology and capital flows to lower-income countries; comparative advantage; remittances. Arguments against – benefits concentrated in countries with infrastructure, skills and stable institutions; least developed countries remain dependent on primary exports with volatile prices and declining terms of trade; capital flight and financial crises; brain drain; MNC profits repatriated; protection by high-income countries in agriculture. Distinguish inequality between countries vs within countries. Evaluation (up to 6): weighted judgement, e.g. average gap between countries has narrowed, largely because of a few large Asian economies, while some countries have been left behind; depends on policy and institutions.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is an expenditure-reducing policy for correcting a current account deficit?
A a devaluation of the currency
B a tariff on imported cars
C an increase in income tax rates
D a subsidy to exporters
parts.answer: C an increase in income tax rates
parts.working: Higher income tax reduces disposable income and total spending, including spending on imports. A, B and D are expenditure-switching policies, because they change relative prices to move spending from imports to domestic goods.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies for correcting a current account deficit, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Switching policies change relative prices so that spending moves from imports to domestic output (e.g. devaluation, tariffs); reducing policies lower total demand so that imports fall (e.g. higher interest rates, tax rises, spending cuts).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition, 1 mark each example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether expenditure-reducing policies are a suitable way to correct a current account deficit in a country with high unemployment.
parts.answer: They reduce imports but at the cost of lower output and higher unemployment; supply-side or switching policies may be more appropriate.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): lower AD reduces imports according to the marginal propensity to import; may also lower inflation and improve competitiveness; but output and employment fall further, with multiplier effects; conflict between external balance and full employment; if the MPM is small, a large fall in income is needed for a small improvement. Evaluation (up to 2): judgement – unsuitable as the main policy in a recession; better to use expenditure-switching or supply-side policies, unless the deficit is caused by excess demand.
