parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm sells its product in a perfectly competitive market at $5 per unit and hires labour in a perfectly competitive labour market at a wage of $70 per day. Daily output for 1 to 5 workers is 20, 38, 54, 66 and 74 units. How many workers will a profit-maximising firm employ?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 5
parts.answer: B 3
parts.working: Marginal products are 20, 18, 16, 12, 8, so MRP = 100, 90, 80, 60, 40. The firm hires while MRP ≥ wage: the 3rd worker adds $80 > $70, the 4th adds only $60 < $70. C assumes hiring continues until total output is high rather than comparing MRP with the wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define marginal revenue product of labour.
parts.answer: The extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more worker: marginal physical product × marginal revenue (or price in perfect competition).
parts.working: 1 change in total revenue from one more worker; 1 MPP × MR.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a firm's demand curve for labour slopes downwards.
parts.answer: Diminishing marginal returns: as more workers are added to fixed capital, MPP and therefore MRP fall; the firm hires up to where MRP = wage, so at a lower wage it hires more workers; the MRP curve is the demand curve.
parts.working: 1 diminishing marginal returns/falling MPP in short run; 1 MRP falls as employment rises; 1 profit-maximising firm employs where wage = MRP, so a lower wage → more workers (MRP curve = demand curve).

practice.stem: A leading Pakistani cricketer earns Rs 80 million a year from playing and sponsorship. The best alternative job open to him is coaching, which would pay Rs 6 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cricketer's economic rent.
parts.answer: Rs 74 million a year
parts.working: 1 80 − 6 = Rs 74 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why economic rent forms a large part of the earnings of top sports players.
parts.answer: Their supply is highly inelastic because talent is rare and cannot be quickly trained; demand (from leagues, sponsors, broadcasters) is high, so the wage is far above transfer earnings.
parts.working: 1 rare natural talent → very inelastic supply; 1 high demand/MRP (TV and sponsorship revenue); 1 so earnings well above transfer earnings, most is economic rent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two factors that affect the elasticity of supply of labour to an occupation.
parts.answer: Any two: length of training/qualifications required; skills needed; geographical and occupational mobility; time period; availability of workers in other occupations; non-monetary benefits.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the demand for labour is a derived demand.
parts.answer: Labour is demanded not for itself but for the goods and services it helps to produce; demand for workers depends on demand for the product.
parts.working: 1 demanded for what it produces; 1 changes in product demand change labour demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that affect the wage elasticity of demand for labour.
parts.answer: Any two: ease of substituting capital for labour; price elasticity of demand for the product; proportion of labour costs in total costs; time period.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: factor identified + direction explained (e.g. easy to replace workers with machines → elastic).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The supply of labour to an occupation is L = 20W − 200, where W is the hourly wage in $ and L the number of workers. The market wage is $30 per hour. What is the total economic rent earned by the workers per hour?
A $4,000
B $6,000
C $8,000
D $12,000
parts.working: L = 400 at W = 30; supply starts at W = 10 when L = 0. Total earnings = 30 × 400 = $12,000. Transfer earnings = area under the supply curve = ½ × 400 × (10 + 30) = $8,000. Economic rent = area above supply, below the wage = ½ × 400 × 20 = $4,000. C is transfer earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why software engineers in Lahore usually earn more than food delivery riders.
parts.answer: Higher MRP: engineers' productivity and the value of software output is high, so demand for them is high; supply is limited by long training and scarce skills (inelastic), whereas riders need few skills, so supply is large and elastic.
parts.working: Up to 2 for demand/MRP reason; up to 2 for supply reason (training, skills, barriers to entry); or other valid reasons such as international demand for engineers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a higher national minimum wage would reduce the wage differential between the two groups.
parts.answer: It would raise riders' pay (if the minimum is above their market wage and enforced) so the gap narrows, but riders may lose jobs or hours, many are self-employed gig workers outside the law, and engineers' pay is unaffected or rises further.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): minimum wage above equilibrium raises pay of low-paid; engineers paid well above minimum so differential falls; possible excess supply/unemployment among riders. Consideration (1+): enforcement in informal/gig work, platform responses, differentials may re-emerge; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with the help of a diagram, how a trade union may raise the wage in a competitive labour market, and the effect on employment.
parts.answer: By collective bargaining the union sets a wage above equilibrium; the supply curve becomes horizontal at the union wage up to the original supply; firms move up the demand (MRP) curve so employment falls.
parts.working: 1 collective bargaining/threat of strike sets wage above equilibrium; 1 diagram: labour market with W and L axes, wage floor; 1 employment falls along MRP/demand curve; 1 excess supply of labour (or effect smaller if demand is wage inelastic / productivity agreements shift MRP).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the effect of a trade union on employment would be different if the employer were a monopsonist.
parts.answer: Yes: a union facing a monopsonist acts as bilateral monopoly; a negotiated wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive level can raise both wage and employment. The outcome depends on bargaining strength and where the wage is set; above the competitive level employment falls.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): monopsony pays below MRP; union wage makes MCL flat; employment can rise. Consideration (1+): if wage set too high employment falls; firms may substitute capital; depends on relative bargaining power; judgement.

practice.stem: Invented article. A food delivery platform in Karachi used 15,000 riders. It cut the payment per delivery from Rs 120 to Rs 100. Three months later 14,100 riders were still working for it. Two smaller platforms also operate in the city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of riders. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of riders might be wage inelastic.
parts.answer: Few alternative jobs for low-skilled workers in the city; riders have already bought motorcycles; many need income urgently and cannot afford to be unemployed; low occupational mobility.
parts.working: 1 + 1 for two reasons; 1 for development linking to small change in labour supplied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the data suggest that the platform company has monopsony power.
parts.answer: Possibly: it could cut pay by 17% and still keep 94% of riders, suggesting few alternative employers; but riders may work for several platforms, the data cover a short period and other factors (unemployment rising) may explain it.
parts.working: 1 monopsony = dominant buyer of labour able to set wage; 1 evidence: large pay cut, small fall in riders; 1 consideration of other explanations/limitations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an individual's supply curve of labour may bend backwards at high wage rates.
parts.answer: A higher wage has a substitution effect (leisure becomes more expensive → work more) and an income effect (higher income → want more leisure, a normal good → work less). At high wages the income effect can outweigh the substitution effect, so hours offered fall.
parts.working: 1 substitution effect explained; 1 income effect explained; 1 at low wages substitution dominates (upward slope); 1 at high wages income effect dominates (backward bend).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider the implications of a backward-bending supply curve for a government that cuts income tax rates to increase hours worked.
parts.answer: A tax cut raises the net wage; for workers on the upward part hours rise, but for high earners on the backward-bending part hours may fall, so the policy may not raise labour supply; effect varies between groups and contracts often fix hours.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): tax cut = higher net wage; outcome depends on which effect dominates for each group; may reduce hours of high earners. Consideration (1+): many workers cannot choose hours; participation decisions (second earners) may respond more; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A monopsony employer faces the labour supply curve W = 4 + 0.5L, so its marginal cost of labour is MCL = 4 + L. The marginal revenue product of labour is MRP = 40 − 0.5L. (W in $ per hour, L in workers.) What wage will the monopsonist pay?
A $16
B $22
C $28
D $40
parts.working: The monopsonist hires where MCL = MRP: 4 + L = 40 − 0.5L → L = 24, then pays the wage on the supply curve: W = 4 + 0.5 × 24 = $16. B ($22) is the competitive outcome where supply = MRP; C ($28) is the MRP at 24 workers, the gap being the monopsony exploitation.

practice.stem: In the market for unskilled factory labour in an invented country, labour demand is Ld = 1000 − 20W and labour supply is Ls = −200 + 40W, where W is the daily wage in $ and L is in thousand workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium wage and level of employment.
parts.answer: W = $20 per day; L = 600 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: A minimum wage of $24 per day is introduced. Calculate the change in employment and the excess supply of labour.
parts.answer: Employment falls by 80 thousand (to 520 thousand); excess supply = 240 thousand
parts.working: M1 Ld = 1000 − 480 = 520; M1 Ls = −200 + 960 = 760. A1 employment −80 thousand and excess supply 240 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a minimum wage could raise both the wage and employment if the labour market were a monopsony.
parts.answer: A monopsonist restricts hiring to pay a low wage (MCL above supply). A minimum wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage makes MCL horizontal at the minimum wage up to the supply curve, so the firm hires more workers at a higher wage.
parts.working: 1 monopsonist hires where MCL = MRP and pays below MRP; 1 minimum wage removes the need to raise the wage for all workers when hiring one more, so MCL = minimum wage; 1 employment rises towards the competitive level if the minimum is set below the competitive wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a national minimum wage is the best way to reduce poverty among low-paid workers.
parts.answer: A minimum wage raises pay for those who keep their jobs and can raise employment under monopsony, but it may cause unemployment in competitive markets, does not reach informal workers or the unemployed, and poverty depends on household circumstances. Alternatives (in-work benefits, negative income tax, training, progressive taxes) may target poverty better; a combination is usually best.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: competitive labour market diagram with minimum wage above equilibrium → higher wage, lower employment, excess supply; monopsony diagram → higher wage and employment; higher spending of low-paid workers; incentive to work. Evaluation: size of minimum relative to median wage; elasticity of demand for labour; informal sector and enforcement (large in low-income countries); poverty is household-based (number of earners, dependants); alternatives: transfer payments, tax credits, universal basic income, education/training to raise MRP, each with costs (funding, disincentives, time lags). Conclusion: 'best' must be judged against alternatives and context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether differences in labour productivity are the main reason why average wages in the information technology sector are much higher than average wages in agriculture.
parts.answer: Productivity (MRP) is a major reason, but supply-side factors (skills, training, barriers, mobility), product demand and prices, market power (unions, monopsony), discrimination, informal employment and government policy also matter.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: marginal productivity theory — wage = MRP in competitive markets; MRP = MPP × MR so both productivity and the value of output matter; diagram comparing two labour markets with different demand (MRP) and supply elasticities; supply of IT workers restricted by education and training; large, mobile supply of unskilled farm labour. Evaluation: MRP is hard to measure in services; product prices matter (agricultural prices low and volatile); monopsony landowners or agro-processors; seasonal and informal work; global demand for IT services; discrimination; government minimum support prices. Judgement on 'main reason'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A chemical factory's marginal private cost is MPC = 20 + 2Q and the marginal external cost of its pollution is a constant $10 per unit. Marginal social benefit equals marginal private benefit: MSB = 110 − 2Q. Which specific tax per unit would achieve the socially optimal output, and what is that output?
A $10 per unit; output 20 units
B $10 per unit; output 22.5 units
C $5 per unit; output 20 units
D $20 per unit; output 20 units
parts.answer: A $10 per unit; output 20 units
parts.working: Market output: 20 + 2Q = 110 − 2Q → Q = 22.5. MSC = 30 + 2Q; optimum 30 + 2Q = 110 − 2Q → Q = 20. A tax equal to the marginal external cost ($10) makes MPC + tax = MSC, so output falls to 20. B gives the output before the tax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'nudge' in government policy.
parts.answer: A change to the way choices are presented that steers people towards a better decision without banning options or changing financial incentives much.
parts.working: 1 influences behaviour through choice architecture/framing; 1 freedom of choice kept (no ban, no large tax).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how automatic enrolment of employees into a workplace pension scheme is an example of a nudge.
parts.answer: Workers are placed in the scheme by default and must actively opt out; because of inertia and present bias most stay in, so saving rises while choice is preserved.
parts.working: 1 default option/opt-out; 1 uses inertia or present bias to raise saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using nudges to correct market failure.
parts.answer: e.g. effects can be small or fade over time; people may still opt out; they do not raise revenue; seen as manipulative; hard to design for different groups.
parts.working: 1 limitation; 1 explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how extending property rights could reduce overfishing in a coastal fishery.
parts.answer: Open-access fish stocks are a common resource, so each boat overfishes. Giving communities or firms ownership/quotas of the stock makes them bear the cost of depletion, so they limit catches to protect future income.
parts.working: 1 overfishing arises because no one owns the stock (common resource/tragedy of the commons); 1 property rights/individual transferable quotas assign ownership; 1 owners internalise the cost and conserve stocks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two problems with using property rights to solve this problem.
parts.answer: Any two: hard to define and enforce rights at sea; monitoring costs; fish move across boundaries; poor fishers may lose access (equity); transaction costs of bargaining.
parts.working: 1 each.

practice.stem: The weekly market for plastic shopping bags in a city has demand Qd = 900 − 100P and supply Qs = −100 + 100P, where P is the price in Rs per bag and Q is in thousand bags. To reduce litter, the government puts a specific tax of Rs 2 per bag on sellers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new price paid by consumers and the new quantity.
parts.answer: Rs 6; 300 thousand bags

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the government's weekly tax revenue.
parts.answer: Rs 600 thousand
parts.working: 1 2 × 300 thousand = Rs 600 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how much of the tax per bag is paid by consumers and how much by producers.
parts.answer: Consumers Rs 1 per bag; producers Rs 1 per bag
parts.working: 1 original equilibrium P = Rs 5 (900 − 100P = −100 + 100P), so consumers pay 6 − 5 = Rs 1; 1 producers receive 6 − 2 = Rs 4, so they bear 5 − 4 = Rs 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two firms are in a tradable pollution permit scheme. Firm X can cut a tonne of emissions at a cost of $30 and Firm Y at a cost of $70. The permit price is $50 per tonne. What is likely to happen?
A X buys permits from Y and pollutes more.
B Y cuts its emissions and sells permits to X.
C X cuts its emissions and sells permits to Y.
D Neither firm trades because both costs differ from the permit price.
parts.answer: C X cuts its emissions and sells permits to Y.
parts.working: X can cut emissions for less than the permit price, so it abates and sells spare permits at $50; Y finds buying a permit at $50 cheaper than abating at $70. Emissions are cut where it is cheapest. A reverses the roles.

practice.stem: In the market for household solar water heaters in an invented country, MPB = 80 − Q, MSB = 100 − Q and MPC = MSC = 20 + Q, where prices are in $ and Q is in thousand heaters per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the free-market output and the socially optimal output.
parts.answer: Free market: 30 thousand; social optimum: 40 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government pays a subsidy of $20 per unit to producers. Calculate the total cost of the subsidy.
parts.answer: $800 thousand ($0.8 million)
parts.working: M1 with subsidy MPC falls to Q; 80 − Q = Q → Q = 40 thousand. A1 20 × 40 thousand = $800 thousand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government may set the subsidy at the wrong level.
parts.answer: The external benefit is hard to measure in money (information failure), so the subsidy may be too high or too low; lobbying may also distort it.
parts.working: 1 difficulty valuing external benefits/imperfect information; 1 consequence: over- or under-provision.

practice.stem: Invented data. To reduce winter smog and congestion, a city government introduces a daily charge of Rs 500 for cars entering the central business area of Lahore. Car trips into the area fall from 400,000 to 340,000 a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in car trips and the daily revenue from the charge.
parts.answer: 15% fall; Rs 170 million a day

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a road-user charge can correct the negative externalities of car use.
parts.answer: Drivers ignore the costs they impose on others (congestion, smog). The charge raises the private cost of driving towards the social cost, so drivers with low benefit switch mode or time, reducing trips towards the social optimum.
parts.working: 1 external costs of congestion and pollution; 1 charge internalises the externality (MPC + charge ≈ MSC); 1 trips fall towards where MSC = MSB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider one reason why the charge may not achieve the socially optimal number of trips.
parts.answer: The external cost is hard to measure, so the charge may be set too low or high; demand for car trips may be inelastic with poor public transport; traffic may divert to roads outside the zone.
parts.working: 1 reason; 1 explanation; 1 judgement/consideration (e.g. effect depends on using revenue to improve buses).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a large tax on cigarettes may not reduce smoking by very much.
parts.answer: Cigarettes are addictive with few substitutes, so demand is price inelastic: the tax raises price but quantity falls only slightly; smokers may also switch to cheaper illegal or untaxed products.
parts.working: 1 addictive/habit-forming, few substitutes; 1 price inelastic demand → small fall in quantity; 1 smuggling/illegal market or cheaper brands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether such a tax is still worthwhile for the government.
parts.answer: Yes in some ways: it raises large revenue (inelastic demand) that can fund healthcare and anti-smoking campaigns, and may deter young people whose demand is more elastic; but it is regressive, may encourage smuggling, and does little to cut external costs if consumption barely falls.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): revenue, long-run elasticity higher, effect on new smokers, internalising external costs. Consideration (1+): regressive, illegal markets, enforcement; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm producing fertiliser has marginal private cost MPC = 10 + Q. Its production causes a constant marginal external cost of $12 per unit. Marginal social benefit equals marginal private benefit: MSB = 100 − 2Q (P in $, Q in units). What is the deadweight welfare loss if output is left to the free market?
A $12
B $24
C $48
D $360
parts.working: Free market: 10 + Q = 100 − 2Q → Q = 30. MSC = 22 + Q; optimum: 22 + Q = 100 − 2Q → Q = 26. Welfare loss triangle between MSC and MSB from Q = 26 to 30, with height 12 at Q = 30: ½ × (30 − 26) × 12 = $24. C forgets the ½ (it is a triangle, not a rectangle); D is the total external cost of all 30 units, not the welfare loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether tradable pollution permits are more effective than direct regulation in reducing carbon emissions from power stations.
parts.answer: Permits fix the total quantity of emissions and let firms that can cut cheaply do so, so the target is reached at least cost and firms have an incentive to innovate; regulation is simpler, more certain for each plant and easier to enforce in some countries. Effectiveness depends on the cap, monitoring, permit allocation and market conditions.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: negative externality diagram (MSC > MPC); how a cap-and-trade scheme works and why it achieves the cut at lowest total abatement cost; permit price as incentive; regulation (emission limits, technology standards, bans) — certain outcome per plant, but same rule for all ignores different costs. Evaluation: setting the cap and allocating permits (free allocation, lobbying, too many permits → low price); monitoring and enforcement costs; price volatility; carbon leakage; regulation inflexible but suitable where few large plants or where hotspots matter; information failure in both. Conclusion on 'more effective' with conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that providing information and using nudges are better ways to reduce the consumption of sugary drinks than placing a tax on them.
parts.answer: Information and nudges tackle the root cause (information failure, present bias) cheaply and preserve choice, but effects are often small; a tax directly raises price, cuts consumption if demand is elastic enough, raises revenue and pushes firms to reformulate, but is regressive and may be weak if demand is inelastic. A combination is often most effective.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: demerit good/negative externality and information failure diagram (overconsumption where MPB > MSB); information campaigns and labels shift perceived MPB left; nudges (placement, default portion sizes); tax shifts supply left by the tax, price up, quantity down, revenue raised. Evaluation: PED of sugary drinks; regressive burden on low-income households; substitution to untaxed sugary products; evidence that nudges fade; cost and reach of campaigns; tax revenue can fund health programmes; judgement on 'better'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether privatisation is an effective way to correct market failure in the distribution of electricity in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Privatisation may improve efficiency through the profit motive (lower losses and theft, better billing, investment) but electricity distribution is a natural monopoly with externalities and equity issues; without strong regulation, private owners may raise prices and neglect poor areas. Effectiveness depends on regulation and competition.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: market failures in electricity (natural monopoly, positive externalities of access, information problems, government failure in state-owned firms: losses, overstaffing); privatisation → profit incentive → productive and dynamic efficiency; access to private capital. Evaluation: private monopoly may restrict output and raise price (monopoly diagram) — needs price-cap regulation; regulatory capture; rural areas unprofitable → subsidies needed; tariffs politically sensitive; evidence varies by country; alternatives such as reform of state firms, competitive tendering. Conclusion on effectiveness and conditions.

practice.stem:
Invented income tax schedule:
First Rs 600,000 of annual income: 0%
Rs 600,001 to Rs 1,200,000: 10%
Above Rs 1,200,000: 20%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by a person with an annual taxable income of Rs 2,000,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this person's average rate of tax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this tax system is progressive.
parts.answer: The average rate of tax rises as income rises because higher slices of income are taxed at higher marginal rates (0% → 10% → 20%).
parts.working: 1 average tax rate rises with income; 1 marginal rate above average rate/higher bands.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a Lorenz curve diagram, the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve is 0.18, and the area below the Lorenz curve is 0.32. What is the Gini coefficient?
A 0.18
B 0.36
C 0.56
D 0.64
parts.working: Gini = A ÷ (A + B) = 0.18 ÷ (0.18 + 0.32) = 0.18 ÷ 0.5 = 0.36. C divides 0.18 by 0.32; A forgets to divide by the total area under the equality line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a universal basic income.
parts.answer: A regular, unconditional cash payment made by the state to every adult, whatever their income or employment status.
parts.working: 1 regular payment to all citizens/adults; 1 not means-tested or conditional on work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a universal basic income would reduce inequality more effectively than means-tested benefits.
parts.answer: It avoids the poverty trap and stigma, has full take-up and low administration costs, so it reaches all the poor; but paying everyone is very expensive, so the amount may be too low to cut inequality unless financed by progressive taxes; means-tested benefits target money on the poorest.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): means-tested benefits are withdrawn as income rises → high effective marginal tax rates/poverty trap; low take-up, stigma, admin cost; UBI simple and keeps work incentives at the margin; distribution depends on how it is financed. Evaluation (up to 2): fiscal cost, possible inflation, may reduce labour supply (income effect), equal payment to rich and poor; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether progressive income taxes are the most effective way to reduce inequality of income and wealth in a developing economy.
parts.answer: Progressive taxes narrow post-tax income gaps, but in many developing economies few people pay income tax, the informal sector is large and evasion is common; wealth inequality needs wealth, property or inheritance taxes. Spending on education and health, transfers, minimum wages and land reform may be more effective; a mix is needed.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): Level 4 (15–20) accurate, well-explained analysis of both sides, relevant diagram(s) fully used, and a reasoned conclusion that answers the question in context; Level 3 (10–14) mostly accurate analysis, some evaluation but conclusion partly asserted; Level 2 (5–9) limited or partly inaccurate analysis, evaluation mostly descriptive; Level 1 (1–4) a few relevant points. One-sided answers are capped at Level 2. Analysis: Lorenz curve/Gini; how progressive taxes raise the average rate with income and fund transfers; effect on disposable income. Evaluation: narrow tax base, informal economy, evasion and avoidance; disincentives to work and invest; capital flight; income taxes do little for wealth inequality (land and property); regressive indirect taxes may dominate the tax system; alternatives — cash transfers (e.g. targeted programmes for poor households), universal education and health, property taxes, minimum wage, microfinance — with their limitations. Conclusion on 'most effective'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by government failure in microeconomic intervention.
parts.answer: When government intervention to correct a market failure leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than before (a net welfare loss).
parts.working: 1 intervention in a market; 1 results in a worse/less efficient outcome than without it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the example of a maximum price set below the equilibrium price for wheat flour, consider how such intervention may lead to government failure.
parts.answer: The price ceiling causes excess demand: shortages, queues, rationing by waiting, black markets, hoarding and smuggling; farmers and millers have less incentive to supply, so output falls. But the policy may protect the poor if combined with subsidies or a buffer stock, so failure depends on design and enforcement.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): diagram with max price below equilibrium; Qd > Qs; shortages, illegal markets at higher prices, lower quality; reduced supply incentive; administrative costs; unintended consequences. Evaluation (up to 2): information problems vs benefits to low-income consumers; can be avoided with release of government stocks, targeted subsidies; judgement on whether the outcome is worse than the free market.

topics.name: The price system and the microeconomy

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Printers and ink cartridges are complements. The price of printers falls sharply. What is most likely to happen in the market for ink cartridges?
A price falls and quantity bought rises
B price rises and quantity bought rises
C price rises and quantity bought falls
D price and quantity bought are unchanged
parts.answer: B price rises and quantity bought rises
parts.working: Cheaper printers → more printers bought → demand for cartridges shifts right → higher equilibrium price and quantity. A is wrong: it describes an increase in supply, not demand. D ignores the link between complements.

practice.stem:
The daily market for tomatoes in Karachi is described by:
Qd = 240 − 4P
Qs = −30 + 5P
where P is the price in Rs per kg and Q is in thousand kg per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = Rs 30 per kg, Q = 120 thousand kg per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: The city government fixes the price at Rs 24 per kg. Calculate the excess demand at this price.
parts.answer: Excess demand = 54 thousand kg per day
parts.working: M1 Qd = 240 − 96 = 144; Qs = −30 + 120 = 90. A1 excess demand = 54 thousand kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how, without price control, the price mechanism would remove a shortage in this market.
parts.answer: Buyers compete and bid the price up; higher price contracts quantity demanded and extends quantity supplied until the market clears at Rs 30.
parts.working: 1 mark each: shortage leads buyers/sellers to raise price (signal); higher price gives incentive to sellers → extension of supply (movement along supply); higher price rations → contraction of demand; process continues until Qd = Qs at equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Beef and leather are in joint supply. Demand for beef from restaurants in Lahore rises. Other things equal, what happens in the leather market?
A Supply of leather falls and its price rises
B Demand for leather rises and its price rises
C Supply of leather rises and its price falls
D Demand for leather falls and its price falls
parts.answer: C Supply of leather rises and its price falls
parts.working: More cattle are slaughtered to meet beef demand, so more hides are produced as a by-product: the supply curve of leather shifts right, price falls and quantity rises. B confuses joint supply with joint demand; the demand for leather has not changed.

practice.stem: Invented data. In 2025 floods cut a South Asian country's cotton crop by 28%. The world price of raw cotton rose from 78 US cents per pound in 2024 to 96 US cents per pound in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the world price of cotton between 2024 and 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with the help of a demand and supply diagram, the likely effect of the rise in the cotton price on the market for polyester fibre.
parts.answer: Polyester is a substitute: demand for polyester shifts right, raising its equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.working: 1 polyester and cotton are substitutes (competitive demand); 1 demand curve for polyester shifts right (diagram with labelled axes P, Q and D1→D2); 1 equilibrium price and quantity both rise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cottonseed oil is produced from the seeds left after cotton is ginned. Consider the effect of the smaller cotton crop on the market for cottonseed oil.
parts.answer: Joint supply: a smaller crop reduces supply of cottonseed, so supply of oil shifts left, price rises and quantity falls; the size depends on stocks, imports and PED.
parts.working: 1 joint supply identified; 1 supply of cottonseed oil shifts left → price up, quantity down; 1 consideration, e.g. effect smaller if stocks held or imports of other edible oils available, or if demand for the oil is price elastic as other cooking oils substitute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the market for a good is linked to the markets for its complements and for goods produced in joint supply with it, and consider whether a fall in the price of a good will always change the equilibrium in a related market.
parts.answer: Complements: lower price of good A raises demand for complement B (P and Q of B rise). Joint supply: changes in output of A change supply of its by-product. A related market changes only if the price fall causes a change in quantity of A and the link is strong.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of complements (joint demand), joint supply, a related market. Analysis: price of A falls → extension of demand for A → demand for complement shifts right (diagram); if price of A falls because of lower demand, output of A falls → supply of joint product shifts left → its price rises (diagram). Evaluation: effect depends on how strong the link is (cross elasticity), on the PED of A (if inelastic, little extra quantity), on whether the fall in price is caused by demand or supply, and on time; a weakly related good will hardly change. Judgement: not always, and the size varies.

practice.stem: The Punjab government is considering a subsidy for each electric motorcycle sold in Lahore. Most motorcycles in the city currently run on petrol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the relationship between electric motorcycles and electricity, and between electric motorcycles and petrol motorcycles.
parts.answer: Electric motorcycles and electricity: complements (joint demand). Electric and petrol motorcycles: substitutes (competitive demand).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether a government subsidy for electric motorcycles in Lahore will reduce the price of petrol.
parts.answer: Possibly a small fall in petrol demand, but the effect on the petrol price is likely to be small: Pakistan's petrol price depends on world oil prices, the exchange rate, taxes and government pricing, and motorcycles are only part of petrol demand.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): subsidy lowers price of e-motorcycles → more bought → fewer petrol motorcycles bought (substitutes) → demand for petrol falls → leftward shift of petrol demand → lower equilibrium price, other things equal; also demand for electricity rises (complement). Evaluation (up to 2): petrol price is largely set by world crude price and government levy, not local demand; motorcycles are a small share of total fuel use; existing petrol bikes last years so effect is slow; supply of petrol may be elastic (imports) so price change is small; judgement needed.

practice.stem: The market for fitness bands in Dubai is described by Qd = 500 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P, where P is the price in US$ and Q is in thousands per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $30, Q = 200 thousand per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rising incomes change demand to Qd = 560 − 10P and a fall in component costs changes supply to Qs = 80 + 5P. Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $32, Q = 240 thousand per month

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why, when demand and supply both increase, the direction of the change in equilibrium price cannot be predicted without knowing the size of each shift.
parts.answer: Both shifts raise quantity, but an increase in demand raises price while an increase in supply lowers it, so the net price change depends on which shift is larger.
parts.working: 1 increase in demand alone → higher price and quantity; 1 increase in supply alone → lower price, higher quantity; 1 so quantity definitely rises but price rises only if the demand shift is larger (here demand rose by 60 thousand at each price, supply by 30 thousand, so price rose).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A household's monthly income rises from Rs 40,000 to Rs 46,000. The number of restaurant meals it buys in a year rises from 200 to 236. What is its income elasticity of demand for restaurant meals, and what kind of good are they?
A 0.83, a normal good that is a necessity
B 1.2, a normal good that is income elastic
C −1.2, an inferior good
D 1.2, an inferior good
parts.answer: B 1.2, a normal good that is income elastic
parts.working: %ΔQ = 36/200 = 18%; %ΔY = 6,000/40,000 = 15%; YED = 18 ÷ 15 = +1.2. Positive and greater than 1 → normal, income elastic (luxury). A inverts the formula (15 ÷ 18).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: A supermarket in Islamabad raises the price of loose tea from Rs 1,200 to Rs 1,380 per kg. Over the next month its sales of instant coffee rise from 5,000 to 5,450 jars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for instant coffee with respect to the price of tea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the sign of your answer shows about the two goods.
parts.answer: Positive: they are substitutes.
parts.working: 1 positive XED → substitutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way the supermarket could use this information.
parts.answer: e.g. when tea prices rise, stock more coffee / raise coffee price slightly, as demand for coffee will increase.
parts.working: 1 use identified (stocking, pricing, promotion); 1 linked to the positive but low XED (coffee demand rises only modestly, by 0.6% per 1% rise in tea price).

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem:
Invented estimates of income elasticity of demand (YED) for goods bought by households in Pakistan:
Wheat flour: 0.2
Motorcycles: 1.8
Second-hand clothing: −0.4
Private tuition: 1.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the inferior good in the table and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Second-hand clothing: its YED is negative (−0.4).
parts.working: 1 second-hand clothing; 1 negative YED means demand falls as income rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Real household incomes are forecast to fall by 5%. Calculate the percentage change in demand for motorcycles and for second-hand clothing.
parts.answer: Motorcycles: -9%; second-hand clothing: +2%
parts.working: 1 motorcycles 1.8 × (−5) = −9%; 1 second-hand clothing −0.4 × (−5) = +2%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a motorcycle manufacturer could use the YED estimate when planning production.
parts.answer: With YED 1.8, sales are very sensitive to income: cut planned output/stocks and staff hiring when incomes are expected to fall, expand when growth is expected; consider cheaper models.
parts.working: 1 income elastic, so demand changes more than proportionately with income; 1 plan output, stock or capacity in line with forecast income (e.g. reduce output about 9% if incomes fall 5%); 1 further use, e.g. diversify into lower-priced models or export markets with rising incomes.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand
practice.stem: A games company estimates that the cross elasticity of demand between its consoles and its games is −2.5. It sells 40,000 games a month and plans to cut the price of its consoles by 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected percentage change in sales of games and the new monthly sales.
parts.answer: +20%; 48,000 games a month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether cutting the price of its consoles is likely to increase the firm's total profit.
parts.answer: Probably, if the extra profit on games (strong complements, XED −2.5) outweighs lower revenue per console; it depends on console PED, margins on games and competitors' reactions.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): strong complements → large rise in game sales; games often have higher profit margins than consoles; extra console buyers also buy games for years. Consideration (1+): lower revenue per console may cause losses on hardware; XED is an estimate and may change; rivals may also cut prices; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Income and cross elasticity of demand

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether income elasticity of demand is more useful than cross elasticity of demand to a firm planning its production for the next five years.
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: YED is usually more useful for long-term planning because incomes change predictably over five years, but XED matters more in markets with close rivals or complements.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. YED points: measures response to income; normal/inferior/luxury; over five years real income growth forecasts allow capacity, product range and market choice (e.g. a firm with YED > 1 expands as the economy grows; inferior-good producers plan for decline). XED points: substitutes and complements; helps predict effect of rivals' price changes and pricing of complementary products; useful for bundling and competition strategy. Evaluation: estimates are based on past data and may change; income forecasts are uncertain; XED changes as new substitutes appear; usefulness depends on market structure and type of product; PED and PES may also matter; both are needed. Judgement must answer 'more useful'.

practice.stem: A cinema in Islamabad cuts its ticket price from Rs 1,000 to Rs 800. Weekly ticket sales rise from 2,500 to 3,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for the tickets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the cinema's weekly total revenue.
parts.answer: Increase of Rs 100,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how your answer to (b) is linked to your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Demand is price elastic (|PED| > 1), so a price cut raises quantity by a larger percentage and total revenue rises.
parts.working: 1 elastic demand; 1 percentage rise in quantity outweighs percentage fall in price → TR rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bus company raises its fares by 20%. Its total revenue from fares rises by 8%. What is the price elasticity of demand for its bus journeys?
A −0.4
B −0.5
C −0.6
D −2.5
parts.working: New TR = 1.2 × new Q = 1.08 × old TR, so new Q = 1.08 ÷ 1.2 = 0.9 of old Q: a 10% fall. PED = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5. A wrongly divides the revenue change by the price change (8 ÷ 20).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of demand for petrol is likely to be lower in the short run than in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: few substitutes, vehicles already owned, habits and commuting fixed → inelastic. Long run: people switch to fuel-efficient or electric vehicles, public transport, move home/work → more elastic.
parts.working: Up to 2 for short-run reasons (lack of close substitutes, necessity for work travel, existing petrol vehicles); up to 2 for long-run reasons (time to find substitutes such as CNG/electric vehicles, car-sharing, relocation) with link to responsiveness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a government should use price elasticity of demand when deciding which goods to tax.
parts.answer: Yes for revenue (tax inelastic goods raises revenue with small fall in sales) and to judge the effect on consumption; but inelastic goods are often necessities, so tax may be regressive, and PED estimates are uncertain.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): inelastic demand → tax revenue high and stable, burden mostly on consumers; elastic demand → large fall in consumption (useful for demerit goods only if elastic). Consideration (1+): equity/regressive effect on poor; aim of tax matters (revenue vs reducing consumption); PED changes over time; judgement.

practice.stem: The demand for a brand of bottled water is Qd = 120 − 2P, where P is the price in Rs and Q is in thousand bottles per week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand when the price rises from Rs 10 to Rs 12.
parts.working: M1 Q falls from 100 to 96: −4%; P rises 20%. A1 −4 ÷ 20 = −0.2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand when the price rises from Rs 50 to Rs 55.
parts.answer: PED = -5
parts.working: M1 Q falls from 20 to 10: −50%; P rises 10%. A1 −50 ÷ 10 = −5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of demand changes along this demand curve even though its slope is constant.
parts.answer: PED depends on percentage changes, not absolute ones. The same absolute change in Q is a small percentage at high quantities and a large percentage at low quantities, while the opposite holds for price.
parts.working: 1 slope measures absolute change (ΔP/ΔQ) but PED uses percentage changes; 1 at low prices/high quantities, %ΔQ is small and %ΔP large → inelastic; 1 at high prices/low quantities, %ΔQ large and %ΔP small → elastic (PED moves from 0 towards −∞ up the curve).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the factors that determine the price elasticity of demand for a product and consider whether a firm selling a branded product, such as a soft drink, can make the demand for its product more price inelastic.
parts.answer: Determinants: number and closeness of substitutes, proportion of income, necessity/habit, time period, definition of the market. A firm can reduce substitutability through branding, advertising and loyalty, but success is limited by rivals' actions.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definition and formula of PED; determinants listed. Analysis: explain how each determinant changes responsiveness (e.g. close substitutes → consumers switch when price rises → elastic). Application: brand advertising, product differentiation, loyalty schemes, exclusive distribution reduce perceived substitutes → steeper demand curve, allowing price rises that raise revenue. Evaluation: rivals also advertise; advertising is costly; consumers of soft drinks are price-sensitive and many substitutes exist; effect may be temporary; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event would cause a movement along the demand curve for rice, rather than a shift of the demand curve?
A a poor harvest that raises the price of rice
B a rise in the price of wheat flour
C a rise in household incomes
D an advertising campaign promoting rice
parts.answer: A a poor harvest that raises the price of rice
parts.working: A poor harvest shifts supply left; the higher price causes a contraction along the existing demand curve. B, C and D change a condition of demand, so they shift the demand curve itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a change in quantity supplied and a change in supply.
parts.answer: Change in quantity supplied: movement along the supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price. Change in supply: shift of the whole curve caused by a non-price factor.
parts.working: 1 each correct distinction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two events that would shift the supply curve of mangoes in Multan to the left.
parts.answer: Any two: a heatwave or pest damaging the crop; higher fertiliser, diesel or labour costs; a new indirect tax; growers switching land to more profitable crops.
parts.working: 1 each, up to 2.

practice.stem:
Weekly demand for milk (litres) by three households in a street:
Price Rs 200: household X 7, Y 5, Z 4
Price Rs 220: X 6, Y 5, Z 3
Price Rs 240: X 5, Y 4, Z 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market demand at each price.
parts.answer: Rs 200: 16 litres; Rs 220: 14 litres; Rs 240: 11 litres
parts.working: Horizontal summation. 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fourth household moves into the street. It buys 3 litres a week at each of the three prices. Calculate the new market demand at Rs 220 and state what happens to the market demand curve.
parts.answer: 17 litres; the market demand curve shifts to the right.
parts.working: 1 14 + 3 = 17; 1 rightward shift (more demanded at every price).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the market demand curve slopes downwards.
parts.answer: e.g. as price falls, the good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes (substitution effect) and consumers' real income rises (income effect), so more is demanded; new buyers enter the market at lower prices.
parts.working: 1 reason identified; 1 explained.

practice.stem: The supply of plastic chairs from factories near Gujranwala is Qs = −40 + 8P, where P is the price in hundreds of rupees (so P = 20 means Rs 2,000) and Q is in thousand chairs per month. A rise in electricity tariffs raises the cost of producing each chair by Rs 500 (5 in these units), shifting the supply curve upwards by this amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity supplied at a price of Rs 2,000 per chair (P = 20) before and after the increase in costs.
parts.answer: Before: 120 thousand chairs per month; after: 80 thousand chairs per month
parts.working: 1 Qs = −40 + 8 × 20 = 120; 1 new supply Qs = −40 + 8(P − 5), so at P = 20, Qs = −40 + 120 = 80 thousand chairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors other than costs of production that could shift the supply curve for a manufactured good.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. improved technology (more output from same inputs → shift right); indirect taxes or subsidies; number of firms in the market; weather/natural events; prices of other goods the firms could produce.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each factor: 1 identified, 1 explained with direction of shift.

practice.stem: Invented data. Over one year the average price of cooking oil in Pakistan rose by 35% while the quantity bought fell by 5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether these data are consistent with a downward-sloping demand curve.
parts.answer: Yes: a higher price with a lower quantity bought fits a movement up along a downward-sloping demand curve, e.g. caused by a fall in supply.
parts.working: 1 price up, quantity down = movement along D; 1 caused by a leftward shift of supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the rise in price was more likely to result from a change in demand or a change in supply.
parts.answer: More likely a fall in supply (higher import costs, depreciation, taxes) because quantity fell; an increase in demand would raise both price and quantity. Demand may also have risen, but supply effect dominated.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): increase in demand alone → P and Q both rise, so not consistent with Q falling; decrease in supply → P up, Q down, consistent; likely causes: higher world palm-oil prices, rupee depreciation, import duties; the small fall in Q (5%) relative to the 35% price rise suggests inelastic demand. Evaluation (up to 2): both curves may have shifted (population growth raising demand while supply fell more); data cover a year and other factors change; judgement.

practice.stem: Five fans, A to E, want one ticket each for a qawwali concert. The most each is willing to pay is: A Rs 900, B Rs 800, C Rs 700, D Rs 600, E Rs 500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define consumer surplus.
parts.answer: The difference between the maximum amount consumers are willing to pay for a good and the price they actually pay.
parts.working: 1 willingness to pay; 1 minus the market price (area below demand curve and above price).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tickets are priced at Rs 650. Calculate the total consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Rs 450

parts.label: c
parts.text: The organiser cuts the price to Rs 550. Calculate the new total consumer surplus.
parts.answer: Rs 800

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market, demand is P = 50 − 0.5Q and supply is P = 14 + 0.3Q, where P is in $ and Q in units. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium?
A $506.25
B $303.75
C $1,012.50
D $810.00

practice.stem: In the market for rooftop solar panels in Pakistan, demand is P = 120 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q, where P is in Rs thousand per panel and Q is in thousand panels per month. Cheaper imported panels then change supply to P = Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the consumer surplus and producer surplus before the change in supply.
parts.answer: CS = Rs 1,250 million; PS = Rs 1,250 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new consumer surplus and the change in consumer surplus.
parts.answer: New CS = Rs 1,800 million; increase of Rs 550 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: In this example producer surplus also rises. Explain why an increase in supply does not always raise producer surplus.
parts.answer: Price falls, which cuts surplus on units already sold; extra units add surplus. If demand is price inelastic, the price fall is large and PS can fall.
parts.working: 1 lower price reduces PS on existing output; 1 extra output and lower costs add PS; 1 net effect depends on PED / size of price fall (inelastic demand → PS may fall).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether an increase in demand for a product always benefits both consumers and producers. Use the concepts of consumer surplus and producer surplus in your answer.
parts.answer: Producers gain (higher price and output → PS rises). Consumers: total CS may rise or fall — existing buyers pay more, but more buyers enter; outcome depends on PES and the cause of the demand increase. Not always both.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Analysis: diagram with D shifting right; PS clearly rises (higher P and Q); CS: original buyers lose from higher price, new demand curve gives new CS triangle — with a parallel shift and elastic supply CS rises; with perfectly inelastic supply price rises and CS of original buyers falls. Consider cause: tastes (welfare of new buyers counts), population growth. Evaluation: depends on PES (time period, spare capacity), size of shift, whether a maximum price or monopoly exists; distribution between consumer groups; short run vs long run as supply responds. Judgement: producers almost always gain; consumers only sometimes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A supply curve is a straight line that passes through the origin. What is its price elasticity of supply?
A 0 at every price
B equal to 1 at every price
C greater than 1 at every price
D different at every point on the curve
parts.answer: B equal to 1 at every price
parts.working: Along a straight line from the origin, Q is proportional to P, so any percentage change in price gives the same percentage change in quantity: PES = 1. D is the common trap: the slope can differ between such lines but PES is still 1.

practice.stem: The wholesale price of chicken in Lahore rises from Rs 600 to Rs 690 per kg. Over the next fortnight the quantity supplied rises from 20,000 kg to 21,500 kg per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of supply of chicken.
parts.answer: PES = 0.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of chicken is price inelastic in the short run.
parts.answer: Any two explained: time needed to raise birds (several weeks); limited shed capacity; chicken is perishable, so stocks cannot be held; feed and chicks must be ordered in advance.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: reason identified + explained link to slow response of quantity supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define price elasticity of supply.
parts.answer: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price of the good: %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP.
parts.working: 1 responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price; 1 formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether the price elasticity of supply of manufactured goods is always greater than that of agricultural goods.
parts.answer: Usually yes in the short run (factories can add shifts, use stocks; crops have long growing periods and are perishable), but not always: factories at full capacity, complex goods like aircraft or chips have very inelastic supply, while some farm products (poultry, vegetables in greenhouses, stored grain) can respond quickly.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): factors – time to produce, spare capacity, stocks, factor mobility; manufacturing usually has stocks and spare capacity → elastic; agriculture has growing seasons, perishability, land constraints → inelastic. Evaluation (up to 2): counter-examples (full capacity, specialised inputs, semiconductors; stored wheat, fast-growing crops); depends on time period; judgement 'not always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the signalling, incentive and rationing functions of the price mechanism and consider how well these functions work in the market for rented housing in a fast-growing city such as Karachi.
parts.answer: Signalling: rising rents show scarcity. Incentive: higher rents encourage building and letting. Rationing: rents allocate flats to those willing and able to pay. In housing the functions work slowly because supply is inelastic, information is poor and the poor are priced out.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of the three functions. Analysis: increase in demand from migration → rents rise (signal) → landlords and developers have an incentive to build/convert property (extension of supply) → higher rents ration the existing stock. Evaluation: supply of housing is inelastic in the short run (land, planning permission, construction time); informal settlements and incomplete information; rationing by ability to pay leaves low-income families without decent housing, which may be inequitable; rent controls distort signals; judgement on 'how well'.
