parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer price index (2024 = 100) was 112.0 in 2025 and 120.4 in 2026. What was the rate of inflation in 2026?
A 7.0%
B 7.5%
C 8.4%
D 20.4%
parts.working: (120.4 − 112.0) ÷ 112.0 × 100 = 7.5%. C (8.4%) is the change in index points, not a percentage of the 2025 level; D measures the change since the base year.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a consumer price index:
Food: weight 40, price change +10%
Housing and utilities: weight 30, price change +5%
Transport: weight 20, price change +15%
Other items: weight 10, price change −2%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the price index at the end of the year (start of year = 100).
parts.working: M1 multiply each price change by its weight: 40 × 10, 30 × 5, 20 × 15, 10 × (−2). M1 sum = 830, ÷ 100 weights = 8.3. A1 index = 108.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why weights are used when calculating a consumer price index.
parts.answer: Households spend different shares of income on different items, so a price change in a large item (food) affects the cost of living more than one in a small item.
parts.working: 1 weights reflect share of household spending; 1 so the index measures change in cost of a typical basket accurately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define deflation.
parts.answer: A sustained fall in the general price level, so the rate of inflation is negative.
parts.working: 1 sustained/persistent fall; 1 in the general (average) price level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible consequences of deflation for an economy.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. consumers delay purchases expecting lower prices → lower AD and output; real value of debts rises → borrowers cut spending, more defaults; firms' revenues fall → wage cuts or job losses; exports become more price competitive.
parts.working: Up to 2 each: consequence identified + explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country the annual rate of inflation falls from 9% to 4%. Which statement must be correct?
A The general price level has fallen.
B The general price level is still rising, but more slowly.
C The purchasing power of money has risen.
D The economy is experiencing deflation.
parts.answer: B The general price level is still rising, but more slowly.
parts.working: Inflation of 4% is still a rise in the average price level, just a slower one (disinflation). A and D confuse falling inflation with falling prices; C is wrong because money still loses value, only more slowly.

practice.stem: Invented data. A factory worker in Faisalabad earned Rs 50,000 a month in 2025 and Rs 56,000 a month in 2026. The consumer price index rose from 100 in 2025 to 118 in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's money wage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the worker's real wage in 2026 at 2025 prices, to the nearest rupee, and the percentage change in the real wage.
parts.answer: Rs 47,458; a fall of 5.1%

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what has happened to the worker's standard of living.
parts.answer: It has fallen: prices rose by more than the money wage, so the wage buys about 5% fewer goods and services.
parts.working: 1 real wage/purchasing power fell; 1 because inflation (18%) exceeded the money wage rise (12%).

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
parts.answer: Demand-pull: AD shifts right faster than the economy's capacity grows → price level rises with higher real output. Cost-push: SRAS shifts left due to higher costs → price level rises while real output falls.
parts.working: 1 demand-pull: AD increases (e.g. consumer or government spending) as output nears full capacity; 1 diagram AD1→AD2, higher P and Y; 1 cost-push: higher costs (wages, imported raw materials) shift AS left; 1 diagram AS1→AS2, higher P and lower Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider which type of inflation is more likely in an oil-importing economy when the world price of crude oil rises by 40%.
parts.answer: Mainly cost-push: higher fuel and transport costs shift AS left. But demand-pull elements are possible if wages rise in response or the government expands spending; effect depends on oil's share of costs and the exchange rate.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): oil is an input for transport, electricity and manufacturing → costs rise → SRAS left → cost-push; import bill rises, which may reduce AD (more spending on imports), dampening demand-pull. Consideration (1+): second-round wage-price spiral; subsidies to fuel; currency movements; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a high rate of inflation is always more harmful to an economy than deflation.
parts.answer: Not always. High inflation erodes purchasing power, harms savers and fixed-income groups, reduces competitiveness and creates uncertainty; but persistent deflation can delay spending, raise real debt burdens and cause unemployment. Harm depends on the size, cause and whether it is anticipated.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Inflation costs: menu and shoe-leather costs, redistribution from savers/lenders to borrowers, fiscal drag, loss of international competitiveness, uncertainty discouraging investment, hyperinflation risk. Deflation costs: postponed consumption, rising real value of debt, falling profits → unemployment, real interest rates rise when nominal rates can't fall below zero, deflationary spiral. Evaluation: 'good' deflation from productivity gains (AS shift right) vs 'bad' deflation from falling AD; mild, anticipated inflation is less harmful than unanticipated high inflation; effects differ for different groups; the context (debt levels, indexation). Judgement must address 'always'.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country K:
Year: 2024, 2025, 2026
Inflation rate (%): 25, 12, 6
Central bank policy interest rate (%): 22, 18, 11

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price level at the end of 2026, taking the end of 2023 as 100. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using real interest rate ≈ nominal interest rate − inflation rate, calculate the real interest rate in 2024 and in 2026.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the fall in inflation from 2024 to 2026 shows that the economy is performing well.
parts.answer: It helps (more stable prices, real interest rates now positive, which protects savers and confidence), but prices are still rising, high real interest rates may cut investment, output and employment, so other indicators are needed.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): lower inflation reduces uncertainty, improves competitiveness, protects real incomes; prices still rose ~48% over the three years, so living costs remain much higher; positive real rate of 5% discourages borrowing → lower AD, growth and jobs. Consideration (1+): need data on growth, unemployment, current account; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, consumption is $600bn, investment $150bn, government spending $200bn, exports $250bn and imports $300bn. What is aggregate demand?
A $600bn
B $900bn
C $1,200bn
D $1,500bn
parts.answer: B $900bn
parts.working: AD = C + I + G + (X − M) = 600 + 150 + 200 + (250 − 300) = $900bn. D adds imports instead of subtracting them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the aggregate demand curve slopes downwards from left to right.
parts.answer: A lower price level raises real wealth (real balance effect), lowers interest rates (more borrowing and spending) and makes exports cheaper relative to imports, so real expenditure rises.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained effects: wealth/real balance effect; interest rate effect; international trade (competitiveness) effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two causes of a rightward shift of the long-run aggregate supply curve.
parts.answer: Any two: more or better-quality labour (migration, education, training); more capital (investment); new technology; discovery of natural resources; supply-side reforms raising productivity.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the effect of a fall in consumer confidence on the price level and real output.
parts.answer: Households spend less and save more → consumption falls → AD shifts left → lower price level and lower real output.
parts.working: 1 consumption falls; 1 AD shifts left (diagram with labelled axes); 1 price level falls (or rises more slowly); 1 real output falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two components of aggregate demand other than consumption.
parts.answer: Any two: investment; government spending; net exports (exports minus imports).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would shift the short-run aggregate supply curve to the left?
A a rise in consumer confidence
B a fall in the world price of oil
C a rise in money wage rates with no change in productivity
D a cut in the rate of income tax
parts.answer: C a rise in money wage rates with no change in productivity
parts.working: Higher wages without higher productivity raise unit labour costs, so firms supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left. A and D shift AD, not SRAS; B lowers costs and shifts SRAS to the right.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country Q, $bn at constant prices:
2025: C 420, I 95, G 130, X 160, M 175
2026: C 438, I 88, G 150, X 172, M 186

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate aggregate demand in 2025 and 2026 and the percentage change. Give the percentage to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the component whose change made the largest contribution to the change in AD.
parts.answer: Government spending (+$20bn).

parts.label: c
parts.text: With the help of an AD/AS diagram, explain the likely effect of this change in AD on the price level and real output.
parts.answer: AD shifts right: real output rises and the price level rises; the split depends on spare capacity (flat section → mainly output, near full capacity → mainly prices).
parts.working: 1 AD shifts right (diagram labelled price level and real output/real GDP); 1 real output rises; 1 price level rises; 1 relative size depends on how close the economy is to full capacity / shape of AS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a large rise in world oil prices shifts the short-run aggregate supply curve of an oil-importing economy.
parts.answer: Oil is a key input in transport, power and manufacturing, so firms' costs of production rise and they supply less at each price level: SRAS shifts left.
parts.working: 1 higher costs of production; 1 SRAS shifts left (upwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether a large rise in world oil prices is likely to reduce real output more than it raises the price level in an oil-importing economy.
parts.answer: Both effects occur (stagflation). Which is larger depends on the slope of AD and AS, whether AD also falls as the import bill rises, policy responses and how long the shock lasts.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): SRAS left → higher price level and lower real output; AD may also fall because spending leaks to imports and real incomes fall → output falls further while dampening the price rise; if AD is steep/inelastic, effect is mainly on price; second-round wage rises push prices further. Evaluation (up to 2): depends on oil intensity, fuel subsidies, monetary policy response (rate rises cut output more), exchange rate, whether the shock is temporary; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in investment affects both aggregate demand and aggregate supply, and consider whether its effect on the price level is likely to be inflationary.
parts.answer: Investment is a component of AD (short run: AD right) and adds to productive capacity (long run: LRAS right). Price level rises in the short run but may be stable or fall in the long run if capacity rises enough.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: investment as spending on capital goods; AD = C + I + G + (X − M); LRAS/capacity. Analysis: higher I → AD shifts right → higher price level and output (with multiplier); new capital raises productivity → LRAS shifts right → lower price level, higher output. Evaluation: timing (AD effect immediate, AS effect delayed); type of investment (replacement vs new capacity); spare capacity; size of the shifts; judgement on whether net effect is inflationary.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's nominal GDP rises from $800bn to $880bn in a year. Over the same year the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 106. What is the rate of real economic growth, correct to one decimal place?
A 3.8%
B 4.0%
C 10.0%
D 16.6%
parts.working: Real GDP = 880 ÷ 1.06 = $830.2bn (at last year's prices); (830.2 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = 3.8%. B uses the shortcut 10% − 6%, which is only an approximation and is not correct to one decimal place; C is nominal growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between actual economic growth and potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Actual growth: an increase in real GDP (output actually produced). Potential growth: an increase in the economy's productive capacity (LRAS/PPC shifts out).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how more spending on education can lead to potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Education raises skills and the productivity of labour, increasing the quality of the factor labour; the productive capacity of the economy rises, shifting LRAS (or the PPC) outward.
parts.working: 1 better skills/human capital; 1 higher labour productivity; 1 LRAS or PPC shifts right/outward (over time).

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country R:
Year: 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026
Real GDP ($bn): 300, 309, 315, 330
Population (million): 200, 204, 208, 212

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth in 2026. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head between 2023 and 2026. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rise in real GDP per head may overstate the improvement in living standards.
parts.answer: Average figure hides inequality; ignores pollution, longer working hours and loss of leisure; output may be military or exports rather than consumer goods; informal economy changes; quality of life measures like health are excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one cause of actual economic growth that comes from the demand side of the economy.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in consumer spending or exports increases AD; if there is spare capacity, firms raise output so real GDP grows.
parts.working: 1 demand-side cause; 1 explained link to higher real output when spare capacity exists.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether an increase in government spending on roads and electricity grids will lead to sustained economic growth.
parts.answer: Short run: AD rises (actual growth); long run: lower transport and energy costs raise productivity, shifting LRAS → potential growth. Sustained only if projects are well chosen, completed and maintained, and financed without crowding out or debt problems.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): AD effect with multiplier; supply-side effect on productivity and capacity; attracts investment. Consideration (1+): time lags, poor project choice/corruption, borrowing costs, maintenance; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the benefits of economic growth always outweigh its costs for a developing economy such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Growth brings higher incomes, jobs, tax revenue for health and education and less poverty; costs include pollution, depletion of resources, inequality, inflation and current-account pressures. Benefits usually outweigh costs for a low-income country, but not always: it depends on the type, sustainability and distribution of growth.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): Level 3 (9–12) accurate, well-developed analysis of both sides with a diagram where relevant and a justified judgement that answers the question; Level 2 (5–8) sound but partly undeveloped analysis, or evaluation that is asserted; Level 1 (1–4) descriptive points with little analysis. A one-sided answer cannot reach Level 3. Benefits: higher real incomes and living standards, lower unemployment, more tax revenue without higher tax rates, reduced poverty. Costs: environmental damage (smog, water stress), resource depletion, rising inequality, inflation if AD outruns capacity, import surge and current-account deficits (boom–bust cycles), urban congestion. Evaluation: growth led by consumption/imports vs by investment/exports; whether gains reach the poor; opportunity cost of investment (less consumption now); sustainability; policy can reduce costs. Judgement must address 'always'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a labour force of 64 million, of whom 59.2 million are employed. What is the unemployment rate?
A 4.8%
B 7.5%
C 8.1%
D 92.5%
parts.working: Unemployed = 64 − 59.2 = 4.8 million. Rate = 4.8 ÷ 64 × 100 = 7.5%. C divides by the number employed instead of the labour force; D is the employment rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the type of unemployment in each case:
(1) Weavers in Faisalabad lose their jobs when mills install automatic looms.
(2) A new graduate spends three months searching for a suitable job.
(3) Construction workers are laid off when spending falls during a recession.
parts.answer: (1) structural (technological); (2) frictional; (3) cyclical (demand-deficient)
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one consequence of high unemployment for the government's budget.
parts.answer: Tax revenue falls (less income tax and spending taxes) and spending on benefits/support rises, so the budget deficit increases.
parts.working: 1 lower tax revenue or higher welfare spending; 1 budget deficit increases / borrowing rises.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country S: working-age population 120 million; labour force 78 million; unemployed according to the labour force survey 5.46 million; people claiming unemployment benefits 3.12 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate shown by each measure.
parts.answer: Labour force survey: 7%; claimant count: 4%
parts.working: 1 5.46 ÷ 78 × 100 = 7%; 1 3.12 ÷ 78 × 100 = 4%. (Use the labour force, not the working-age population.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the claimant count measure is lower than the labour force survey measure.
parts.answer: Some unemployed people are not eligible for benefits (e.g. partner's income, recently left education, informal workers); some choose not to claim (stigma, small benefit, don't know how); the survey uses the international definition (looking for work and available).
parts.working: Up to 2 each: reason identified + explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a recession causes cyclical unemployment.
parts.answer: Falling AD means firms sell less, so they need fewer workers (labour is a derived demand) and cut jobs.
parts.working: 1 fall in AD/output; 1 lower derived demand for labour → job losses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether structural unemployment is more harmful than cyclical unemployment to an economy.
parts.answer: Structural unemployment is often longer lasting and concentrated in regions/industries; skills become obsolete and it does not disappear when the economy recovers. Cyclical unemployment can be widespread and severe but usually falls as AD recovers. Judgement depends on scale, duration and policy response.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): structural – mismatch of skills/location, long duration, hysteresis, regional decline, needs costly retraining; cyclical – affects many sectors, lost output across the economy, falling AD can deepen recession, but responds to fiscal/monetary policy. Evaluation (up to 2): a deep recession can turn cyclical into long-term unemployment; structural change also brings efficiency gains; depends on labour mobility and retraining; judgement.

practice.stem:
Invented data for an open economy, $bn per year:
Investment 120, Government spending 200, Exports 180
Saving 100, Taxation 210, Imports 220

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total injections and the total withdrawals.
parts.answer: Injections $500bn; withdrawals $530bn

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what will happen to the level of national income.
parts.answer: Withdrawals exceed injections by $30bn, so less is spent on domestic output than is earned; national income will fall until withdrawals equal injections.
parts.working: 1 W > I so spending in the flow falls; 1 national income falls to a new equilibrium where injections = withdrawals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two main flows between households and firms in the circular flow.
parts.answer: Households supply factor services and receive factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit); households spend on goods and services, which is revenue for firms.
parts.working: 1 factor incomes from firms to households; 1 consumer spending from households to firms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the circular flow of income, which is an injection?
A income tax paid by households
B spending on imported goods
C spending by foreigners on a country's exports
D money saved by households in banks
parts.answer: C spending by foreigners on a country's exports
parts.working: Injections are investment, government spending and exports – spending that enters the flow from outside the household–firm loop. A, B and D are withdrawals (taxation, imports and saving).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government sector, and consider whether an increase in spending on imports will always reduce national income.
parts.answer: Households and firms exchange factor services and spending; saving, taxes and imports leak out; investment, government spending and exports are injected. More imports are a withdrawal and reduce national income unless offset by higher injections (e.g. imported capital raising investment and exports, or rising exports).
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: households, firms, government, foreign sector; injections (I, G, X) and withdrawals (S, T, M); equilibrium where I + G + X = S + T + M. Analysis: higher M → greater withdrawal → spending on domestic output falls → national income falls (multiplier). Evaluation: imports of capital goods and raw materials may raise investment and export capacity; foreigners may spend their earnings on the country's exports; if imports replace saving rather than domestic consumption, effect differs; judgement on 'always'.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country T, $bn:
GDP at market prices: 350
Primary income (profits, interest, dividends) received from abroad: 12
Primary income paid to foreign owners: 20
Capital consumption (depreciation): 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate gross national income (GNI).
parts.working: M1 GNI = GDP + primary income from abroad − primary income paid abroad = 350 + 12 − 20. A1 $342bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate net national income (NNI).
parts.working: M1 NNI = GNI − capital consumption (depreciation) = 342 − 30. A1 $312bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why GNI may be lower than GDP for a country where many firms are foreign-owned.
parts.answer: Profits and interest earned by foreign owners from production in the country are counted in GDP but paid abroad, so they are subtracted to give GNI.
parts.working: 1 foreign-owned firms send profits/dividends abroad; 1 these are primary income outflows deducted from GDP.

practice.stem: Invented data for Country U: GDP at market prices $500bn; indirect taxes on spending $60bn; subsidies on products $15bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate GDP at basic prices.
parts.working: M1 GDP at basic prices = GDP at market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies = 500 − 60 + 15. A1 $455bn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the output, income and expenditure methods of measuring GDP should give the same total.
parts.answer: The value of output produced is either spent (expenditure) and the revenue from it is paid out as factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) to those who produced it, so all three measure the same flow.
parts.working: 1 output is sold/spent (output = expenditure, counting changes in inventories); 1 the money received is paid as incomes to factors; 1 so the three measure the same circular flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the three totals differ in practice.
parts.answer: Statistical discrepancy: errors and omissions, hidden/informal economy, different data sources and timing.
parts.working: 1 any valid reason.

practice.stem:
Invented data for Country V:
2020: nominal GDP Rs 50 trillion, GDP deflator 100, population 220 million
2026: nominal GDP Rs 105 trillion, GDP deflator 190, population 245 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in 2026 at 2020 prices, in Rs trillion, to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Rs 55.3 trillion
parts.working: M1 real GDP = nominal ÷ (deflator ÷ 100) = 105 ÷ 1.9. A1 Rs 55.3 trillion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head between 2020 and 2026, to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 2020: 50 trillion ÷ 220 million = Rs 227,273; M1 2026: 55.26 trillion ÷ 245 million = Rs 225,564. A1 -0.8% (a small fall, although real GDP rose by 10.5%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why economists use real GDP per head rather than nominal GDP when comparing living standards over time.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP rises with inflation even if output does not; real GDP removes price changes. Dividing by population shows the average output per person, as a growing population shares the output.
parts.working: 1 real removes the effect of inflation; 1 per head allows for population growth.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is an expenditure-switching policy to reduce a current account deficit?
A a devaluation of the country's currency
B an increase in income tax rates
C a cut in government spending on public services
D a rise in interest rates to reduce consumer spending
parts.answer: A a devaluation of the country's currency
parts.working: A devaluation makes imports dearer and exports cheaper, switching spending by both residents and foreigners towards domestically produced goods. B, C and D are expenditure-reducing: they cut total spending, including spending on imports.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: A North African country has a current account deficit equal to 5 % of its GDP, mainly because of high imports of consumer goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two expenditure-reducing policies a government could use to reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Any two of: higher income tax or sales tax; lower government spending; higher interest rates; a reduction in the money supply/credit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two (contractionary fiscal or monetary measures).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a fall in national income is likely to reduce spending on imports.
parts.answer: With lower incomes households and firms spend less in total, and part of every unit of spending goes on imports (the marginal propensity to import), so imports fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower income → lower total spending/consumption; 1 mark: some of that spending is on imported goods (imports depend on income, normal goods), so import spending falls.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A South Asian country's imports of mobile phones rose to US$2.1 billion last year. Its current account deficit is 3.8 % of GDP. The government proposes a 25 % tariff on imported phones. Most local phone factories assemble phones from imported parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies.
parts.answer: Expenditure-switching policies change the relative price or availability of imports and domestic goods so spending moves towards domestic output (e.g. tariffs, devaluation); expenditure-reducing policies lower total spending in the economy, which reduces spending on imports (e.g. higher taxes or interest rates).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly explained type (with or without an example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether the proposed tariff on mobile phones is likely to reduce the current account deficit.
parts.answer: It may reduce imports of phones if demand is price elastic and domestic substitutes exist, but if demand is inelastic and there are no local producers, spending on imports may fall only a little; retaliation and higher costs for businesses may also reduce exports.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: tariff raises the domestic price of imported phones → quantity of imports falls; switch to domestic assemblers; tariff revenue. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: effect depends on PED for phones (likely inelastic for a necessity), availability of domestic substitutes (domestic phones may use imported parts), retaliation against exports, smuggling, and it treats a symptom not the cause (low competitiveness).

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in interest rates could reduce a current account deficit, and consider the possible costs of this policy for the domestic economy.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates reduce consumption and investment, so national income and spending on imports fall (expenditure-reducing); costs include lower growth and higher unemployment, and an appreciation that may hurt exporters.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: current account deficit; expenditure-reducing policy; meaning of interest rate rise. Analysis: higher cost of borrowing and reward for saving → lower C and I → lower national income → lower spending on imports; lower inflation may improve competitiveness over time. Evaluation: costs — slower growth, higher unemployment, lower investment reduces future capacity; inflows of hot money may cause appreciation, making exports less competitive and partly offsetting the effect; heavy cost for indebted households and firms; judgement on whether the cost is worth paying.

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): Before a 10 % devaluation, a country's exports were worth US$30 billion and its imports US$45 billion a year, both priced in US dollars. In the first year after the devaluation, the US dollar price of its exports fell by 10 % and export volumes rose by 4 %. The US dollar price of its imports was unchanged and import volumes fell by 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the export earnings and import spending, in US$ billion, one year after the devaluation, and state whether the trade deficit has become larger or smaller. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Exports US$28.08 bn; imports US$43.65 bn; the deficit rises from US$15.00 bn to US$15.57 bn, so it becomes larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the trade deficit might become smaller over a longer period after the devaluation.
parts.answer: In the short run demand for exports and imports is price inelastic because contracts are fixed and buyers take time to find substitutes; over time demand becomes more elastic, export volumes rise more and import volumes fall more, so earnings rise and the deficit falls (a J-curve pattern).
parts.working: 1 mark: short-run demand is inelastic (contracts, habits, lack of substitutes); 1 mark: over time PED for exports and imports rises as buyers adjust; 1 mark: when the combined responsiveness is large enough, export earnings rise relative to import spending and the deficit narrows (J-curve).

practice.subtopic: Policies to correct current account imbalances

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether expenditure-switching policies are more effective than expenditure-reducing policies in correcting a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Expenditure-switching avoids a deliberate fall in national income and targets competitiveness, but depends on price elasticities, retaliation and inflation; expenditure-reducing policies work more reliably on imports but at the cost of lower growth and higher unemployment. The more effective choice depends on the cause of the deficit.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: switching (devaluation, tariffs, quotas, export subsidies) changes relative prices so domestic and foreign buyers move to domestic goods; reducing (contractionary fiscal and monetary policy) lowers income and therefore imports; diagrams of AD shifts where useful. Evaluation: switching may fail if demand for imports and exports is price inelastic, if devaluation raises import costs and inflation, or if tariffs bring retaliation/break trade agreements; reducing works whatever the elasticities but creates unemployment and may harm investment; if the deficit is due to excess demand, reducing is appropriate; if due to low competitiveness, switching plus supply-side policy is better; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would most likely cause a country's floating exchange rate to appreciate?
A a rise in its interest rates relative to those in other countries
B a rise in its inflation rate relative to that in other countries
C an increase in its residents' demand for imported goods
D an outflow of investment funds to other countries
parts.answer: A a rise in its interest rates relative to those in other countries
parts.working: Higher relative interest rates attract financial inflows, raising demand for the currency, so it appreciates. B, C and D each raise the supply of the currency or reduce demand for it, causing depreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate and a fixed exchange rate.
parts.answer: A floating rate is determined by the demand for and supply of the currency in the foreign exchange market with no government target; a fixed rate is set by the government or central bank at a chosen value and maintained by intervention (buying/selling currency, interest rates).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a large increase in the number of foreign tourists visiting Thailand would affect the value of the Thai baht in a floating exchange rate system.
parts.answer: Tourists must buy baht to pay for hotels and services, so demand for the baht rises; the demand curve shifts to the right while supply is unchanged; the equilibrium exchange rate rises, so the baht appreciates (and the quantity traded increases).
parts.working: 1 mark: tourists need baht → demand for baht increases; 1 mark: demand curve shifts right (axes: price of baht in foreign currency, quantity of baht); 1 mark: excess demand at the old rate; 1 mark: new higher equilibrium rate — appreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The exchange rate changes from US$1 = PKR 280 to US$1 = PKR 300. A Pakistani exporter keeps the rupee price of a shirt at PKR 4200. What has happened?
A The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
B The rupee has appreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
C The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has risen from $14.00 to $15.00.
D The rupee has appreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has risen from $14.00 to $15.00.
parts.answer: A The rupee has depreciated and the US dollar price of the shirt has fallen from $15.00 to $14.00.
parts.working: More rupees are needed to buy one dollar, so the rupee has depreciated. Dollar price = 4200 ÷ 280 = $15.00 before and 4200 ÷ 300 = $14.00 after. B gives the right prices but the wrong direction for the rupee.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a managed float exchange rate system works, and consider whether it is better than a fixed exchange rate for a small open economy.
parts.answer: In a managed float, market forces set the rate but the central bank intervenes (buying or selling currency, changing interest rates) to limit large or unwanted movements. It combines some flexibility with some stability, but needs reserves and may lack credibility; a fixed rate gives more certainty but removes an adjustment tool.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of managed float and fixed exchange rate; tools of intervention (foreign currency reserves, interest rates). Analysis: if the currency falls too fast, the central bank sells foreign currency and buys domestic currency, raising demand (diagram); it can let the rate adjust gradually to shocks, helping the current account; under a fixed rate the government must defend the peg whatever happens. Evaluation: for a small open economy heavily dependent on trade, stability of a fixed rate helps traders and controls imported inflation, but defending it can exhaust reserves and requires interest rates to follow the anchor country; a managed float keeps monetary independence but may cause uncertainty and speculative pressure; judgement.

practice.stem:
Table 7: Exchange rate of the Country Q dollar (data invented for practice)
January: US$1 = 160 Q-dollars
December: US$1 = 184 Q-dollars

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the value of the Country Q dollar measured in US dollars between January and December. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: −13.0 % (a depreciation of about 13.0 %)
parts.working: M1: value of one Q-dollar in US$ = 1 ÷ 160 = 0.006250 in January and 1 ÷ 184 = 0.005435 in December. A1: (0.005435 − 0.006250) ÷ 0.006250 × 100 = −13.0 %. (The 15 % rise in Q-dollars per US$ is not the same as a 15 % fall in the Q-dollar.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider how the change in the exchange rate is likely to affect inflation in Country Q.
parts.answer: Inflation is likely to rise: imported goods, fuel and raw materials cost more in Q-dollars (cost-push), and cheaper exports raise net exports and AD (demand-pull). The size depends on the import content of consumption, how much firms pass on and whether the depreciation is expected to last.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: higher domestic price of imported consumer goods → CPI rises directly; dearer imported inputs → higher costs → AS shifts left (cost-push); exports become cheaper abroad → higher net exports → AD rises (demand-pull); possible wage-price spiral. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: effect depends on the share of imports in spending, PED for imports, profit margins absorbing costs, contracts priced earlier, and the central bank's response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a depreciation of a country's currency is always beneficial for its economy.
parts.answer: No: a depreciation can raise exports, output and employment and help a current account deficit, but it also raises import prices and inflation, increases the burden of foreign-currency debt and reduces living standards; its benefits depend on elasticities, spare capacity and the cause of the fall.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home → net exports and AD rise → growth and jobs (AD/AS); current account may improve if demand is price elastic enough; competitiveness improves. Costs: imported inflation, higher costs for firms using imported inputs, lower real incomes, larger burden of debt in foreign currency, possible capital flight. Evaluation: depends on price elasticities (short-run J-curve), spare capacity, import content of exports, size of foreign debt, whether trading partners are growing, and whether the depreciation is gradual or a sudden crisis; 'always' is too strong; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms of trade.
parts.answer: The ratio of a country's index of export prices to its index of import prices, multiplied by 100.
parts.working: 1 mark: export price index ÷ import price index × 100 (or the quantity of imports that a unit of exports can buy).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for the year when the export price index is 108 and the import price index is 90.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what this index value shows about the country's position compared with the base year.
parts.answer: The terms of trade have improved by 20 %: each unit of exports now buys 20 % more imports than in the base year.
parts.working: 1 mark: an improvement (index above 100); 1 mark: a given quantity of exports pays for more imports.

practice.stem:
Table 8: Price indices for Country C, a cocoa exporter (2023 = 100; data invented for practice)
2023: export prices 100, import prices 100
2024: export prices 120, import prices 105
2025: export prices 96, import prices 112
Extract: After a record harvest in other producing countries, world cocoa prices fell sharply in 2025. Country C imports most of its fuel and machinery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for 2024 and 2025. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the extract, explain one likely cause of the change in the terms of trade between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: The world price of cocoa, the main export, fell (export prices index from 120 to 96) while import prices of fuel and machinery kept rising, so the terms of trade deteriorated.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the fall in export prices (cocoa) and/or rise in import prices; 1 mark: links this to the fall in the index from 114.3 to 85.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Over a year, a country's index of export prices rises from 100 to 110 and its index of import prices rises from 100 to 125. What is its terms of trade index at the end of the year?
A 88.0
B 113.6
C 115.0
D 85.0
parts.working: Terms of trade = (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100 = 110 ÷ 125 × 100 = 88.0: a deterioration. B inverts the ratio (125 ÷ 110 × 100).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large rise in world oil prices would affect the terms of trade of an oil-importing country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Oil is a large part of its imports, so the import price index rises relative to the export price index and the terms of trade deteriorate (fall).
parts.working: 1 mark: import prices rise; 1 mark: index falls/deteriorates (each unit of exports buys fewer imports).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether this change in the terms of trade will reduce living standards in the country.
parts.answer: Likely yes in the short run: more exports are needed to pay for the same imports, real incomes fall, fuel and transport costs raise inflation and the current account deficit widens; the effect may be smaller if demand shifts to other energy sources, if the price rise is temporary, or if export prices also rise.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: deterioration means more resources must be exported to buy the same oil; higher import bill → current account worsens/currency may depreciate; higher fuel prices → cost-push inflation → real incomes fall; firms' costs rise → output and jobs may fall. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: depends on PED for oil (inelastic → larger import bill), duration of the shock, government subsidies, rising remittances from oil-exporting Gulf countries, and whether export prices rise too.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): A garment-exporting country lowered its export prices to win orders. Between 2024 and 2025 its export price index fell from 100 to 95, its import price index rose from 100 to 104, and the volume of its exports rose by 15 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terms of trade index for 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the value of the country's export earnings between 2024 and 2025. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: value index = price index × volume index ÷ 100 = 95 × 115 ÷ 100 = 109.25. A1: export earnings rose by 9.25 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the deterioration in the terms of trade is harmful to this country.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: export prices fell, but because demand for its exports is price elastic, export volumes rose by more and export earnings rose; the fall in the terms of trade may reflect greater competitiveness. It would be harmful if caused by rising import prices or falling world demand.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: a deterioration means each unit of exports buys fewer imports; but the cause matters — here export prices fell as firms became more competitive and volumes rose 15 %, so earnings rose (calculation), helping output, jobs and the current account; if import prices rise (e.g. oil), real income falls. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on the cause of the change, PED for exports and imports, the import bill (import prices rose 4 %), whether the gain is sustained; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a country that depends on exporting primary products will always benefit from a rise in world commodity prices.
parts.answer: A rise in commodity prices improves its terms of trade and usually raises export earnings, incomes and government revenue, but benefits may be temporary, unevenly shared and may cause appreciation that harms other exporters; it does not always benefit.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: higher export prices → terms of trade improve → more imports per unit of exports; export revenue rises if demand is price inelastic; current account improves; higher incomes, employment and tax revenue (royalties) → growth; supply of exports may expand. Evaluation: the gain depends on whether the price rise reflects higher world demand or a supply shortage at home (poor harvest — lower volumes); commodity prices are volatile, so dependence increases instability; currency appreciation can harm manufacturing and tourism; revenue may go to a few firms or MNCs; rising import prices may offset; it may discourage diversification; justified conclusion on 'always'.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage, and consider whether free trade benefits all countries.
parts.answer: Absolute advantage is producing more of a good with the same resources; comparative advantage is producing at a lower opportunity cost. Trade based on comparative advantage can raise total output and welfare, but not every country or group gains equally.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of absolute and comparative advantage, opportunity cost, free trade. Analysis: a numerical or worked example showing that specialisation by comparative advantage raises total world output even when one country has absolute advantage in both goods; gains shared through the terms of trade; consumers gain from lower prices and more choice. Evaluation: gains depend on the terms of trade, transport costs and factor mobility; some industries and workers lose jobs; countries specialising in primary products face volatile prices; infant industries may never develop; benefits are not automatic for all; judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text:
One worker in Country X can produce either 10 tonnes of rice or 5 units of cloth. One worker in Country Y can produce either 6 tonnes of rice or 4 units of cloth. Which statement is correct?
A Country X has an absolute advantage in both goods, but Country Y has a comparative advantage in cloth.
B Country X has a comparative advantage in both goods.
C Country Y has a comparative advantage in rice.
D Neither country can gain from trade because Country X is more efficient at producing both goods.
parts.answer: A Country X has an absolute advantage in both goods, but Country Y has a comparative advantage in cloth.
parts.working: X produces more of both goods per worker (absolute advantage in both). Opportunity cost of 1 unit of cloth: X = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 tonnes of rice; Y = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 tonnes of rice. Y gives up less rice, so it has the comparative advantage in cloth (and X in rice). D ignores that gains come from differences in opportunity cost.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage
practice.stem:
Table 9: Output per worker per week (data invented for practice)
Country A: 8 tonnes of wheat or 24 units of textiles
Country B: 6 tonnes of wheat or 12 units of textiles

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of wheat in each country.
parts.answer: Country A: 3 units of textiles; Country B: 2 units of textiles.
parts.working: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 textiles (1); 12 ÷ 6 = 2 textiles (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which good each country should specialise in. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Country B should specialise in wheat (lower opportunity cost: 2 textiles vs 3); Country A should specialise in textiles (opportunity cost 1/3 tonne of wheat vs 1/2 in B).
parts.working: 1 mark: B wheat, A textiles; 1 mark: justified by lower opportunity cost (comparative advantage).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a rate of exchange of textiles for wheat at which both countries could gain from trade.
parts.answer: Any rate strictly between 2 and 3 units of textiles per tonne of wheat, e.g. 2.5 units of textiles for 1 tonne of wheat.
parts.working: 1 mark: a rate between the two opportunity cost ratios (2 < rate < 3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one reason why the gains from specialisation might be smaller in practice than the theory suggests.
parts.answer: For example, transport costs may use up the gain; or factors are not perfectly mobile between industries, so workers cannot easily move from wheat to textiles; or opportunity costs rise as production expands (increasing costs).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a valid limitation (transport costs, factor immobility, increasing costs, trade barriers, exchange rates); 1 mark: explains how it reduces the gain.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for trade and comparative advantage

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether specialising according to comparative advantage is the best trade strategy for a low-income country.
parts.answer: Specialisation by comparative advantage raises efficiency and income in the short run, but a low-income country's current comparative advantage is often in primary products with volatile prices and falling terms of trade; diversification and developing new advantages may be better long-run strategies.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: comparative advantage theory; gains from specialisation and trade (higher output, economies of scale, foreign currency earnings, access to imported capital goods); compare with alternatives such as diversification, protection of infant industries, regional trade agreements. Evaluation: risks of over-specialisation (price volatility, weather, exhaustion of resources, deteriorating terms of trade); comparative advantage can change over time through investment in skills and technology (dynamic comparative advantage); protection may lead to inefficiency and retaliation; examples (e.g. garment exports, cocoa, copper); justified conclusion on 'best'.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which transaction is recorded as a credit in the secondary income section of Pakistan's current account?
A money sent home by Pakistani workers employed in Saudi Arabia
B profits sent abroad by a foreign-owned car factory in Pakistan
C a foreign company building a new factory in Pakistan
D rice exported from Pakistan to China
parts.answer: A money sent home by Pakistani workers employed in Saudi Arabia
parts.working: Workers' remittances are current transfers and are recorded in secondary income. B is primary income (a debit), C is foreign direct investment (financial account), D is trade in goods.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four components of the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a country might have a large surplus on its current account.
parts.answer: For example: strong international competitiveness (high productivity, quality, low costs) so exports far exceed imports; high domestic saving and low consumption, so spending on imports is low; an undervalued exchange rate; large exports of a high-priced commodity such as oil.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for explaining how it raises exports relative to imports (or income inflows relative to outflows).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem:
Table 10: Current account of Country N, 2025 (US$ billion; data invented for practice)
Trade in goods: −27.5
Trade in services: −2.9
Primary income: −8.1
Secondary income: +31.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance for 2025.
parts.answer: A deficit of US$7.3 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a current account deficit of this kind is a problem for the country.
parts.answer: It may be: it must be financed by borrowing or by selling assets, and the large deficit on goods shows weak competitiveness. But the deficit is small relative to the trade gap because of large remittances, and if imports are capital goods it may support future growth.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: the deficit must be financed through the financial account (borrowing, running down reserves, FDI); persistent deficits may lead to depreciation and higher debt; large goods deficit suggests low competitiveness and reliance on remittances; primary income deficit reflects interest and profit payments abroad. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: depends on the size relative to GDP, how it is financed (FDI vs short-term loans), what is imported (capital goods vs consumer goods), and whether remittances are stable.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a persistent current account deficit is always harmful to an economy.
parts.answer: Not always: a deficit financed by long-term FDI and used to import capital goods can raise future growth, but a persistent deficit financed by short-term borrowing or reserves can lead to debt problems, currency crises and loss of jobs in import-competing industries.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: meaning of a current account deficit and how it is financed (financial account); harms: lower AD (net exports negative), job losses in exporting and import-competing industries, rising foreign debt and interest payments (primary income outflows), pressure on the exchange rate, loss of reserves, possible need for contractionary policy. Possible benefits: imports of capital goods raise productivity; consumers enjoy higher living standards; deficit may reflect strong growth and inward investment. Evaluation: depends on size relative to GDP, cause (strong demand vs weak competitiveness), type of financing, what is imported, and the exchange rate system; justified conclusion on 'always'.

practice.stem: A Central Asian government is considering whether to protect its new solar-panel industry from imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a tariff and an import quota.
parts.answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, raising their price; a quota is a physical limit on the quantity (or value) of a good that may be imported.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the infant industry argument for protection.
parts.answer: A new domestic industry has high average costs because it cannot yet benefit from economies of scale or experience, so it cannot compete with established foreign firms; temporary protection lets it grow until it becomes competitive.
parts.working: 1 mark: new firms have high costs/lack economies of scale and experience; 1 mark: temporary protection until it can compete, after which it is removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The world price of a good is $200 and a country can import any quantity at this price. Before a tariff, domestic demand is 70 000 units and domestic supply is 20 000 units. The government imposes a 15 % tariff. Domestic demand falls to 64 000 units and domestic supply rises to 26 000 units. What is the government's tariff revenue?
A $1 140 000
B $1 500 000
C $1 920 000
D $780 000
parts.working: Tariff per unit = 15 % × $200 = $30. Imports after the tariff = 64 000 − 26 000 = 38 000 units. Revenue = 38 000 × $30 = $1,140,000. B uses the imports before the tariff (50 000).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an import quota affects domestic consumers and domestic producers of a good, and consider whether the gains to producers are greater than the losses to consumers.
parts.answer: A quota reduces supply in the domestic market, so price rises; producers sell more at a higher price and gain producer surplus, but consumers pay more and buy less, losing consumer surplus. Consumer losses exceed producer gains because of deadweight losses, and unlike a tariff no revenue goes to the government (the quota rent goes to licence holders).
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definition of quota; consumer and producer surplus. Analysis: diagram with world price, domestic demand and supply; quota limits imports so domestic price rises above world price; domestic output rises, consumption falls; producer surplus increases, consumer surplus falls; quota rent to importers/foreign exporters; two deadweight loss triangles (production inefficiency and lost consumption). Evaluation: in standard analysis consumers lose more than producers gain; but there may be wider benefits — jobs saved, strategic industry — and the size depends on elasticities and the quota level; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether protectionism is justified to protect jobs in a developing country's car industry.
parts.answer: Protection may save jobs in the short run and allow the industry to develop, but it raises prices for consumers and firms, protects inefficiency, invites retaliation and may cost jobs elsewhere; it is justified only if temporary and linked to a credible plan to become competitive.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: tariffs/quotas raise import prices → demand shifts to domestically produced cars → output and employment rise in the car industry and its suppliers; infant industry and strategic arguments; tariff revenue. Costs: higher prices for consumers and businesses using vehicles; lower consumer surplus and deadweight loss; reduced incentive to cut costs; retaliation against the country's exports may cost jobs elsewhere; breaches of trade agreements. Evaluation: whether protection is temporary and conditional on productivity gains; size of the domestic market (economies of scale); alternatives such as training or attracting FDI; experiences of protected car industries that stayed uncompetitive; justified conclusion.
