parts.label: a
parts.text: A city government sets a maximum monthly rent for flats that is below the market equilibrium rent. Explain why this causes a shortage of rented flats.
parts.answer: At the lower rent, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls, so demand exceeds supply.
parts.working: 1 mark: maximum rent is below equilibrium so it is binding. 1 mark: more households want to rent at the lower price (extension of demand). 1 mark: landlords supply fewer flats as returns fall (contraction of supply), e.g. convert them to offices or sell them – excess demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an illegal (shadow) market may develop for rented flats.
parts.answer: Because some tenants are willing to pay more than the legal maximum, landlords can charge extra payments secretly.
parts.working: 1 mark: at the quantity supplied, tenants' willingness to pay is above the legal maximum. 1 mark: so landlords ask for illegal side payments (e.g. large 'key money' deposits), and flats go to those who can pay rather than those in most need.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one effect of the maximum rent on the quality of rented flats.
parts.answer: Quality falls because landlords have less incentive and income to maintain them.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government sets a maximum price for bread above the current equilibrium price. What is the immediate effect?
A a shortage of bread
B a surplus of bread
C no change in the price or quantity of bread
D a rise in the price of bread to the maximum price
parts.answer: C no change in the price or quantity of bread
parts.working: A maximum price only affects the market if it is below equilibrium. Set above equilibrium it is not binding, so price and quantity stay the same. D is wrong because the maximum is a ceiling, not a target.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market, demand is Qd = 200 − 4P and supply is Qs = 20 + 2P, where P is the price in dollars. The government sets a maximum price of $20. What is the size of the resulting shortage?
A 20 units
B 40 units
C 60 units
D 80 units
parts.answer: C 60 units
parts.working: Equilibrium: 200 − 4P = 20 + 2P gives P = $30, Q = 80. At $20, Qd = 120 and Qs = 60, so the shortage is 60. D is the equilibrium quantity, not the shortage.

practice.stem:
The table shows the demand and supply schedules for rice in a country (invented data).
Price (Rs per kg): quantity demanded (thousand tonnes), quantity supplied (thousand tonnes)
150: 900, 500
175: 800, 600
200: 700, 700
225: 600, 800
250: 500, 900

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: Rs 200 per kg; 700 thousand tonnes
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a minimum price of Rs 250 per kg and buys any surplus. Calculate the surplus and the cost to the government of buying it.
parts.answer: Surplus 400 thousand tonnes; cost Rs 100 billion
parts.working: Surplus = 900 − 500 = 400 thousand tonnes (M1 A1); cost = 400,000 tonnes × 1000 kg × Rs 250 = Rs 100,000,000,000 = Rs 100 billion (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the change in farmers' total revenue from rice as a result of the scheme.
parts.answer: Rises by Rs 85 billion (from Rs 140 billion to Rs 225 billion)
parts.working: Before: 700,000 × 1000 × 200 = Rs 140 billion; after: 900,000 × 1000 × 250 = Rs 225 billion (M1); increase Rs 85 billion (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of this scheme for consumers.
parts.answer: Consumers pay a higher price (Rs 250 instead of Rs 200) and buy less, losing consumer surplus; they also pay taxes to finance the surplus.
parts.working: 1 mark point, 1 mark development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a diagram, explain why a maximum price set below the equilibrium price may cause a shortage, and consider whether such a policy will help low-income households.
parts.answer: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price; poor households may or may not benefit depending on rationing and supply response.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definition of a maximum price; correctly labelled demand and supply diagram with maximum price line below equilibrium; shortage shown as Qd − Qs. Analysis (3): lower price extends demand and contracts supply; quantity actually traded falls; producers may cut quality; shortage leads to queues and shadow markets. Evaluation (2): households who obtain the good gain from the lower price; but those who cannot get it lose; benefit depends on PES and PED, rationing system (e.g. ration cards), enforcement; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Invented data: in a country, the retail price of sugar rose to Rs 165 per kg after a poor sugar-cane harvest. The government then imposed a maximum retail price of Rs 140 per kg. A month later, newspapers reported that many shops had no sugar on their shelves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the maximum price is below the previous market price. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two likely effects of the maximum price on the sugar market.
parts.answer: Shortage as Qd rises and Qs falls; illegal market or hoarding; supply diverted to other uses or smuggled abroad.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained effects: shortage (excess demand) with empty shelves; illegal resale at higher prices; hoarding by traders expecting the control to end; mills cut supply or export; queues and time costs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether a maximum price is more effective than a cash transfer to poor households for making sugar affordable.
parts.answer: A cash transfer targets the poor and avoids shortages; a maximum price is cheaper for the budget but benefits all buyers and causes shortages.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): maximum price helps everyone who buys, including rich households and confectionery firms; causes shortage; no budget cost. Cash transfer targets poor, keeps market price, no shortage, but costs the government and may be spent on other goods. Evaluation (1): judgement, e.g. a cash transfer is likely more effective if there is a reliable register of poor households.

practice.stem: In the market for a basic medicine, demand is P = 100 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q, where P is the price in dollars and Q is the quantity in thousands of packs per month (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity, and the consumer surplus and producer surplus at equilibrium.
parts.answer: P = $60, Q = 40 thousand; consumer surplus $800 thousand; producer surplus $800 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government imposes a maximum price of $40. Calculate the new consumer surplus and producer surplus, assuming the units supplied go to the consumers who value them most.
parts.answer: Consumer surplus $1000 thousand; producer surplus $200 thousand
parts.working: Quantity supplied at $40: 40 = 20 + Q so Q = 20 (M1). CS = trapezium between demand and $40 from 0 to 20 = ½ × (60 + 40) × 20 = 1000 (A1). PS = ½ × 20 × 20 = 200 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deadweight (welfare) loss and comment on whether consumers as a group gain from the maximum price.
parts.answer: Welfare loss $400 thousand; consumers who obtain the good gain (CS rises by $200 thousand) but 20 thousand units of demand are no longer met.
parts.working: Total surplus 1600 − 1200 = 400 (B1). Comment (B1): consumers as a group gain only if goods reach those who value them most; queuing or illegal markets would reduce this gain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a guaranteed minimum price for wheat is the best way for a government to support farmers' incomes.
parts.answer: A minimum price raises incomes of farmers who sell, but creates surpluses, higher food prices and fiscal costs; alternatives may be better.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): diagram of minimum price above equilibrium; surplus Qs − Qd; government must buy and store the surplus; farmers' revenue rises (price × quantity sold); larger farmers with more output gain most; consumers pay more, which hurts poor households for whom wheat flour is a staple; storage costs, wastage, opportunity cost of government spending; possible over-production of wheat at the expense of other crops. Comparison with alternatives: direct cash transfers to small farmers, input subsidies, buffer stocks, crop insurance, investment in irrigation and research. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on PED and PES, budget position, how well the scheme is targeted, world prices; 'best' requires a comparison and a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A government introduces a minimum retail price of Rs 360 for a pack of cigarettes. The previous market price was Rs 300. Assume the price elasticity of demand for cigarettes is −0.4 (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the quantity of cigarettes demanded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in total consumer spending on cigarettes.
parts.working: New spending ÷ old spending = 1.20 × 0.92 = 1.104 (M1), a rise of 10.4 % (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why a minimum price on cigarettes may not greatly reduce smoking, and suggest one problem it could create.
parts.answer: Demand is price inelastic, so consumption falls only slightly while spending rises; it may encourage illegal or smuggled cigarettes.
parts.working: 1 mark: PED is inelastic (addiction, few substitutes). 1 mark: quantity falls by only 8 % while smokers spend more, which may hurt poor smoking households. 1 mark: problem, e.g. smuggling/counterfeit cigarettes, extra revenue goes to sellers not the government (unlike a tax).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.38. What does this show?
A income has become more equally distributed
B income has become less equally distributed
C average income in the country has fallen
D the number of people living in poverty has risen
parts.answer: B income has become less equally distributed
parts.working: A higher Gini coefficient means the Lorenz curve is further from the line of equality, so distribution is less equal. It says nothing about the level of average income (C) or the absolute number in poverty (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between income and wealth, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (e.g. monthly wages); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (e.g. a house or land).
parts.working: 1 mark each correct distinction with example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how inequality of wealth can lead to inequality of income.
parts.answer: Wealth generates income (rent, interest, dividends, profit), so those with more assets receive more income.
parts.working: 1 mark: assets yield income such as rent and dividends. 1 mark: wealth also allows better education and business start-up, raising future earnings, so the gap widens across generations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two causes of income inequality other than inequality of wealth.
parts.answer: Differences in skills/education; discrimination; regional differences; unemployment; differences in bargaining power.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid causes.

practice.stem:
Invented income tax bands for a country (annual income):
first Rs 600,000: 0 %
Rs 600,001 to Rs 1,200,000: 5 %
Rs 1,200,001 to Rs 2,400,000: 15 %
above Rs 2,400,000: 25 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by Bilal, who earns Rs 1,000,000 a year, and by Sana, who earns Rs 3,000,000 a year.
parts.answer: Bilal Rs 20,000; Sana Rs 360,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of tax paid by each person, and state Sana's marginal rate of tax.
parts.answer: Bilal 2 %; Sana 12 %; Sana's marginal rate 25 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this tax system is described as progressive.
parts.answer: The average rate of tax rises as income rises (2 % to 12 %), so higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate rises with income. 1 mark: use of the figures calculated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the causes of income inequality within a country and consider whether some degree of inequality is necessary for an economy to work well.
parts.answer: Causes include differences in skills, education, wealth, discrimination and bargaining power; some inequality provides incentives, but too much harms growth and welfare.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of income inequality; measurement by Lorenz curve or Gini coefficient; causes such as differences in education and skills, wealth/inheritance, labour market discrimination, regional differences, unemployment, tax and benefit systems. Analysis (3): explain how each cause leads to different wage or non-wage incomes, e.g. scarce skills command high wages. Evaluation (2): wage differences signal where labour is needed and reward effort, risk and training; but extreme inequality reduces social mobility, health and demand, and may cause social unrest; justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country.
Year: share of income of poorest 20 % of households, share of income of richest 20 %
2015: 8 %, 45 %
2025: 7 %, 49 %
Real national income grew by 40 % between 2015 and 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest 20 % to that of the poorest 20 % in 2015 and in 2025. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the change in the ratio suggests about the distribution of income.
parts.answer: Income has become less equally distributed, as the richest group's share rose while the poorest group's share fell.
parts.working: 1 mark: less equal. 1 mark: use of data (ratio rose from 5.6 to 7.0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the data prove that the poorest 20 % of households were worse off in 2025 than in 2015.
parts.answer: No: the data are shares, not amounts; if total real income grew enough, the poorest may have had higher real incomes despite a smaller share.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 3): shares vs absolute incomes; real GDP growth of 40 % (invented) means the poorest 20 %'s real income changed by 1.4 × 7/8 − 1 = +22.5 %; but price changes for basic goods, household size and non-income factors (services, wealth) also matter. Evaluation (1): a judgement, e.g. relatively worse off but probably not absolutely.

practice.stem: Invented data: the share of national income received by each fifth (quintile) of households in a country, from poorest to richest, is 6 %, 10 %, 15 %, 22 % and 47 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cumulative share of income received by the poorest 60 % of households.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the Lorenz curve as straight lines joining the cumulative points, calculate the area under the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient. Give the Gini coefficient to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Area under Lorenz curve = 0.312; Gini coefficient = 0.38

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what would happen to the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient if a new tax and transfer scheme took income from the richest 20 % and gave it to the poorest 20 %.
parts.answer: The Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cumulative shares at each point rise, so the curve moves towards the 45° line. 1 mark: the area between the curve and the line of equality falls, so the Gini coefficient falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a progressive income tax is the best way to reduce income inequality in a lower-middle-income country.
parts.answer: It can narrow post-tax income gaps, but its effect is limited where few people pay income tax and the informal sector is large; spending and other taxes may matter more.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): how a progressive tax works (rising average rate) and narrows post-tax incomes; revenue can fund transfers, health and education. Limits: small tax base, large informal sector, tax avoidance and evasion, disincentive effects on work and enterprise, capital flight; poorest households are below the threshold so gain nothing directly. Alternatives: cash transfers, free education and health (raise human capital), wealth or property taxes, minimum wages, land reform. Evaluation (up to 4): effectiveness depends on tax collection capacity and how revenue is spent; long-term inequality is better reduced by education; a judgement on 'best'.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why would a free market fail to provide a public good such as a flood defence wall?
A the good is rival in consumption
B consumers would demand too much of it
C people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot earn revenue
D the government has better information than consumers
parts.answer: C people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot earn revenue
parts.working: Because a public good is non-excludable, people can be free riders, so firms cannot charge and will not supply it. A is wrong: public goods are non-rival.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many people in rural areas do not have regular dental check-ups, even when they can afford them. Explain how information failure can lead to the under-consumption of dental check-ups.
parts.answer: People underestimate the long-term benefits (preventing serious disease), so their demand is below the level that would maximise their welfare.
parts.working: 1 mark: information failure = consumers lack full/accurate information. 1 mark: they do not realise that problems can be prevented cheaply / focus on short-term cost. 1 mark: so demand and consumption are lower than they would choose with full information – a merit good is under-consumed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two policies the government could use to increase consumption of dental check-ups.
parts.answer: Free or subsidised check-ups; information campaigns in schools; direct provision through clinics.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why smokeless tobacco products are regarded as demerit goods.
parts.answer: Consumers underestimate the harm (e.g. oral cancer), and may be addicted, so consumption is higher than is in their own interest.
parts.working: 1 mark: demerit good = over-consumed in a free market. 1 mark: information failure – users underestimate health risks. 1 mark: addiction / habit, so the good's harm to the user is not fully reflected in demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of banning the sale of such products.
parts.answer: Advantage: consumption should fall sharply, improving health. Disadvantage: an illegal market may develop, with no quality control and no tax revenue.
parts.working: 2 marks each: advantage explained (removes legal supply, clear signal); disadvantage explained (illegal markets, enforcement costs, loss of jobs/tax revenue, consumers may switch to other harmful products).

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why public goods would not be provided in a free market, and consider whether the government should provide all public goods itself.
parts.answer: Non-excludability causes free riding, so there is a missing market; the government must ensure provision, but it may contract private firms to produce them.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): definitions of non-rival and non-excludable; examples (national defence, street lighting, lighthouses, flood defences). Analysis (3): firms cannot charge non-payers, so consumers do not reveal willingness to pay; free-rider problem; zero marginal cost of an extra user means charging would be inefficient; so the market is missing. Evaluation (2): government must finance them through taxation but need not produce them – private firms can build and maintain under contract, possibly more efficiently; deciding the right quantity is difficult without prices; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a ban is a better policy than an indirect tax for reducing the consumption of a demerit good.
parts.answer: A ban gives the biggest reduction in theory but causes illegal markets; a tax keeps the market legal and raises revenue but has small effect when demand is price inelastic.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): a ban removes legal supply, sends a clear signal, but creates illegal markets, enforcement costs, loss of tax revenue and possible harm from unregulated products; indirect tax shifts supply left, raises price and reduces quantity, generates revenue to fund health care or education, but if PED is inelastic consumption falls little and the tax is regressive. Discuss the role of information (education campaigns), the nature of the good (addictive or not, how harmful), enforcement capacity. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on the good and the country – a ban may suit very harmful goods with easy enforcement; a tax suits goods where moderate consumption is accepted; a judgement.

practice.subtopic: Reasons for intervention (merit, demerit and public goods)
practice.stem:
Invented data on the percentage of children fully vaccinated in a country.
Year: urban districts, rural districts
2020: 88 %, 62 %
2025: 88 %, 71 %
Free mobile vaccination clinics began visiting rural villages in 2021.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in vaccination rates between urban and rural districts in 2025, and state whether it was larger or smaller than in 2020.
parts.answer: 17 percentage points in 2025, smaller than 26 percentage points in 2020

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why vaccinations may be under-consumed in rural districts if left to the market.
parts.answer: Information failure (parents underestimate benefits), cost and travel time, low incomes, myths and mistrust.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: merit good definition (1); information failure explained (1); low incomes and distance raise the effective price (1); result – consumption below the socially desirable level (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data show that free mobile vaccination clinics are the best policy to raise vaccination rates.
parts.answer: The data suggest the clinics helped, but other factors may have contributed and the cost is not shown.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): rural rate rose 9 points after clinics began while the urban rate stayed at 88 %, which supports the policy; but correlation is not causation – information campaigns, rising incomes or school requirements might also explain it; no data on cost per extra child vaccinated; rate still 71 %, so barriers remain (information, trust). Alternatives: conditional cash transfers, school-entry requirements, community health workers. Evaluation (up to 2): a justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Before a specific tax is imposed on a good, its price is $50 and 100 units are sold. After a specific tax of $10 per unit, the price paid by consumers is $56 and 90 units are sold. What is the government's tax revenue?
A $360
B $540
C $900
D $1000
parts.working: Revenue = tax per unit × quantity sold after the tax = $10 × 90 = $900. D wrongly uses the original quantity; A is the producers' share ($4 × 90) and B the consumers' share ($6 × 90).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a specific tax and an ad valorem tax.
parts.answer: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit; an ad valorem tax is a percentage of the price.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Specific: supply curve shifts up in parallel. Ad valorem: the vertical gap widens as price rises (curve pivots).

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the help of a diagram described in words, explain why the burden (incidence) of an indirect tax falls mainly on consumers when demand is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Supply shifts up by the tax; with steep demand the price rises by most of the tax and quantity falls little.
parts.working: Diagram: original D and S, S shifts vertically up by the tax (1). With inelastic (steep) demand, price paid by consumers rises by most of the tax (1). Price received by producers (new price minus tax) falls only a little (1). Consumers' share = rise in price × new quantity, larger than producers' share; quantity falls little (1).

practice.stem: In the market for solar water heaters, demand is Qd = 120 − 2P and supply is Qs = −30 + 3P, where P is the price in dollars and Q is in thousands per year (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity before the subsidy.
parts.answer: P = $30, Q = 60 thousand

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government pays producers a subsidy of $10 per unit. The supply equation becomes Qs = −30 + 3(P + 10). Calculate the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.answer: P = $24, Q = 72 thousand

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the subsidy to the government, and the share of the subsidy per unit received by consumers and by producers.
parts.answer: Cost $720 thousand; consumers $6 per unit; producers $4 per unit
parts.working: Cost = 10 × 72 = $720 thousand (B1). Consumers' price falls from $30 to $24, so they gain $6 per unit (B1). Producers receive $24 + $10 = $34, a gain of $4 per unit (B1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why consumers receive the larger share of the subsidy in this market.
parts.answer: Demand is less price elastic than supply at the original equilibrium, so more of the benefit passes to consumers.
parts.working: B1: at P = 30, Q = 60 the PED is 2 × 30/60 = 1.0 and the PES is 3 × 30/60 = 1.5; the less elastic side receives the larger share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether an indirect tax on sugary drinks is likely to reduce their consumption significantly.
parts.answer: It raises price and reduces quantity, but the effect depends on PED, the size of the tax, pass-through to consumers and the availability of untaxed substitutes.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): diagram showing supply shifting up by the tax; new higher price and lower quantity; incidence depends on PED/PES; if demand is price inelastic (habit, brand loyalty, low share of income for richer groups) consumption falls little; producers may absorb part of the tax or reformulate recipes with less sugar (a desired effect); consumers may switch to untaxed sugary foods; tax is regressive; revenue could fund health education. Evaluation (up to 4): significance depends on the tax rate, the price sensitivity of young and low-income consumers (more elastic), complementary policies (labelling, school bans); a justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: A government's cash-transfer programme pays Rs 10,500 every quarter (three months) to each of 9 million low-income families. The country's GDP is Rs 105 trillion (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the cash-transfer programme. Give your answer in Rs billion.
parts.answer: Rs 378 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the programme as a percentage of GDP. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a transfer payment and why it is not counted as part of GDP.
parts.answer: A payment from the government for which no good or service is provided in return; it redistributes existing income rather than paying for new output.
parts.working: 1 mark definition. 1 mark: no production takes place in return, so counting it would double-count income.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments
practice.stem: A buffer stock agency for coffee beans aims to keep the price between a floor of $1.80 per kg and a ceiling of $2.20 per kg. After a very good harvest, the free-market price would fall to $1.50 per kg, so the agency buys 300,000 tonnes of coffee beans at $1.80 per kg (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost to the agency of the purchases it makes after the good harvest. Give your answer in $ million.
parts.answer: $540 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the agency would do if a poor harvest caused the free-market price to rise to $2.50 per kg.
parts.answer: Sell coffee from its stock to increase supply and bring the price down to the ceiling of $2.20.
parts.working: 1 mark: sell from the stock. 1 mark: the extra supply shifts the supply curve right and keeps the price at or below $2.20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why such a scheme might fail in the long run.
parts.answer: Floor set too high (persistent surpluses and rising costs); storage costs and perishability; stocks run out after several poor harvests; producers expand output; funding problems.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained reasons.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the direct provision of health care by the government can increase the consumption of a merit good, and consider the problems that direct provision may cause.
parts.answer: Free provision removes the price barrier and raises consumption towards the desired level; but it is costly, may cause excess demand and can be inefficient.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of direct provision (government produces and supplies, often free at the point of use); health care as a merit good under-consumed due to information failure and low incomes. Analysis (3): zero price means quantity demanded rises (movement along demand to where price = 0); access no longer depends on income; equity improves. Evaluation (2): high opportunity cost for the budget; excess demand leads to waiting lists; lack of profit motive may reduce efficiency and quality; information failure remains if people still do not use services; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Direct provision, buffer stocks and transfer payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether buffer stock schemes are an effective way to stabilise the prices of agricultural products.
parts.answer: They can smooth short-term fluctuations, but often fail because of wrongly set price bands, storage costs, perishability and lack of funds.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): agricultural prices are unstable because supply varies with weather and both demand and supply are price inelastic in the short run; diagram of a price band, buying in good harvests and selling in poor ones; benefits: stable farm incomes, planning, investment, stable food prices for consumers. Problems: setting the band correctly (if too high, permanent surpluses); storage and wastage costs; perishable goods cannot be stored; a run of poor harvests empties the stock; political pressure; large funds needed; for exported crops, other countries' output matters. Evaluation (up to 4): more effective for storable goods (grains, metals) with a band near the long-run average price; judgement.

topics.name: Basic economic ideas and resource allocation

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. What does this point show?
A all resources are fully and efficiently employed
B some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
C the combination cannot be reached with current resources
D the country has had an increase in productive capacity
parts.answer: B some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
parts.working: A point inside the PPC means output could rise without giving up any other good, so resources are unemployed or misallocated. C describes a point outside the curve, not inside it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A flood destroys roads, bridges and factories in a country. Using a production possibility curve described in words, explain the effect on the country's productive capacity.
parts.answer: The PPC shifts inwards because the quantity of capital (a factor of production) has fallen.
parts.working: 1 mark: axes are two goods/services (e.g. agricultural goods and manufactured goods), not price and quantity. 1 mark: capital stock is destroyed, so the maximum output possible falls. 1 mark: the whole PPC shifts inwards (towards the origin); if mainly factories are lost the shift is larger on the manufactured goods axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this differs from the effect of a rise in unemployment caused by a fall in demand.
parts.answer: Unemployment moves the economy to a point inside an unchanged PPC.
parts.working: 1 mark: productive capacity is unchanged, so the PPC does not shift. 1 mark: actual output falls, shown by a movement from a point on the curve to a point inside it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An economy moves along its production possibility curve from 60 units of capital goods and 300 units of consumer goods to 80 units of capital goods and 260 units of consumer goods. What is the opportunity cost of each extra unit of capital goods?
A 0.5 units of consumer goods
B 2 units of consumer goods
C 3.25 units of consumer goods
D 40 units of consumer goods
parts.answer: B 2 units of consumer goods
parts.working: Consumer goods given up = 300 − 260 = 40; extra capital goods = 80 − 60 = 20; 40 ÷ 20 = 2 units of consumer goods per unit. D is the total sacrifice, not the cost per unit; A inverts the ratio.

practice.stem:
The table shows the production possibilities of a farming region in Punjab that grows only wheat and cotton (invented data).
Combination: wheat (thousand tonnes), cotton (thousand bales)
A: 0, 500
B: 100, 470
C: 200, 420
D: 300, 340
E: 400, 220
F: 500, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra tonne of wheat when production moves from combination C to combination D.
parts.answer: 0.8 bales of cotton per tonne of wheat
parts.working: Cotton given up = 420 − 340 = 80 thousand bales (M1); ÷ 100 thousand tonnes of wheat = 0.8 bales per tonne (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra tonne of wheat when production moves from combination E to combination F.
parts.answer: 2.2 bales of cotton per tonne of wheat
parts.working: 220 thousand bales ÷ 100 thousand tonnes = 2.2 bales per tonne (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers to (a) and (b), explain why the production possibility curve for this region is concave (bowed outwards) from the origin.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost rises as more wheat is produced because resources are not equally suited to both crops.
parts.working: 1 mark: opportunity cost of wheat increases (0.8 → 2.2). 1 mark: land and labour best suited to cotton are moved into wheat last / factors are not perfectly mobile or equally productive in both uses. 1 mark: so each extra unit of wheat needs more cotton to be given up, making the slope steeper and the curve concave.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the combination 200 thousand tonnes of wheat and 450 thousand bales of cotton can be produced. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No, it is unattainable.
parts.working: B1 not attainable; B1 at 200 thousand tonnes of wheat the maximum cotton output is 420 thousand bales, so 450 lies outside the PPC with current resources and technology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the help of a production possibility curve diagram, explain the effect of a new technology that raises productivity in the textile industry only, and consider whether such a change will always increase the economic welfare of the country.
parts.answer: The PPC pivots outwards along the textile axis only; welfare usually rises but not always.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): PPC shows maximum combinations of two goods (textiles and other goods) with given resources and technology; opportunity cost; correct axis labels. Analysis (3): the maximum output of textiles rises while the maximum of other goods is unchanged, so the curve pivots outwards from the other-goods intercept; at every point except that intercept the country can now produce more; the opportunity cost of textiles falls. Evaluation (2): welfare may not rise if the economy is inside its PPC (unemployment), if workers displaced by machines stay unemployed, if extra output creates pollution, or if textiles are mostly exported and the gains go to a few owners; a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A small island economy can produce either 400 tablet computers or 1000 tonnes of rice per month, or any combination on a straight-line production possibility curve between these two points (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tablet computer.
parts.answer: 2.5 tonnes of rice
parts.working: 1000 ÷ 400 = 2.5 tonnes of rice (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of rice the country can produce if it makes 150 tablet computers.
parts.answer: 625 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the straight-line shape of this production possibility curve assumes about the country's resources.
parts.answer: Resources are equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost is constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: constant opportunity cost (same slope throughout). 1 mark: this assumes factors are equally productive in making tablets and rice / perfectly transferable, which is unlikely in reality.

practice.stem:
Invented data for two countries, average for 2015–2024:
Country X: investment as a share of GDP 32 %; average annual real GDP growth 6.1 %
Country Y: investment as a share of GDP 14 %; average annual real GDP growth 2.8 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the average growth rates of the two countries over the period.
parts.answer: Country X's average growth (6.1 %) was about 2.2 times that of Country Y (2.8 %), i.e. 3.3 percentage points higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: X grew faster. 1 mark: data manipulated, e.g. 3.3 percentage points higher or about 2.2 times as fast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the help of a production possibility curve described in words, explain how a decision to produce more capital goods now can affect a country's future output.
parts.answer: Choosing a point with more capital goods and fewer consumer goods now raises the capital stock, shifting the PPC outward in future.
parts.working: Axes labelled capital goods and consumer goods (1). Moving along the PPC towards capital goods means an opportunity cost of current consumer goods (1). Extra capital raises productive capacity (1). Future PPC shifts outwards further than for a country choosing more consumer goods, allowing more of both goods later (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data prove that Country Y should increase the share of output it devotes to investment.
parts.answer: Not proven: the data show an association, but growth also depends on other factors; a higher investment share has a current consumption cost.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): higher investment links to faster capacity growth (X); sacrifice of current consumption may harm living standards of poor households; return depends on type/quality of investment; growth also depends on labour skills, technology, demand, political stability; the data cover only two countries and averages, so correlation not causation. Evaluation (up to 2): a judgement, e.g. investment is likely to help but the data alone cannot prove it; it depends on whether Y has spare capacity or weak demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the production possibility curve is a useful way to explain the economic problem facing a low-income country.
parts.answer: Useful for showing scarcity, choice, opportunity cost and growth, but limited because it is a simplified two-good model.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks for analysis: PPC illustrates scarcity (finite resources), choice between combinations, opportunity cost (slope), unemployment (inside), growth (outward shift) and the trade-off between capital and consumer goods, which is key for a low-income country with low savings. Limitations: only two goods; assumes fixed resources and technology; does not show distribution of output, quality of life, or which point is best (a normative choice); points outside may be reached through trade or aid. Up to 4 marks for evaluation: a supported judgement, e.g. useful as a starting framework but policy decisions need further evidence on income distribution and markets. Level 3 (9–12): balanced, applied to low-income country, justified conclusion; Level 2 (5–8): some analysis, limited evaluation; Level 1 (1–4): descriptive.

practice.stem: Invented data for a country (US$ billion, at constant prices): potential output in 2024 was 500 and actual output was 470. In 2025 potential output grew by 5 % and actual output grew by 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap (potential minus actual output) as a percentage of potential output in 2024 and in 2025. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using a production possibility curve described in words, explain what happened to actual and potential growth between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: The PPC shifted outwards (potential growth 5 %) and the production point moved outwards (actual growth 3 %), but the point ended up further inside the new curve.
parts.working: 1 mark: outward shift of PPC shows potential growth. 1 mark: movement of the production point away from the origin shows actual growth. 1 mark: because actual grew less than potential, the gap between the point and the curve widened (more unused resources).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best example of a free good?
A drinking water supplied by a city water board
B sunlight used by a family to dry washing on a roof
C a free textbook provided by the government to school pupils
D a public park in Islamabad with no entry charge
parts.answer: B sunlight used by a family to dry washing on a roof
parts.working: A free good has no opportunity cost: it is not scarce, and using it does not take resources from other uses. Sunlight is unlimited relative to demand. C and D have zero price to the user but use scarce resources, so they are economic goods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a public good.
parts.answer: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable.
parts.working: 1 mark non-rival: one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available to others. 1 mark non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a private firm is unlikely to provide street lighting in a residential area of Lahore.
parts.answer: Because of the free-rider problem, the firm could not charge users and would make no revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: street lighting is non-excludable, so non-payers cannot be prevented from using it. 1 mark: consumers have an incentive to be free riders and not reveal their willingness to pay. 1 mark: the firm cannot earn revenue to cover costs, so the market fails to provide it (missing market).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A provincial government provides free lunches to all primary school pupils. How should these lunches be classified?
A a public good, because they are provided by the government
B a public good, because no price is charged
C a private good, because they are rival and excludable
D a free good, because they have no opportunity cost
parts.answer: C a private good, because they are rival and excludable
parts.working: One pupil's lunch cannot be eaten by another (rival) and people can be prevented from getting one (excludable), so it is a private good, whoever provides it; it may also be a merit good. A is the common error of linking public goods to who supplies them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why motorcycle helmets are classified as a merit good.
parts.answer: Riders underestimate the benefit of a helmet (protection from serious head injury), so in a free market fewer helmets are bought and worn than is in the riders' own interest.
parts.working: 1 mark: a merit good is one that would be under-consumed if left to the free market / benefits are greater than consumers realise. 1 mark: information failure – riders underestimate the risk of an accident or the severity of head injuries (or are over-confident about short journeys). 1 mark: so demand and consumption are below the level that best serves the rider (and society, e.g. lower hospital costs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government might make the wearing of helmets compulsory rather than subsidise their price.
parts.answer: A subsidy lowers the price, but riders who underestimate the benefit may still not buy or wear a helmet; a law changes behaviour directly.
parts.working: 1 mark reason (the cause of under-consumption is information failure, not mainly price / regulation has a low budget cost). 1 mark development, e.g. even a cheaper helmet may be left at home, while a law backed by fines makes every rider wear one; it also costs the government little compared with a subsidy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a merit good and a public good, and consider whether secondary education in Pakistan should be regarded as a merit good.
parts.answer: Public goods are defined by non-rivalry and non-excludability; merit goods by under-consumption due to information failure; education is usually a merit good, though this involves a value judgement.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): public good definition (non-rival, non-excludable, free-rider, missing market); merit good definition (under-consumed in free market, information failure, judged by government). Analysis (3): education is rival and excludable, so it is not a public good; households may underestimate future earnings and wider benefits, poor families face cost barriers or need children's labour; so consumption is below the level society desires. Evaluation (2): classification as merit good is partly a value judgement; for well-informed households demand may already be high; private schools show it can be supplied by the market; a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A motorway between two cities charges drivers a toll at booths on every entrance. At night, when traffic is light, vehicles travel freely; during the morning rush hour it is heavily congested. Explain why the motorway is best described as a quasi-public good rather than a pure public good.
parts.answer: It is partly rival (congestion) and partly excludable (tolls), so it has some but not all characteristics of a public good.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition/idea of quasi-public good. 1 mark: at night one extra car does not reduce space for others (non-rival), but at rush hour extra users slow others down, so it becomes rival. 1 mark: toll booths mean non-payers can be excluded, so it is excludable. 1 mark: therefore it does not fully meet both conditions of a pure public good.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the government might still choose to finance the motorway from taxation.
parts.answer: Large external benefits/high fixed cost mean the market may under-provide it; tolls could reduce efficient use when the road is empty.
parts.working: 1 mark reason, 1 mark development (e.g. charging a toll when the road is empty discourages use that costs nothing extra; the economy-wide benefits of trade and travel are not captured by tolls).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether the classification of goods as merit goods or demerit goods is always based on objective evidence.
parts.answer: Not always: some classifications rest on strong evidence (tobacco harm), but many involve value judgements by governments.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): definitions of merit and demerit goods; role of information failure; evidence-based cases (smoking, vaccinations) where harm or benefit is measured scientifically; cases that are value judgements (alcohol, certain entertainment, arts, sugary foods) where the government's view replaces consumers' own preferences; paternalism; classification can vary between countries and over time; positive vs normative statements. Evaluation (up to 4): a weighed judgement, e.g. the evidence may be objective, but the decision that consumption is 'too high' or 'too low' is always partly normative. Level 3 (9–12) balanced with justified conclusion; Level 2 (5–8); Level 1 (1–4).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a planned economy, how are most decisions about what to produce made?
A by consumers spending in markets
B by firms seeking the highest profit
C by the state through central planning
D by trade unions bargaining with employers
parts.answer: C by the state through central planning
parts.working: In a planned (command) economy the state owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce. A and B describe the price mechanism in a market economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that a planned economy may face in allocating resources.
parts.answer: e.g. information problems and weak incentives.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two explained problems: (1) planners lack information about consumer preferences and costs, leading to shortages and surpluses; (2) weak profit/wage incentives reduce effort, innovation and quality; (3) bureaucracy and slow response to change; (4) limited consumer choice. 1 mark for identification, 1 for explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a mixed economy.
parts.answer: Both private and public sectors; prices allocate most goods but government intervenes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: private and public ownership exist together; market prices allocate many goods; the government provides public/merit goods, regulates markets or redistributes income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a mixed economy is the best way to allocate a country's scarce resources.
parts.answer: Often yes, because it combines the incentives of markets with government correction of market failure, but the outcome depends on the balance and on government failure.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 8): the economic problem (what, how, for whom); market economy strengths (price signals, efficiency, choice, incentives) and weaknesses (public goods not provided, inequality, information failure, demerit goods); planned economy strengths (equity, coordination of large projects) and weaknesses (information, incentives); mixed economy aims to gain the advantages of both. Evaluation (up to 4): depends on the size and quality of the public sector, corruption and government failure, stage of development; 'best' depends on value judgements about equity vs efficiency; justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Invented data for a country that moved from a planned economy to a market economy, starting in Year 1.
Year: real GDP index (Year 1 = 100), inflation rate (%), unemployment rate (%)
Year 1: 100, 4, 1
Year 2: 88, 300, 8
Year 3: 84, 95, 14
Year 4: 90, 30, 12
Year 5: 99, 12, 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in real GDP between Year 1 and Year 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain why the move from a planned to a market economy might cause inflation and unemployment in the short run.
parts.answer: Price controls removed → prices jump to market levels; inefficient state firms close → workers lose jobs while new firms take time to grow.
parts.working: Inflation (2): removal of maximum prices lets prices rise to equilibrium where there were shortages; 300 % inflation in Year 2. Unemployment (2): subsidies to loss-making state enterprises end, so they cut jobs or close; labour is occupationally immobile and new private firms take time to develop; unemployment rose from 1 % to 14 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assess whether the data suggest that the move to a market economy was a mistake.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: short-run costs were high, but by Year 5 growth had resumed and inflation fallen.
parts.working: Analysis (up to 4): Years 2–3 show large costs (inflation, unemployment, falling output); by Year 5 real GDP had recovered to 99 and inflation fell to 12 %, suggesting gains in efficiency; data say nothing about quality/choice of goods or distribution; unemployment still high at 9 %. Evaluation (up to 2): a judgement, e.g. too early to say; depends on the pace of reform and support for those who lost jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the factor of production that each of the following represents and the reward paid to it: (i) a plot of farmland in Sindh; (ii) a delivery van owned by a bakery; (iii) a nurse working in a hospital.
parts.answer: (i) land – rent; (ii) capital – interest; (iii) labour – wages
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct factor with its reward.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the entrepreneur in a market economy.
parts.answer: The entrepreneur organises the other factors and takes the risk of business; the reward is profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: combines/organises land, labour and capital to produce goods. 1 mark: bears risk/uncertainty and receives profit (or loss).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is classified as capital in economics?
A money saved in a bank deposit account
B shares in a company bought by a household
C a sewing machine used in a garment factory
D a fishing lake owned by a farmer
parts.answer: C a sewing machine used in a garment factory
parts.working: Capital is a man-made aid to production, such as machinery. Money and shares (A, B) are financial assets, not real capital; the lake (D) is a natural resource, so land.

practice.stem: A furniture workshop in Chiniot employs 5 workers. When each worker made complete chairs, the workshop produced 20 chairs a day. After the work was divided into separate tasks (cutting, carving, joining, polishing), the same 5 workers produced 32 chairs a day (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in output per worker after the workshop introduced division of labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why division of labour may have raised output per worker.
parts.answer: Workers become skilled at one task through repetition; time is saved by not switching tasks / tools; workers suited to tasks.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two explained reasons: practice improves skill and speed; less time lost moving between tasks and tools; workers can be matched to tasks they are best at; easier to use specialised machinery; training is shorter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of division of labour for the workers.
parts.answer: Boredom from repetitive work (or loss of variety of skills / risk of unemployment if the task is automated).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid disadvantage to workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how specialisation and the division of labour can increase an economy's output, and consider whether a country should specialise in producing a narrow range of goods.
parts.answer: Specialisation raises productivity and output; but over-specialisation creates risks.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): meaning of specialisation (individuals, firms, regions, countries) and division of labour; need for exchange/money. Analysis (3): higher productivity through skill, time saving, use of machinery and economies of scale; lower unit costs; more output from given resources (PPC shifts outward / move to higher output). Evaluation (2): national specialisation increases dependence on world prices (e.g. a single crop or mineral), exposes the country to demand shocks and structural unemployment; diversification may reduce risk; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is normative?
A Pakistan's inflation rate was higher in 2023 than in 2021.
B A rise in the price of petrol will reduce the quantity of petrol demanded.
C The government should spend more on primary schools than on motorways.
D Raising the minimum wage may increase unemployment among young workers.
parts.answer: C The government should spend more on primary schools than on motorways.
parts.working: C contains a value judgement ('should') and cannot be tested by evidence. D is positive: it is a testable prediction even though it uses 'may'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify which of the following statements are positive and which are normative.
(1) The unemployment rate among graduates in the country rose from 9 % to 12 %.
(2) Income inequality in the country is unacceptably high.
(3) A tax on sugary drinks would reduce their consumption.
(4) Clean drinking water is more important than mobile phone coverage.
parts.answer: Positive: (1) and (3). Normative: (2) and (4).
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why economists make the assumption of ceteris paribus when building economic models.
parts.answer: To isolate the effect of one variable by holding all other factors constant.
parts.working: 1 mark: ceteris paribus means other things remain equal. 1 mark: in the real world many variables change at once and controlled experiments are not possible, so the assumption lets economists study one cause and effect at a time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why economics is described as a social science.
parts.answer: It studies human behaviour using scientific method but cannot run controlled experiments, and people do not behave consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: it uses scientific method (theories, models, testing against data). 1 mark: it studies human behaviour in society, which is less predictable, and laboratory experiments are rarely possible.

practice.stem: A household in a country with 30 % annual inflation keeps Rs 100,000 in cash at home for one year. It earns no interest (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four functions of money.
parts.answer: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the real value of the household's savings after one year, in Year 0 prices. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how very high inflation weakens two functions of money.
parts.answer: Store of value: money loses purchasing power. Standard of deferred payment / unit of account: future amounts and prices become unreliable.
parts.working: 2 marks each: store of value – each rupee buys less over time, so people switch to gold, property or foreign currency; unit of account – prices change so often that comparisons are hard; standard of deferred payment – lenders are repaid in money worth less, so they become unwilling to lend; medium of exchange – in extreme cases people turn to barter or foreign currency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the characteristics that an item needs in order to function well as money, and consider whether balances held in mobile phone wallets have these characteristics.
parts.answer: Acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, limited supply, homogeneity; mobile wallets have most of them but depend on trust, technology and access.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): list and explain characteristics – generally acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, scarce/limited in supply, uniform/recognisable. Analysis (3): mobile wallet balances are easily divisible and portable, do not wear out, are units of the national currency so uniform and scarce; widely accepted where merchants have agreed. Evaluation (2): acceptability depends on network coverage, phone ownership and trust in the provider; not usable during power or network failures; may be part of broad rather than narrow money; justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Ayesha lives in Karachi. She has been offered a job at a bank paying Rs 65,000 a month. Instead, she chooses a two-year full-time diploma costing Rs 300,000 a year in fees (invented data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the opportunity cost of Ayesha's decision.
parts.answer: The job at the bank (the next best alternative), including the income it would have paid.
parts.working: 1 mark: the next best alternative forgone – the bank job.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total economic cost to Ayesha of the two-year diploma (the fees plus the earnings she gives up).
parts.working: Earnings forgone 65,000 × 24 = Rs 1,560,000 (M1); plus fees 2 × 300,000 = Rs 600,000; total Rs 2,160,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Ayesha may still have made a rational choice.
parts.answer: She expects the future benefits (higher earnings, satisfaction) to exceed the opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: rational choice compares costs and benefits. 1 mark: the diploma may raise lifetime earnings or job satisfaction by more than Rs 2.16 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the basic economic problem of scarcity exists in all economies, and consider whether scarcity is less of a problem for high-income countries than for low-income countries.
parts.answer: Wants are unlimited while resources are finite, so all economies must choose; richer countries face scarcity too, though basic needs are less affected.
parts.working: Knowledge (3): scarcity = unlimited wants vs limited resources; need for choice; opportunity cost; the three questions what/how/for whom. Analysis (3): resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise) are finite everywhere; as incomes rise new wants appear (health care, environment, leisure); even rich countries face trade-offs (e.g. health vs defence, ageing populations). Evaluation (2): in low-income countries scarcity affects basic needs (food, clean water), so its human cost is greater; in high-income countries it concerns more optional wants; absolute scarcity is universal but relative severity differs; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following acts as an automatic stabiliser in an economy?
A a progressive income tax system
B a one-off decision to build a new motorway
C a cut in the central bank's policy interest rate
D a new tariff on imported cars
parts.answer: A a progressive income tax system
parts.working: As incomes fall in a recession, people move into lower tax bands, so tax paid falls faster than income and disposable income is cushioned, with no new government decision needed. B is discretionary fiscal policy (a deliberate decision), C is monetary policy. D is a protectionist measure, not a stabiliser.

practice.stem:
Table 1: Tax revenue of Country P, 2025 (PKR billion; data invented for practice)
Income tax: 2900
Corporate (company) profits tax: 1100
General sales tax: 3400
Customs duties: 1200
Excise duties: 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a direct tax and an indirect tax, and identify the direct taxes in Table 1.
parts.answer: A direct tax is paid straight to the government by the person or firm on whom it falls, out of income or wealth; an indirect tax is levied on spending and can be passed on in the price. Direct taxes: income tax and corporate profits tax.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct distinction (on income/wealth vs on spending, incidence can be shifted); 1 mark for identifying income tax and corporate profits tax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate indirect taxes as a percentage of total tax revenue. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a general sales tax is likely to be regressive.
parts.answer: Poorer households spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods, so the tax paid takes a larger percentage of a low income than of a high income.
parts.working: 1 mark: regressive means the share of income paid in tax falls as income rises; 1 mark: low-income households spend (rather than save) most of their income, so sales tax paid is a higher % of their income.

practice.stem: A government in South-East Asia plans to cut the basic rate of income tax from 20 % to 17 % to support spending during a slowdown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a progressive income tax.
parts.answer: A tax where the proportion of income paid in tax (the average rate) rises as income rises, because higher slices of income are taxed at higher marginal rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate rises as income rises; 1 mark: higher marginal rates on higher bands of income (or an example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether a cut in income tax rates will increase aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Usually yes, because disposable income and consumption rise, but the effect may be small if households save the extra income, buy imports, or lack confidence.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: lower tax → higher disposable income (1) → higher consumption (1) → AD (C + I + G + X − M) shifts right (1); possible extra effect on incentives. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: the rise may be small if the extra income is saved (low confidence, debt repayment), spent on imports, or goes mainly to high earners with a low propensity to consume; or offset if spending is cut to pay for it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between automatic stabilisers and discretionary fiscal policy, and consider which is more useful in reducing the effects of a fall in aggregate demand.
parts.answer: Automatic stabilisers change tax revenue and spending without a decision as income changes; discretionary policy is a deliberate change. Stabilisers act quickly but only cushion; discretionary policy can be larger but suffers time lags.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definitions of fiscal policy, automatic stabilisers (progressive taxes, unemployment benefits) and discretionary policy (deliberate changes in tax rates or spending); examples. Analysis: in a downturn, tax revenue falls and benefit spending rises automatically, supporting disposable income and AD; discretionary policy, e.g. extra infrastructure spending, shifts AD right by a chosen amount; AD/AS diagram. Evaluation: stabilisers work immediately and without political delay but only reduce, not reverse, a fall in AD; discretionary policy can be targeted and larger but has recognition, decision and implementation lags and may arrive too late; usefulness also depends on the size of the welfare system and the government's ability to borrow; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, the first PKR 600 000 of annual income is tax-free, the next PKR 600 000 is taxed at 5 % and all income above PKR 1 200 000 is taxed at 15 %. A worker earns PKR 1 800 000 a year. What are the worker's marginal and average rates of income tax?
A marginal rate 15 %, average rate 6.7 %
B marginal rate 6.7 %, average rate 15 %
C marginal rate 15 %, average rate 15 %
D marginal rate 5 %, average rate 6.7 %
parts.answer: A marginal rate 15 %, average rate 6.7 %
parts.working: Tax = 0 + 5 % × 600 000 + 15 % × 600 000 = 30 000 + 90 000 = PKR 120,000. Average rate = 120,000 ÷ 1 800 000 = 6.7 %. The marginal rate is the rate on the last rupee earned, 15 %. B reverses the two definitions.

practice.stem:
Table 2: Government finances of Country R (US$ million; data invented for practice)
Year 1: nominal GDP 52 000; government spending 10 400; tax revenue 8320
Year 2: nominal GDP 50 400; government spending 10 900; tax revenue 7860

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP in Year 1 and in Year 2. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain how automatic stabilisers might account for the change in the budget deficit between Year 1 and Year 2.
parts.answer: GDP fell, so incomes, spending and profits fell; tax revenue fell automatically while spending on unemployment and welfare benefits rose automatically, so the deficit increased with no new policy decision.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the fall in nominal GDP (52 000 to 50 400) as a sign of recession; 1 mark: lower incomes/spending/profits → lower revenue from income, sales and profits taxes (revenue fell 8320 → 7860); 1 mark: rising unemployment → more benefit payments, so spending rose (10 400 → 10 900); 1 mark: these changes happen without a government decision and cushion the fall in AD, so the rise in the deficit is partly cyclical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether expansionary fiscal policy is the best way to reduce unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy can raise AD and reduce cyclical unemployment, but its success depends on spare capacity, the multiplier, debt levels and time lags; it does little for structural unemployment, and monetary or supply-side policy may be better in some cases.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: higher government spending or lower taxes → higher AD → firms raise output and demand more labour; with a negative output gap there is little inflationary pressure (AD/AS diagram with AD shifting right on the flatter part of AS); spending can be targeted at regions or labour-intensive projects; comparison with monetary policy (interest rate cuts) and supply-side policies (training) is required by 'best'. Evaluation: works for cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment but not structural or frictional; time lags; leakages to imports; a large existing debt may limit borrowing or raise interest rates; confidence may stay low; monetary policy may be faster but weak if interest rates are already near zero; a combination may be best; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government could use fiscal policy to reduce demand-pull inflation, and consider whether doing so will harm economic growth.
parts.answer: Contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, lower spending) reduces AD and so the pressure on prices; it may slow growth in the short run, but stable prices can support long-run growth.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: demand-pull inflation is caused by AD rising faster than the economy's capacity; contractionary (deflationary) fiscal policy. Analysis: higher income tax or sales tax reduces disposable income and consumption; cuts in government spending reduce G directly; AD shifts left, reducing the price level rise (AD/AS diagram near full capacity). Evaluation: real output may fall and unemployment rise in the short run; cutting capital spending may reduce future LRAS; but if the economy is at full capacity the fall in output may be small, and lower inflation improves confidence, investment and competitiveness, helping long-run growth; judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government's budget deficit fell from $40 billion last year to $25 billion this year. Assuming the government finances its deficit only by borrowing, which statement must be correct?
A The national debt fell this year.
B The national debt still rose this year, but by less than last year.
C Government spending fell this year.
D Tax revenue rose this year.
parts.answer: B The national debt still rose this year, but by less than last year.
parts.working: The national debt is the stock of past borrowing; any deficit adds to it, so a $25 billion deficit raises the debt by $25 billion, which is less than last year's $40 billion rise. A confuses a smaller deficit (flow) with a falling debt (stock); C and D are possible, but the deficit could fall through either, so neither must be true.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A lower-middle-income country collects tax equal to only 9.5 % of its GDP of PKR 110 000 billion. Fewer than 4 % of adults file income-tax returns, and a large informal sector pays little tax. A lender has asked the government to raise the ratio to 12 % within three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra tax revenue the government would collect if the tax-to-GDP ratio rose from 9.5 % to 12 % with GDP unchanged.
parts.answer: PKR 2,750 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether widening the tax base is a better way to raise tax revenue than raising existing tax rates.
parts.answer: Widening the base is usually better for efficiency and fairness, but it is slower and harder to enforce; raising rates gives quicker revenue but may reduce incentives and encourage evasion. A judgement depends on administrative capacity and the size of the informal sector.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: widening the base (bringing traders, retailers, agricultural incomes and property into the net) raises revenue without higher rates, spreads the burden more fairly, and reduces distortions; raising rates on the few who already pay may reduce work and investment incentives, encourage evasion and avoidance, and can be regressive if it relies on sales tax; higher rates may raise revenue quickly. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: a broader base needs records, digital payments and political will, so it is slow; in the short run higher rates may be needed; overall judgement (e.g. a broader base is better for sustained revenue).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether a government should always aim to balance its budget.
parts.answer: Not always: deficits can be justified in recessions or for productive investment, and surpluses during booms; but persistent deficits raise debt and interest costs, so a balanced budget over the economic cycle is a more sensible aim than a balanced budget every year.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: meaning of a balanced budget, deficit and surplus; benefits of balance: no rise in national debt, lower interest payments, confidence of lenders, avoids possible crowding out and future tax rises; costs: in a recession, cutting spending or raising taxes to balance the budget reduces AD further and deepens unemployment (AD/AS); deficits can finance infrastructure and education that raise future LRAS and tax revenue; a surplus in a boom can reduce demand-pull inflation. Evaluation: depends on the stage of the cycle, the size of existing debt, whether borrowing is in foreign currency, and what the borrowing pays for (investment vs current spending); conclusion that 'always' is too strong, balance over the cycle is more realistic.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): To reduce its budget deficit, a government has raised its general sales tax rate from 17 % to 18 %. An opposition party argues that it should have cut government spending instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A good has a price of PKR 1000 before tax. Calculate the percentage increase in its price when the sales tax rate rises from 17 % to 18 %, assuming the tax is fully passed on to consumers. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: price with tax rises from PKR 1170 to PKR 1180. A1: 10 ÷ 1170 × 100 = 0.85 %. (Not 1 %: the base is the tax-inclusive price.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether raising the sales tax rate is a better way to reduce the budget deficit than cutting government spending.
parts.answer: A sales tax rise raises revenue quickly from a broad base but is regressive and adds to inflation; spending cuts avoid higher prices but can damage public services and growth. The better choice depends on what spending is cut and on the distribution of the burden.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: sales tax raises revenue from a wide base and is hard to avoid on formal-sector sales; it causes a one-off rise in the price level (cost-push) and falls more heavily on the poor (regressive); it reduces consumption and AD. Spending cuts reduce the deficit directly and do not raise prices, but cuts to health, education or infrastructure reduce future growth and welfare; both reduce AD in the short run. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on whether essentials are exempt, on how efficient current spending is, on the state of the economy, and on PED of taxed goods; a justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which policy is a supply-side policy?
A a reduction in the central bank's policy interest rate
B government subsidies for vocational training courses
C an increase in unemployment benefit payments
D a temporary cut in sales tax to boost spending
parts.answer: B government subsidies for vocational training courses
parts.working: Training raises the skills and productivity of the labour force, increasing the economy's productive capacity (LRAS). A and D mainly change aggregate demand (monetary and demand-side fiscal policy); C raises spending on benefits and may even weaken incentives to work.

practice.stem: A government in East Africa plans to double its spending on technical and vocational colleges over five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define supply-side policy.
parts.answer: Government policy aimed at increasing the productive capacity (potential output) of the economy by improving the quantity and/or quality of factors of production or the efficiency of markets.
parts.working: 1 mark: increases productive capacity/potential output/LRAS; 1 mark: via quantity or quality of resources, or efficiency of markets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how increased government spending on technical education could affect the long-run aggregate supply of an economy.
parts.answer: Workers gain skills, so labour productivity rises; firms can produce more with the same inputs and costs fall; the economy's productive capacity rises, shifting LRAS to the right (and the PPC outwards), though only after a time lag.
parts.working: 1 mark: improves quality of labour/human capital; 1 mark: higher labour productivity/lower unit costs; 1 mark: increases potential output, LRAS shifts right (diagram description); 1 mark: time lag of several years before effects appear / also adds to AD in the short run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between market-based and interventionist supply-side policies, and consider which type is likely to increase output more quickly.
parts.answer: Market-based policies rely on incentives and competition (tax cuts, deregulation, privatisation); interventionist policies use government spending and direct action (education, infrastructure, R&D grants). Speed depends on the specific policy; neither type is always faster.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: definition of supply-side policy; market-based examples and interventionist examples. Analysis: both aim to shift LRAS right; market-based policies change incentives to work, invest and compete; interventionist policies improve the quality and quantity of factors directly. Evaluation: deregulation or tax incentives can act within months, while education and large infrastructure projects take years; however, market-based policies depend on how firms and workers respond, which may be weak, and may increase inequality; interventionist spending also raises AD quickly; a judgement on which is faster in a given context.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is an interventionist supply-side policy rather than a market-based one?
A privatisation of a state-owned airline
B removing regulations that restrict entry into the telecommunications market
