C a reduction in the top rate of income tax
D government investment in a new national rail network
parts.answer: D government investment in a new national rail network
parts.working: Interventionist supply-side policy uses direct government action or spending to raise productive capacity, such as infrastructure. A, B and C are market-based: they reduce the role of the state and rely on incentives and competition.

practice.stem:
Table 3: Output per worker in Country V (US$ per year, constant 2020 prices; data invented for practice)
2020: 5600
2025: 6100
The government plans to privatise its state-owned steel and electricity companies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in output per worker between 2020 and 2025. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Consider whether privatising state-owned enterprises is likely to raise productivity further.
parts.answer: Privatisation may raise productivity through the profit motive, competition and access to private capital, but gains are uncertain if a public monopoly simply becomes a private monopoly or if regulation is weak.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for analysis: profit motive and shareholder pressure → cost cutting and better management; access to private finance → investment in new technology; competition (if markets are opened) → efficiency; removes political interference. Up to 1 mark for evaluation: a private monopoly may lack incentive to improve; job losses may cut output in the short run; depends on regulation and on whether the market is contestable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether reducing labour-market regulations, such as limits on hiring and firing, is the most effective supply-side policy to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: Labour-market deregulation can make firms more willing to hire and reduce frictional and some structural unemployment, but it may reduce job security and wages and does little where unemployment is caused by low skills or weak demand; training and education may be more effective for structural unemployment.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: flexible labour markets reduce the cost and risk of hiring, so firms take on more workers; quicker matching reduces frictional unemployment; lower non-wage costs increase competitiveness; compare with other supply-side policies: training and education (structural unemployment), better job-matching services, reducing benefit traps, geographic mobility (housing). Evaluation: deregulation may increase insecure work and inequality, reduce worker morale and productivity; does not help cyclical unemployment; effect depends on the type of unemployment, on how strict regulations were to begin with, and on the size of the informal sector (where rules are often not enforced anyway); justified conclusion on 'most effective'.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): Inflation in a South Asian economy has risen to 14 %, partly because of power shortages and congestion at its main port. The finance minister says supply-side reforms will 'bring prices down within a year'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why supply-side policies often take a long time to have an effect.
parts.answer: Building infrastructure, educating workers or changing behaviour in response to incentives takes years, so productive capacity rises only slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a slow process (training/education, construction, new firms entering); 1 mark: so the shift in LRAS happens after a long time lag.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policies can reduce inflation in the short run.
parts.answer: Mostly not: their main effect on capacity comes in the long run, and extra government spending on infrastructure may even add to AD in the short run. Some measures, such as cutting import duties on inputs or removing supply bottlenecks, can reduce costs fairly quickly, so the effect depends on the policy and the cause of inflation.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: supply-side policy shifts LRAS/AS right, lowering the price level for a given AD (AD/AS diagram); this needs time (training, infrastructure); in the short run interventionist spending raises AD and may increase demand-pull inflation; tax cuts raise disposable income and AD; but some measures act quickly on costs, e.g. removing tariffs on imported inputs, clearing port bottlenecks, deregulating energy supply, which reduce cost-push pressure. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on cause of inflation (cost-push vs demand-pull), type of policy, credibility; usually monetary/fiscal policy is needed in the short run; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether supply-side policy is more effective than fiscal policy in achieving economic growth in a low-income country.
parts.answer: Supply-side policy is essential for sustained growth because it raises potential output, but in a low-income country it is slow and needs funds; fiscal policy can raise actual growth quickly where there is spare capacity, and much supply-side policy is itself funded through the budget. A combination is likely to be most effective.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: distinguish actual and potential growth; fiscal policy (higher G, lower taxes) raises AD and actual output where there is a negative output gap; supply-side policies (education, health, infrastructure, property rights, deregulation) shift LRAS right, raising potential growth without inflation; diagrams. Evaluation: in low-income countries, capacity constraints (power, skills, transport) limit the effect of extra demand, which may become inflation or imports; but supply-side policy is slow, costly and may depend on aid or borrowing; weak institutions and corruption may reduce the effect of both; overlap — infrastructure spending is both; judgement on 'more effective' with conditions.

practice.stem: A central bank in South America is concerned that inflation is well above its 3 % target.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two instruments of monetary policy.
parts.answer: Any two of: the central bank's policy interest rate; the money supply (e.g. open market operations, reserve requirements); quantitative easing; the exchange rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct instruments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how an increase in interest rates could reduce the rate of inflation.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reduce disposable income of borrowers and may raise the exchange rate; consumption, investment and net exports fall, AD grows more slowly and demand-pull pressure on prices eases.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher cost of borrowing → less credit-financed consumption/investment; 1 mark: higher reward for saving / higher loan repayments reduce disposable income; 1 mark: possible appreciation → cheaper imports, fewer exports; 1 mark: AD falls/grows more slowly → less demand-pull inflation.

practice.stem:
Table 5: Car loans in Country M (data invented for practice)
Quarter 1: bank lending rate 12 %; car loans approved 48 000
Quarter 4: bank lending rate 16 %; car loans approved 39 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the number of car loans approved between Quarter 1 and Quarter 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why higher interest rates reduce the number of car loans.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates raise monthly repayments, so a car bought on credit becomes more expensive and fewer households can afford or are willing to borrow.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher cost of borrowing/higher repayments; 1 mark: reduces affordability or willingness to buy on credit (or banks lend less to riskier borrowers).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank raises its policy interest rate. Which effect is most likely?
A The country's currency depreciates.
B Household borrowing to buy cars and other durable goods falls.
C The interest cost of the government's debt falls.
D Households save a smaller proportion of their income.
parts.answer: B Household borrowing to buy cars and other durable goods falls.
parts.working: Higher interest rates raise the cost of loans, so credit-financed spending on durables falls, reducing consumption and AD. A is wrong: higher rates usually attract financial inflows and cause appreciation; D is wrong because saving becomes more rewarding.

practice.stem:
Table 4: Country K (data invented for practice)
January 2024: central bank policy rate 15 %; inflation rate 12 %
December 2024: central bank policy rate 22 %; inflation rate 29 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the approximation real interest rate = nominal interest rate − inflation rate, calculate the real interest rate in January 2024 and in December 2024.
parts.answer: January 2024: +3 %; December 2024: −7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the increase in the policy rate may not have reduced inflation quickly.
parts.answer: Because inflation rose faster than the policy rate, the real interest rate actually fell (became negative), so borrowing became cheaper in real terms; in addition, monetary policy works with long time lags, and inflation caused by rising import and energy prices (cost-push) is not reduced much by higher interest rates.
parts.working: 1 mark: real rate fell from +3 % to −7 %, so policy was looser in real terms; 1 mark: time lags (12–24 months) before AD responds; 1 mark: if inflation is cost-push (energy, imports, currency depreciation) higher rates do little to the cause; 1 mark: other relevant reason, e.g. much spending is not financed by bank credit / large informal sector, or government borrowing continued to rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a reduction in interest rates might increase aggregate demand, and consider why it might fail to do so during a severe recession.
parts.answer: Lower rates reduce the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, raising consumption and investment, and may depreciate the currency, raising net exports; in a severe recession low confidence, high debt and banks' unwillingness to lend may weaken these effects.
parts.working: Mark bands (8): knowledge and understanding up to 3, analysis up to 3, evaluation up to 2. Knowledge: monetary policy; the components of AD; meaning of a cut in the policy rate. Analysis: cheaper credit → more spending on durables and housing; lower loan repayments raise disposable income; investment projects become profitable; lower rates may cause capital outflows → depreciation → exports rise, imports fall; AD shifts right (diagram). Evaluation: if consumers and firms are pessimistic they may not borrow; banks may ration credit; rates may already be close to zero; time lags; depends on how much spending is financed by credit; judgement.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A family in Lahore has a variable-rate loan of PKR 2 000 000 on which it pays interest only. The bank's lending rate rises from 18 % to 21 % after the central bank raises its policy rate to fight inflation caused mainly by higher prices of imported fuel and edible oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the family's annual interest payment and express it as a percentage of the original payment. Give the percentage to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Increase of PKR 60,000 a year, a 16.7 % rise

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assess whether raising interest rates is an effective way to control inflation caused by rising import prices.
parts.answer: Only partly: higher rates may strengthen the currency and reduce second-round wage and price rises, but they do not lower world prices, and they reduce output and employment, squeezing households already hit by higher prices.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: inflation from import prices is cost-push (AS shifts left); higher interest rates reduce AD (consumption via higher repayments as in the data, investment), which limits second-round effects and inflation expectations; higher rates may attract capital inflows and appreciate the currency, reducing import prices; but they reduce output further, adding to the fall in real GDP (stagflation). Up to 2 marks for evaluation: depends on whether the import price rise is temporary, on how sensitive the exchange rate is to interest rates, on the share of households with variable-rate loans, and on the credibility of the central bank; justified judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy in reducing inflation.
parts.answer: Monetary policy is often more flexible and independent of politics, and works through several channels, but it has time lags and is weak against cost-push inflation; fiscal policy acts directly on AD but is slower to change and politically difficult. Effectiveness depends on the cause of inflation and the economy's circumstances.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: monetary policy: higher interest rates/reduced money supply → lower C, I and possibly net exports via appreciation → AD falls; independent central banks can act quickly and build credibility on inflation expectations. Fiscal policy: higher taxes, lower spending reduce AD directly and can be targeted; AD/AS diagram for demand-pull inflation. Evaluation: monetary policy affects all regions and sectors equally, may harm investment and raise government debt interest; works poorly where few people borrow from banks; fiscal tightening is politically unpopular, slow (budget timetable) and may cut useful public investment; neither works well against cost-push inflation; coordination matters; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT one of a government's main macroeconomic policy objectives?
A low and stable inflation
B a low level of unemployment
C a fixed price for petrol
D sustainable economic growth
parts.answer: C a fixed price for petrol
parts.working: The main macroeconomic objectives are economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices (low inflation) and balance of payments stability (plus, often, income redistribution). A fixed petrol price is a microeconomic intervention in one market, not a macroeconomic objective.

practice.stem:
Table 6: Targets and outcomes for Country H, 2025 (data invented for practice)
Real GDP growth: target at least 5 %; actual 6.1 %
Inflation: target 5–7 %; actual 11.4 %
Unemployment: target no more than 6 %; actual 5.2 %
Current account balance: target deficit no larger than 2 % of GDP; actual deficit 4.3 % of GDP

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which of the government's targets were met in 2025.
parts.answer: Economic growth (6.1 % ≥ 5 %) and unemployment (5.2 % ≤ 6 %) met; inflation and current account targets missed.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth target met; 1 mark: unemployment target met (and recognition that the other two were missed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain one conflict between the government's macroeconomic objectives.
parts.answer: Fast growth and low unemployment came with high inflation and a large current account deficit: rising AD pushed the economy close to full capacity, so prices rose (demand-pull), and higher incomes increased spending on imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a conflict from the data (growth/unemployment vs inflation, or growth vs current account); 1 mark: rising AD → output and employment rise; 1 mark: near capacity → demand-pull inflation (11.4 % vs 5–7 % target) or higher incomes → more imports; 1 mark: links to the data (current account −4.3 % vs −2 % limit) / higher inflation makes exports less competitive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess whether keeping inflation low should be a government's most important macroeconomic objective.
parts.answer: Low inflation supports confidence, investment and competitiveness and protects the poor, so it is a strong candidate; but in a recession or with high unemployment, growth and employment may matter more, and the priority depends on the country's current problems.
parts.working: Mark bands (12): analysis up to 8 (knowledge applied, clear chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 4 (weighed judgement that answers the question). Analysis: the four main objectives; benefits of low and stable inflation: protects real incomes and savings (especially of those on fixed incomes), reduces uncertainty, encourages investment, keeps exports competitive, avoids menu and shoe-leather costs; conflicts between objectives (e.g. low inflation vs low unemployment in the short run); costs of unemployment and low growth. Evaluation: the priority depends on circumstances: with inflation at 25 %, controlling it comes first; with deflation risk or high unemployment, growth and jobs matter more; low inflation can be seen as a means to sustainable growth rather than a rival; central bank inflation targets show many governments give it priority; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In Keynes's liquidity preference theory, which motive for holding money is most sensitive to changes in the rate of interest?
A the speculative motive
B the transactions motive
C the precautionary motive
D the store of value motive
parts.answer: A the speculative motive
parts.working: Speculative balances are held instead of bonds; when interest rates are high, bonds are attractive and the opportunity cost of holding money is high, so speculative demand falls. Transactions demand (B) depends mainly on income.

practice.stem: A central bank in South Asia has raised its policy rate three times this year and has also lent emergency funds to a small commercial bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between narrow money and broad money.
parts.answer: Narrow money is money that can be spent immediately: notes and coins (plus banks' reserves at the central bank or sight deposits, depending on the measure); broad money also includes less liquid bank and savings deposits that can be turned into spending power.
parts.working: 1 mark: narrow = notes, coins/highly liquid; 1 mark: broad = narrow money plus time/savings deposits (less liquid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two functions of a central bank.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g.: carries out monetary policy (sets the policy interest rate, controls the money supply) to meet an inflation target; acts as lender of last resort to commercial banks in a crisis; is banker to the government (manages its accounts and borrowing); supervises and regulates banks; issues notes and coins; manages foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate.
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining what it involves or why it matters.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): In an East African country, the number of people using mobile-phone wallets has risen from 9 million to 31 million in six years. Market traders, taxi drivers and utility companies now accept wallet payments, and the share of payments made in cash has fallen from 70 % to 40 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two characteristics of money that a digital wallet balance must have if it is to function as money.
parts.answer: For example: general acceptability — shops and people must be willing to accept it in payment; divisibility — it can be used for small and large amounts; durability/security — balances cannot be destroyed or easily forged; portability — payments can be made anywhere; limited supply/stable value so it holds purchasing power.
parts.working: For each of two characteristics: 1 mark for naming it, 1 mark for applying it to digital wallet balances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a shift from cash to digital payments could affect commercial banks' ability to create credit.
parts.answer: Less cash is withdrawn and held outside the banking system, so the cash leakage falls; more deposits stay with banks and are available as reserves, so the credit multiplier and banks' ability to lend increase (subject to demand for loans and regulation).
parts.working: 1 mark: less cash held by the public/smaller cash leakage; 1 mark: more deposits/reserves stay in banks; 1 mark: larger credit (bank) multiplier → more lending possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Commercial banks keep 8 % of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. A customer deposits $40 million of new cash. Assuming no cash leaks out of the banking system, what is the maximum total increase in bank deposits?
A $500 million
B $460 million
C $320 million
D $43.2 million
parts.answer: A $500 million
parts.working: Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5, so maximum deposits = 12.5 × $40 million = $500 million. B ($460 million) is the maximum increase in new loans, which excludes the original deposit.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): A customer deposits PKR 10 million of cash in Bank A. All banks keep 10 % of every deposit as reserves and lend out the rest, and all loans are redeposited in the banking system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new loans made in each of the first three rounds of lending, starting with Bank A.
parts.answer: Round 1: PKR 9.0 million; round 2: PKR 8.1 million; round 3: PKR 7.29 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum total increase in bank deposits that could result from the original deposit.
parts.answer: PKR 100 million
parts.working: Credit multiplier 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; 10 × 10 = PKR 100 million (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual increase in deposits is likely to be smaller than this.
parts.answer: For example: borrowers hold part of the loans as cash (cash leakage), so it does not return to banks; banks may keep reserves above the minimum during uncertain times; there may be too few creditworthy borrowers or weak demand for loans; capital requirements may limit lending.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it reduces redeposits or lending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which commercial banks' ability to create credit is limited.
parts.answer: Banks can create deposits by lending a multiple of their reserves, but their ability is limited by reserve and capital requirements, cash leakages, the demand for loans, the supply of creditworthy borrowers, central bank policy and confidence. The extent of the limit varies over the economic cycle.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: functions of commercial banks; process of credit creation and the credit multiplier (1 ÷ reserve ratio) with a numerical example; liquidity vs profitability conflict; limits: required reserve/liquidity ratios, capital adequacy rules, cash leakage, banks' own prudence, demand for loans, interest rates set by the central bank, competition from non-bank lenders. Evaluation: in booms limits are weak and credit may expand rapidly (asset bubbles); in recessions demand for loans and bank confidence are the main limits even with ample reserves; financial innovation and digital payments reduce cash leakage; the multiplier model oversimplifies modern banking; justified judgement on 'extent'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PT), the money supply rises by 8 %, the velocity of circulation is unchanged and the number of transactions rises by 3 %. By approximately how much does the price level change?
A a rise of 4.9 %
B a rise of 8.0 %
C a rise of 11.2 %
D a fall of 2.7 %
parts.answer: A a rise of 4.9 %
parts.working: P = MV ÷ T, so P changes by 1.08 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 4.9 % (roughly 8 % − 3 %). B assumes T is fixed, as in the strict monetarist version, but here T rises.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): In an economy the demand for money is given by Md = 600 − 40r, where Md is in $ billion and r is the rate of interest in per cent. The money supply is fixed by the central bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium rate of interest when the money supply is $360 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The central bank increases the money supply to $400 billion. Calculate the new equilibrium rate of interest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a liquidity trap and why, in a liquidity trap, a further increase in the money supply would not reduce the rate of interest.
parts.answer: At a very low interest rate people expect bond prices to fall (interest rates to rise), so they are willing to hold any extra money rather than buy bonds; the demand for money becomes perfectly elastic, so extra money supply is simply held and the interest rate does not fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: very low interest rate where demand for money becomes perfectly elastic (horizontal); 1 mark: expectation that bond prices will fall/interest rates rise, so speculative demand absorbs extra money; 1 mark: shifting the money supply curve right leaves the interest rate unchanged, so monetary policy cannot stimulate investment this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that controlling the money supply is the most effective way to control inflation.
parts.answer: Monetarists argue, using the quantity theory, that inflation is caused by excess money growth and is best controlled by limiting it; Keynesians argue that velocity and output are not stable, that money supply is hard to control, and that inflation has other causes (cost-push, demand from fiscal policy). Money supply control can be effective in some cases (hyperinflation, monetary financing of deficits) but is rarely the most effective tool on its own.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: MV = PT; monetarist assumptions (V and T fixed or stable) → P rises proportionately with M; transmission through interest rates and spending; Keynesian view — V varies, T can rise when there is spare capacity, money demand sensitive to interest rates; difficulty of controlling money supply when banks create credit; central banks now usually target interest rates; alternatives: interest rate policy, fiscal policy, supply-side policy, exchange rate policy. Evaluation: depends on the cause of inflation (excess money creation vs cost-push from oil or depreciation), on whether the economy is near full capacity, on central bank credibility; evidence that money and inflation are closely linked in the long run and in hyperinflations, weaker in the short run; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would show potential economic growth rather than only actual economic growth?
A an outward shift of the economy's long-run aggregate supply curve
B a movement from a point inside the production possibility curve to a point on it
C an increase in aggregate demand when there is a large negative output gap
D a fall in unemployment caused by higher consumer spending
parts.answer: A an outward shift of the economy's long-run aggregate supply curve
parts.working: Potential growth is an increase in productive capacity, shown by an outward shift of LRAS (or of the PPC). B, C and D show actual growth from using existing spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between actual and potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Actual growth is an increase in real output (real GDP) produced; potential growth is an increase in the economy's productive capacity — the maximum output it could produce.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of potential economic growth.
parts.answer: For example: investment in capital goods increases the capital stock; improvements in technology raise productivity; education and training improve the quality of labour; a larger labour force (population growth, migration, higher participation); discovery of natural resources.
parts.working: For each of two causes: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it increases productive capacity (LRAS shifts right).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible costs of rapid economic growth.
parts.answer: Any two of: environmental damage and pollution; depletion of non-renewable resources; demand-pull inflation; current account deficit as imports rise; greater income inequality; congestion and stress; opportunity cost of investment (less consumption now).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how economic growth could increase income inequality.
parts.answer: Growth may be concentrated in sectors such as finance, technology or mining that employ skilled workers and owners of capital, whose incomes rise fastest; unskilled or rural workers gain little, and returns to capital may rise faster than wages, so the gap widens.
parts.working: 1 mark: gains concentrated in certain sectors/regions; 1 mark: skilled workers and owners of capital gain most; 1 mark: unskilled/rural/informal workers gain little, so the Gini coefficient rises.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): Country G's nominal GDP was 50 000 billion in 2024 and 56 100 billion in 2025 (in local currency). The GDP deflator was 100 in 2024 and 108 in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in 2025 at 2024 prices and the rate of real economic growth between 2024 and 2025. Give real GDP to one decimal place and the growth rate to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Real GDP 2025 = 51,944.4 billion; real growth = 3.89 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why real GDP is a better measure of economic growth than nominal GDP.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP rises when prices rise even if output does not; real GDP removes the effect of inflation, so it shows the change in the volume of goods and services produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: nominal GDP includes inflation (here nominal rose 12.2 %); 1 mark: real GDP measures change in output/volume.

practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): In 2025 a South Asian country's real GDP grew by 4.2 % and its population grew by 2.4 %. Much of the growth came from farming that depends on pumping groundwater, and from clearing forest for new farmland.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the growth rate of real GDP per head in 2025. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.working: M1: 1.042 ÷ 1.024 = 1.01758; A1: growth of real GDP per head = 1.76 % (approximately 4.2 % − 2.4 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the country's present rate of economic growth may not be sustainable.
parts.answer: For example: growth based on rapid use of non-renewable resources such as groundwater and forests reduces future capacity; pollution and environmental damage lower future productivity and health; growth driven by borrowing or a consumer boom may cause inflation and current account deficits; rapid population growth puts pressure on land and water.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining why it threatens future growth (meeting present needs without compromising future generations).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that investment in human capital is the most important cause of long-run economic growth.
parts.answer: Human capital raises productivity, adaptability and innovation and is central to growth, but its effect depends on physical capital, technology, institutions and demand for skilled labour; it is one of several key causes, and the most important cause varies by country.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: meaning of human capital (education, training, health); effects on labour productivity, innovation and ability to use technology; LRAS shifts right/PPC outwards; compare with physical capital investment, technological progress, natural resources, labour force growth, institutions and property rights. Evaluation: returns to education depend on quality, not years of schooling; skilled workers may emigrate (brain drain); without capital and infrastructure skills are underused; time lags are long; endogenous growth view gives human capital a central role; justified conclusion with reference to country type.

practice.stem: Extract (invented for practice): A Southeast Asian country's real GDP is US$300 billion. The government targets real growth of 5 % a year while cutting carbon emissions from electricity by 30 % by 2035. Coal still provides 60 % of its electricity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the country's real GDP after four years if it grows at 5 % a year. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: US$364.65 billion
parts.working: M1: 300 × 1.05⁴; A1: 364.65 (not 300 × 1.20 = 360, which ignores compounding).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a carbon tax on electricity generators could affect the country's long-run aggregate supply.
parts.answer: In the short run it raises generators' costs, shifting AS left; in the long run it encourages investment in renewable energy and energy efficiency and reduces the pollution damage to health and farmland, which may protect or increase LRAS.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher costs of production in the short run (AS shifts left); 1 mark: incentive to invest in cleaner technology/renewables; 1 mark: reduced pollution protects health, productivity and natural capital, so long-run capacity is maintained or rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Consider whether the government can achieve both rapid economic growth and environmental sustainability.
parts.answer: Possibly, if growth comes from cleaner technology, renewables and efficient resource use (green growth); but in the short run there is often a trade-off because coal is cheap and clean energy needs heavy investment.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for analysis: trade-off — fossil-fuel growth increases emissions; green investment raises costs now; but innovation and renewables can decouple growth from emissions and create jobs. Up to 1 mark for a judgement depending on finance, technology and time scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether policies to achieve sustainable economic growth must reduce the rate of economic growth.
parts.answer: In the short run, sustainability policies such as carbon taxes, regulations and resource conservation can raise costs and slow growth; but in the long run they protect natural capital and health and can create new industries, so sustainable growth need not be slower and may be faster over a long period.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: meaning of sustainable growth; policies: environmental taxes, tradable permits, regulation, subsidies for renewables, investment in human capital and technology; short-run effects — higher costs, AS shifts left, lower output in polluting sectors; long-run — less depletion, fewer climate and health costs, innovation and green industries shift LRAS right; measurement issues (GDP ignores environmental depletion). Evaluation: depends on the time period, on the policy design (market-based vs command), on whether clean technology is affordable, on international coordination, and on a country's stage of development; low-income countries may face sharper trade-offs; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an open economy with a government, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal rate of tax is 0.15 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.25 (all measured as fractions of national income). Government spending rises by $30 billion. What is the final increase in national income?
A $60 billion
B $120 billion
C $300 billion
D $40 billion
parts.answer: A $60 billion
parts.working: Multiplier = 1 ÷ (MPS + MRT + MPM) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2; increase in income = 2 × $30 billion = $60 billion. C uses only the MPS (multiplier 10), ignoring taxes and imports.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between injections and withdrawals in the circular flow of income of an open economy with a government sector.
parts.answer: Injections are additions of spending to the circular flow that do not come from domestic households' income: investment, government spending and exports. Withdrawals (leakages) are parts of income not passed on as spending on domestic output: saving, taxation and imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: injections named (I, G, X); 1 mark: withdrawals named (S, T, M); 1 mark: explanation — injections add to spending on domestic output, withdrawals remove income from the flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what happens to national income when injections are greater than withdrawals.
parts.answer: Spending on domestic output exceeds the income leaking out, so firms see stocks fall and raise output; incomes rise, and as income rises withdrawals rise too, until withdrawals equal injections at a new, higher equilibrium income.
parts.working: 1 mark: total spending/demand exceeds output, stocks fall; 1 mark: output and income rise (multiplier process); 1 mark: withdrawals rise with income until W = J at a new equilibrium.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice), in $ billion for one period: national income 1200; saving 120; taxation 180; imports 60; investment 90; government spending 150; exports 90.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate total injections and total withdrawals in the period.
parts.answer: Injections = 330 billion; withdrawals = 360 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain what is likely to happen to national income in the next period.
parts.answer: National income will fall, because withdrawals (360) exceed injections (330), so spending on domestic output is less than income/output; firms cut production until withdrawals fall to equal injections.
parts.working: 1 mark: income falls; 1 mark: because W > J, so aggregate demand is less than output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the role of the financial sector in linking saving and investment in the circular flow.
parts.answer: Households' savings are deposited with banks and other financial institutions, which lend them to firms for investment; if the financial sector channels saving into investment efficiently, the saving withdrawal is offset by an investment injection; the interest rate helps balance them.
parts.working: 1 mark: savings held by banks/financial institutions; 1 mark: lent to firms (and government) for investment; 1 mark: links withdrawal (S) to injection (I); if saving is not lent on, income falls.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem: Data (invented for practice): When national income in a country rose by $400 billion, households' spending on domestically produced goods rose by $240 billion. The government now plans to spend an extra $12 billion on rural roads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the marginal propensity to consume domestically produced goods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the multiplier and the eventual increase in national income caused by the extra government spending.
parts.answer: Multiplier 2.5; national income rises by $30 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the actual increase in national income may be smaller than this.
parts.answer: For example: the government may borrow to finance the spending, raising interest rates and crowding out private investment; if the economy is near full capacity, prices rise rather than output; time lags mean the full effect takes years; withdrawals (e.g. saving) may rise if confidence is low; extra spending may go to imports.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for identification, 1 mark for explaining how it reduces the final rise in real income.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether an economy with a high marginal propensity to import should rely on increasing exports, rather than increasing government spending, to raise its national income.
parts.answer: A high marginal propensity to import reduces the multiplier for any injection, so it does not by itself favour exports over government spending; but exports bring foreign currency and improve the current account, while government spending leaks heavily into imports. Exports depend on world demand and competitiveness, which the government cannot easily control, so a mix is likely to be best.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: open-economy circular flow; both exports and government spending are injections with the same multiplier; high MPM → small multiplier → limited effect of either; extra government spending with a high MPM worsens the current account; export-led growth earns foreign exchange, may attract investment and economies of scale; methods to raise exports (depreciation, supply-side policy, trade agreements). Evaluation: exports depend on trading partners' growth, exchange rates and protectionism; government spending can be targeted at domestic labour-intensive projects with low import content; spending on infrastructure may raise export capacity too; debt constraints; justified conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an economy, investment is $120 billion, government spending is $200 billion and exports are $180 billion; these do not depend on income. Saving, taxes and imports are 15 %, 20 % and 15 % of national income respectively. Exports then rise by $50 billion. What is the new equilibrium level of national income?
A $1100 billion
B $1050 billion
C $1000 billion
D $1333 billion
parts.answer: A $1100 billion
parts.working: Equilibrium where injections = withdrawals: 500 = 0.5Y, so Y = 1000. After exports rise, 550 = 0.5Y, so Y = 1100. B adds only the $50 billion rise in exports and ignores the multiplier of 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps
practice.stem:
Table 11: Real GDP of Country D ($ billion; data invented for practice)
Year 1: actual 820; potential 850
Year 2: actual 860; potential 870
Year 3: actual 905; potential 890
Year 4: actual 930; potential 910

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output gap as a percentage of potential output for each year. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.working: Output gap = (actual − potential) ÷ potential × 100. Year 1: (820 − 850) ÷ 850 × 100 = −3.53 %; Year 2: (860 − 870) ÷ 870 × 100 = −1.15 %; Year 3: (905 − 890) ÷ 890 × 100 = 1.69 %; Year 4: (930 − 910) ÷ 910 × 100 = 2.20 %. 3 marks all four correct; 2 marks for three; 1 mark for correct method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the first year in which there was an inflationary (positive) output gap and explain why inflation might rise in that year.
parts.answer: Year 3: actual output exceeded potential output, so firms were working beyond normal capacity; labour and resource shortages push up wages and costs and demand exceeds supply, so prices rise (demand-pull).
parts.working: 1 mark: Year 3; 1 mark: explanation — output above capacity → shortages, overtime, rising wages/costs → inflation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult for a government to measure the output gap accurately.
parts.answer: Potential output cannot be observed directly; it must be estimated from trends in productivity, the labour force and capital, which change with technology and shocks; GDP data are revised and the informal economy is not fully measured, so the estimated gap may even have the wrong sign.
parts.working: 1 mark: potential output is not observable/estimated; 1 mark: depends on assumptions about productivity, labour force, natural rate of unemployment; 1 mark: data revisions/informal sector/time lags in data.

practice.subtopic: Circular flow, multiplier and output gaps

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that, because of the multiplier, an increase in government spending will always be an effective way to end a recession.
parts.answer: The multiplier means extra government spending raises national income by more than the initial injection, which can help end a recession with spare capacity; but the size of the multiplier may be small in an open economy with high taxes and imports, and crowding out, time lags, debt and confidence can weaken the effect. 'Always' is too strong.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: circular flow, injections and withdrawals; multiplier = 1 ÷ (MPS + MRT + MPM), numerical illustration; AD shifts right, closing a negative output gap; accelerator effects may add investment. Evaluation: a small multiplier in very open economies (high MPM) or with high tax rates; crowding out of private investment if borrowing raises interest rates; Ricardian equivalence (households save for expected future taxes); time lags in planning projects; quality of spending (productive vs wasteful); debt sustainability and lender confidence; effectiveness greater in a deep recession with low interest rates; justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a country, the working-age population is 140 million, the labour force is 84 million and 78.12 million people are employed. What are the unemployment rate and the labour force participation rate?
A unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 60.0 %
B unemployment rate 4.2 %, participation rate 60.0 %
C unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 55.8 %
D unemployment rate 4.2 %, participation rate 55.8 %
parts.answer: A unemployment rate 7.0 %, participation rate 60.0 %
parts.working: Unemployed = 84 − 78.12 = 5.88 million; unemployment rate = 5.88 ÷ 84 × 100 = 7.0 % (of the labour force, not the working-age population, which gives 4.2 % in B). Participation rate = 84 ÷ 140 × 100 = 60.0 %.

practice.stem: A textile region in a South Asian country has lost many jobs as factories move to automated production, while technology firms in the capital report shortages of programmers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between frictional unemployment and structural unemployment.
parts.answer: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment while people move between jobs or search for their first job; structural unemployment is longer-term unemployment caused by a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the available jobs, after changes in the structure of the economy (e.g. decline of an industry).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the natural rate of unemployment and one factor that could reduce it.
parts.answer: The natural rate is the level of unemployment that exists when the labour market is in equilibrium, with no demand-deficient unemployment — made up of frictional and structural unemployment; it can be reduced by, for example, better job-matching information, training and retraining schemes, or improved geographical mobility.
parts.working: 1 mark: unemployment at labour market equilibrium/when AD is at full employment level/no cyclical unemployment; 1 mark: consists of frictional + structural (voluntary) unemployment; 1 mark: one valid supply-side factor that reduces it, with brief reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether reducing structural unemployment should be a higher priority for a government than reducing demand-deficient (cyclical) unemployment.
parts.answer: Structural unemployment is long-lasting and lowers potential output, so reducing it raises the natural rate of employment permanently; cyclical unemployment is temporary but can be large in a recession and can turn into structural unemployment through hysteresis. The priority depends on which type dominates at the time.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: causes of each type (mismatch of skills/location from structural change, automation, globalisation vs deficient AD in a downturn); costs: lost output, lower tax revenue, higher benefit spending, social costs, deskilling; policies: supply-side (training, mobility, information) for structural vs fiscal and monetary expansion for cyclical; diagrams (labour market or AD/AS). Evaluation: in a deep recession cyclical unemployment is the main problem and quick to fix with demand policies; structural policies are slow and costly; but persistent structural unemployment harms growth and inequality; hysteresis links the two; context of countries with large informal sectors; justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
Table 12: Inflation and unemployment in Country E (data invented for practice)
Year 1: inflation 4.1 %; unemployment 8.2 %
Year 2: inflation 5.3 %; unemployment 6.9 %
Year 3: inflation 6.8 %; unemployment 5.6 %
Year 4: inflation 9.5 %; unemployment 5.4 %
Year 5: inflation 12.0 %; unemployment 5.5 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between inflation and unemployment shown in the data.
parts.answer: From Year 1 to Year 3 higher inflation is associated with lower unemployment (an inverse relationship, as in the short-run Phillips curve); from Year 3 to Year 5 inflation keeps rising sharply while unemployment stays at about 5.5 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse relationship in Years 1–3 (inflation 4.1 → 6.8 %, unemployment 8.2 → 5.6 %); 1 mark: in Years 3–5 unemployment stops falling/stays around 5.4–5.6 % while inflation rises to 12.0 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, explain the pattern in Years 3 to 5.
parts.answer: Unemployment has reached the natural rate (about 5.5 %). Workers now expect higher inflation and demand higher money wages, so the short-run Phillips curve shifts up; further rises in AD only increase inflation, and unemployment returns to the natural rate — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
parts.working: 1 mark: natural rate of unemployment around 5.5 %; 1 mark: inflation expectations adjust upwards/workers bargain for higher money wages; 1 mark: short-run Phillips curve shifts upwards; 1 mark: long-run Phillips curve vertical at the natural rate — no lasting trade-off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that there is a trade-off between unemployment and inflation in the long run.
parts.answer: The original Phillips curve suggested a stable trade-off, but the expectations-augmented view argues that in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate, so there is no long-run trade-off; however, hysteresis, very low inflation and wage rigidity mean the long-run curve may not be perfectly vertical.
parts.working: Mark bands (20): knowledge, understanding and analysis up to 14 (accurate theory, developed chains of reasoning, diagram where useful), evaluation up to 6 (justified judgement on the actual question, with conditions). Analysis: original Phillips curve (inverse relationship, demand-pull explanation); expectations-augmented Phillips curve: short-run trade-off, adaptive expectations, shifting short-run curves, vertical long-run Phillips curve at the natural rate (NAIRU); rational expectations view (no trade-off even in the short run if policy is anticipated); stagflation evidence in the 1970s. Evaluation: hysteresis — long recessions raise the natural rate; at very low inflation, downward wage rigidity may create a trade-off; flattening of the Phillips curve in recent decades; supply shocks shift curves; implications for policy (supply-side policy to lower the natural rate); justified conclusion.
